TWO ROSES. 0 brilliant, blooming, bright-red rose, Whose scented odour heavenward goes, I love thy beauty, colour, size. Thou sweetest flower beneath the skies I But putter far than I love thee I love the love who gßv'et thee me. Though she with thee might well commune, As thou with her couldst truly vie, Thou hast a richness in thy bloom, And she has beauty in her eye: Her look inspires eternal bliss • Thine breathes forth Nature's loveliness. Thou art a rose, and to is she; Each blossoms in the bright to-day. Pure as thou art may her life be, Until it shed its parting ray I E'en as at Light thy portal close. • Eo shall her eyelids find repose. MOMABI HARDY.

THE " NEILSON SYSTEM" OF HAeVESTING CROPS.—The continued wet weather keeps to the fore the question of "How to make Hay." The system advocated by Mr. Neil- son, of Halewood. which we fully described in a series of articles a few weeks ago, is being tried in various parts; and for the purposes of these trials the implement makers have brought oat numerous descriptions of fans. Amongst them Messrs. Thwaites Bros., of Bradford,have issued a pamphlet givirg an account of Mr. Neilson's system, and containing a full list, with many illustrations,, of their various makes of Root's patent exhausters. These will beionnd to almost any size, for either hand, horse, or steam power; and at prices which, in moet case, look remarkably seasonable. THE HARVEST /N THE MIDLANDS.—Tbo harvest in the central Midlands commenced in South Leieesterelvire on Monday by the cutting of several &ICS of oats. During the last ten days the growing crops have made remarkeale progress, and with continued fine weather the crop will not only be a fairly good one, but will not be nearly to late as was at one time enticipated. Wheat in some cases is very aood indeed, but in the majority of instances the ears are Saa.ly filled, and have a starved aonearance. Barley is uni- formly good; and oats, although very late on cold clay lands, will be e very fair average crop. The potato disease is very bad, and in a great many instexcee one-third of the crop is only Et for pig food. The hay is now nearly all secured in good condition, aced has proved a must abundant elders—in feet, on the average, three times heavier than that of last year. CORK BUTTER MARKET.—The report of the Commie- elopers on Agriculture contains the following memorandum: —"To the evidence connected with an important branch of Irish industry, and directly affecting a large class of agri- culturists, we deem it advisable to call attention. The way in which trade may be hampered and it progress obstructed by the abuse of arrangements orininally designed for its promotion is strikirgly Moot-Med by the .hi-tery of the Cork Butter Market, which will he feeund in the evidence sub- roittal to your Majesty. I'Vhaterer the vane of the Cork batter market in former times to the farmers may have been, it has now ceased to be an institution that cal be favour- ably spoken of. Owing to the great facilities for the trans- port of produce there is a much larger dernand for fresh butter than formerly, anal a corresponding diminution in the value of very salt butter. The present arrangements of the Cork butter market evidently tend to reduce the value of the highest class of butter, and to unduly raise that of a lower clam, so as to produce an approximate uniformity in price, which is not good either for the farmer or for the consumer. The Cork butter market is in to real sense an open market.; on the contrary, the control of the Corporation of Cork over it is illusory, and the management is in.the hands of a close Corporation, who discourage individual enterprise, and, through the system of advances to farmers, keep them in a state of subjection injurious to their interests as acri- euTtnriets. Such is the general effect of the evidence which has been submitted to us, and which, owing to the compre- hensive terms of reference, has necessarily extended over a very wide range, embracing, in addition to the general state of agriculture at home, the condition of agriculture and of tenure in foreign countries, and also including a variety of subjects, such as the land laws, the syetem of local taxation, tithe rent-charge, railway rates, and other matters. None of them could be actually deecribed as causes of depression, but their importance is fully recognised by the Commission, and they have cerdidered and made recommendations with regard to them in a subsequent part of their report." _lea-tenons ANIMAL DISEASES..—A. word Cr two about an adrenal disease known as splecie fever will bring us to the welblenown zymotic (liseases which carry off so many human beings. As early as 1850 it was observed that the blood of animals which had died from splenic fever teemed with microscopic organisms resembling minute transparent rode ; and it has been placed beyond all doubt that this fever is flee to the growth and development of these minute organisms. Placed under favaurable coeditiona, the rods I grow till they often become a hundred times their original I length. After a time, little dote appear in them, which finally grow to minute egg shaped bodies, presenting an ap- pearance somewhat like a long row of seeds in a pod. liy- anelby. the pod—as we may call it—gees to pieces, and the seeds or spores are let loose. Many experiments have been made with both rods and spores duinea-pies, rabbit?, and mice were inoculated with the blood of diseased animals containing the rods, the result beirg that within twenty or thirty hours they invariably died of spienie fever. By dry- hog the blood which contained only the rods, it was found that it did not retain its infectious properties longer than about 3 month; bat blood containing the developed enema, dried and reduced to dust, even after being kept four years, proved as deadly as at first. In 1868, M. Chauveen made some interesting discoveriee concernirg the infectious matter in cow-pox, sheep-pox, at:nail-pox, hydrophobie. slanders, and syphilis. Taking some of the matter, be found ,! that it consisted of a fluid in which were numerous minute ! granular particles, some of them so minute as to pass through the finest filters. When diluted with water, the larger particles subsided, the finer granules, however, re- maining suspended in the water, and the liquid still retain- ing its infectious properties: but by diffusion in dietilled water, these minute particles were completely separated, and • the liquid then proved harrnlese. It was thus shown that the infection was communicated by thee minute organleed particles, and that even a tingle one of these pesseeeee etteh inconceivable fecundity that it will produce quite as power- ful effects as if a large quantity of concentrated matter bad hseal introf.inced into the system. Sufficient evidence has thus been obtained to prove that many tllee,lees are Propa- gated by minute organisms; and it is now a well-ascertained fact that scarlatina, diphtheria, measles, typhus and typhoid ;avers are spread in .the same fashion;

ARTIFICIALLY COLOURING GROWING FLONVERS.—SnI2I+3 curious and interesting experiments in the artificial colour- ing of flowers have been reported by Mr. Nesbitt. Solutions being made of various aniline dyes, he placed in each a white narcissus. Several of the dyes, including red, blue, and green, were absorbed, and produced beautiful effects. Six of the colours were not absorbed, though the flowers were left for some days in the solution, while the absorp- tion_ of pink took less than an hour.

Since. the recent successfal experiment of Mr. Shadbolt in balloon photography, the Municipal Council of Perils has offered a prize of £4O to the Academy of Aerostation for the best photograph of Paris from a captive balloon. In Mr. Shadbolt'e photograph Of 'the Stamford Hill district, ialsna from an elevation of two thousand feet, railways, vehicles, and even people were distinctly visible. This feat of photo- graphy, which bee never been accomplished before, is of real scientific value, and would be of special service in war. A New FIIZE•RESISTING AnEtsea—Considerable attention has for many years past been given to the means of render- ing wood and other substances uninflamnaahle, and with varied .912::Cess. The latest attempt in this direction is that of Herr B. Hoff, Professor of Chemistry at the Royal and Imperial Technical Academy at Jeroelay, Galicia, who for some years past has devoted himself to a study of the sub- ject, and has recently succeeded in effecting this object. What the means are by which the result is "attained, we are not informed, except that it is a simple and inexpensive chealical process, and that the materials consist of the cheapest factory evalte. Wood thus treated, when sob- mitted to a high temperature, neither produces flame nor attains a great heat. We have submitted samples of wo-el so treated to the action of a gas flame, with the result that the woad neither burst into a blaze nor became red hot; it simply gave off a light smoke and the surface became cos ed with a thin film or fine black pewder, the result of its car- bonteation. Should a practical trial on an extended scale lead to equally good results, it would follow—other things being equal—that we shall pos2ese-a very efficient means of protecting the timber portions of our dwellings and other structures against ignition, should a fire occur—lron. It also renders unctuous and other animal sub- stances soluble in water. It is uses in making liniments and embrocations. Soap has also a slight aperient action; it is also a mild anti-acid, and is said to possess advantages over the alkalies given alone. It is also given in rheumatic affec- tions, and in goat where swellings occur in the joints, and are called chalk stones. It is supposed to dissolve ttsese, There is no doubt at all but that it Li very useful in external applications for bruises and sprains. It has also been ad- ministered with -effect in cares of poisoning by corrosive substances, such as oil of vitriol, aquafortis, and corruive sablima.te. Soap is also used to test the hardness of water. When soap comes in contact with lime in water it is decom- posed, ttearate of lime, or lime-soap, being formed. In Greer to test the harclneeS of any simple of water, that is, to fled out how much lime is held in solution in it, a solu- tion of Castile soap in alcohol is employed. What is called a standard solution of soap is made; that is, a certain known weight of soap is dissolved in a certain weight or measure of alcohol. A given measure of the water to be tested is put into a bottle, and some of the solution of soap is dropped in ; the stopper is placed in the bottle, which is well shaken. If no permanent froth or lather is formed on the surface of the water more of the soap solution is aedeti, and the mixture .is again shaken, anff the operation is repeated tilt a perma- nent lather is obtained. It is then ascertained how much of the alcoholic selation has been used, and this tells the quantity of soap decomposed. and from this is calculated the q °anti)), of lime present which decomposed it.—Seience for All.

THE -EXAMINER, S.ATURDAY, Atc-IT receipt of places or pensions. He hhtSeit was Lord Privy- Seal of Scotland (£2,675), *.chich, I believe, was a life office, and which he obtained in 1811. He died in 1851. If he held the office till ll'ea death, he must have netted over £lOO,OOO therefram. Then there was a Lady Elizabeth, who I presume, was his sister, and who was granted in 1801 a pension of £3OO, and lived on till 1852. The second Vis- count's eldest son was a General in the Army, Governor of Edinburgh Castle, and Colonel of the 60th Foot. His second son was a Vice-Admiral, and was for some years a Lord of the Admiralty, with a salary of £lO,OOO. His third son, the present Lord, was Storekeeper-General of the Navy. His fourth son went into the Church, and obtained the Crown living of Epworth, value £9BB and a house. The family motto is, Quad potui perfecti—" I have done what I could ;" and it must be allowed that they have done a great deal in putting public money into their own pockets. Now, let us pass to the Zetland branch, the chief of which formerly held the title of Baron Dundas. The second son of the first Lord Dundas was a Colonel in the Army. Another son, by favour of the Fitzwilliams, into whose family his father had married, for many years held two rectories, with two houses and £829 per annum. Afterwards his son was appointed to one of them (Harpole' £529 and a house. Another son was a Vice-Admiral, and for some time a Lord of the Admiralty (i,000); and another was a Lieutenant- General. There was also a William Dundas, M.P., a cousin I believe, of Lord Melville, who held three or four Scotch sinecures for many years, whose united annual value was between three and four thousand pounds. I find also a Dundas as Commander-in-Chief and Governor of Landguard Fort; another as Joint-Keeper of the Signet ; another as Governor of the Cape of Good Hope; another as Governor of the Prince of Wales's Island; another as Commissioner of Excise; another as Conanissioner of the Navy at Bombay; another with a pension of £3OO for himself and £3OO for his children; and another, a female, with a pension of £7BO. It is quite possible that one man held more than one office, and it is very likely that I have omitted to mention some offices altogether; if so, my excuse must be the number of the tribe. I must not omit to mention that it was a Dundas who suggested in the House of Commons, during the disturbances over Lord Robert Grosvenor's Sunday Closing Bill, that the mob should be dispersed by cannon. Of late years this fortunate family have not had such opportunities of living upon the public purse; yet I find one—the Hon. Robert Dundas—who had been in the Admiralty forty-two years, and who, on his re,irement in 1869, had a salary of £1,300, receiving an annual allowance of £1,072. Another was a Colonial Governor for twenty-two years.; and yet another has been in turn Solicitor-Generat and Judge Advocate- Genera! twice.

THE PRISON LIFE OF MICHAEL DAVITT.

BY TILE AUTB.OR OF SKETCHES OF CONtVICT LIFE," Erc. -- CHAPTER IV.—DARTMOOR Continued). The winters at Dartrnoor are terribly severe ; so much so that cases of froet-bite are comuron ; and the convicts were "so often troubled with chilblains, and thereby rendered un- able to work, that in 1872 they were allowed protection for their hands in the shape of serail bags made something in the shaee of a glove. Devitt was compelled to break stones when the snow was on the ground ;to stand or sit with his feet in the snow, and when it is remembered that the Dartmoor winter begins about the end of October, and last often into May, and even June, we can understand the hard- ships he had La undergo. In order that my readers may thoroughly understand what convict life is at Dartmoor I will try to describe a aerinter day, as given me by a man who served nearly the whole of a seven years' sentence there. Although the convicts are in bed at eight p.m., the nights seem all too short, for the excessive labour creates a long- ing for more sleep. During the night, all is as quiet as the grave, although there may be 320 prisoners in one ball. The warder on night duty walks about in his carpet slippers, and the principal warder comes into the ball every two hours, hut so accustomed do the convicts become to his visits that the clanging of the iron door does not disturb them. Just before five a.m, signs may be heard, that indicate the convicts' knowledge that it is nearly time to rise, but should the watchman-warder find any convict out of bed before the bell rings, he will probably report the man and get him punished. The WI rings, and in a moment all is commotion. The shivering convicts get out of their hammocks, wash and dress themselves, make up their beds by folding tbe clothes across the hammock in such a way that the inspecting officer may see that the sheets and blankets have not been torn or Mused in any way. At 5-20 the cell doors are unlocked, and four of the convicts—who do it in turn for a week—turn out to sweep and wash certain parts of the landing, each man, however, washing the space in front of his cell. My informant shall now tell his own story. • "I any, chummy, Ido believe it's foggy! Another days' spell," whispered one of my neighbours, a tall raw-boned fellow, not over fond of hard. work. I hope not. I'd rother go out on the hog and keep my- self warm with the spade than starve all day in my cell. Besides._ I've finished my book."

"I'll lend you mine. Here it is. Look out, the screw's not got his lamps this way." My neighbour's library book turned out to be the Pilgrim's Progress " fic.re take it hack ; I read that years ago." " Now, then, GT, you're tailing; report you. [This to my neighbour on the other side.] "It wasn't me, sir ; it was 60." " Contralicting an officer ; that's another offence, 67." The accused convict is quiet. knowing that any further attempt to exonerate himself will only exasperate the officer, and get him a heavier punishment. At six o'clock all the convicts have bad their breakfasts served out—a pirt f gruel and twelve oances of bread. At G. 45 we marched to chapel, and two or three prayers and a hymn having been hurriedly got through, we are marched back again. One of the renowned Dartmoor fogs is cm, and they dare not take us out to work, fearing some of us might esca pa._

"rake number 3 and 4 wards into the oakum-shed, and look alive about it," roars out the principal warder. "Blue me, if they ain't going to make U 3 pick oalitun," said my tall neighbour; " what a rascally shame." But instead of taking our ward into the oakum shed they march us into (ha hats, and, six a t a time, order us to strip all off. Some turncoat has been "rounding" on his mates that there is "snout " [tobacco] in the ward, and we are to be searched. It is known that the oakum shed is a place in which trafficking goes on—selling tiny morsels of tobacco for meat, pudding, dz.c. Although professing themsAves to be half-starved, many convicts will sell their food for tobacco. The officers had not been wrongly informed ; they found about half a yard of thin twist on one of the men and food on three others. The four were taken to the cells and then we were marched to the oakum shed.

"That was a narrow squeak for me," said Long Tom, as my tall neighbour was called. "I had a pudding saved. but I was so deuced peckish in the middle of the night that I het it. Wonder what he'll cop," "Three days' choky and 28 days' penal ; that's what he'll get, see if he don'r,2' said another, an old lag." We were seated in the oakum shed, engaged in picking coir to put in the beds, but as talking was not then pro- hibited, and no task was enforced, there was not muck work done.
" ! there'e %%'ç shall have to twn out after . . . all.

T tang Tom was right, and in a few minutes wa latete mustered in the prison parade ground, and marched off to the bogs. Ourparfy was trenching—turn:ng over the Fjound, and making it ready for draining. An old lag, " doiPc, ten," and who had served two previous sentences of penaCservi- tude, was the "marker out" of the work, The ground had to be dug down to the gravel foundation, in some parts the bog top soil was a foot in depth, and then gradually sloped to four or five feet. It was easy to " spit" it out in square pieces, the strongest man, and most accustomed to the spade, getting through his piece in half an hour. Then he could stand and watch the remainder, sometimes, which was not objE cted to by the warder, helping a novice, to keep him out of trouble. The last. man to finish his task was often credited with seven marks for his work, especially if it was usual for him to be last. The number of days in every convict's sentence, exclusive of the first nine months, which he spends in separate con- finements is multiplied by six, and the product represents the number of marks the convict must earn ere he can be recommended for a ticket of leave. The scale of marks is, tide the official Hales, "eight marks per diem for steady, hard labour, and the full performance of their allotted task ; seven for a less degree of industry ; six for a fair, but moderate day's work. If by his industry on public works the convict gains eight marks per diem, and does not forfeit any for misconduct, he earns the full remission of one-fourth allowed by the Secretary of State."] Long' Tom was in our party, and though probably the strongest man in it, he was often the last, but no one ever offered to help him, knowing it was pure idleness kept .him behind. We had not been at work more than an hour ere a "black dress" man Ml out and wanted to see the doctor. [A "black dress" man is one who has been guilty of assaulting a warder, for the §entdnce such an offence being a flogging and six months in chains, with a dress half black, half grey.] "I on saw the doctor this 'morning," said the warder, a tyrannical "bog trotter," "And he said you were putting it on. If you don't go on with your work I'll have you hand- cuffed and run in."

"Then you'll never run in :thy other poor devil of a lag'," shouted the man as he ran at the officer with his spade. One fearful blow on the back of the head, the convicts looking breathlessly on ; but ere another could be dealt on the staggering officer, vainly trying to draw his sword, Long Tom felled the man with his spade, and the warder of a neigbouring party running up, Black Sam had the darbies put on, and lay on the ground as if dead. A pail full of dirty bog water soon brought him round, but ale would not rise, venting his imprecations on Long Tom for his inter- ference.
"You - pig! Why didn't you let Ino finish him ; ra as soon he hung as have another bishing (flogv,ing); and if they don't shift me from this - hQle, I'll swing from some - screw or another."

The principal warder on duty came round, and at the point o$ kr:civil guard's bayonet thyvretched convict was drhen trWany .1-lesitAtion or lagingiresulting in a gentle probe with the bayonet point—for brutality is rampant in convict prisons. That's the best strOe'bf- business Lva. done for mmy day," said Long Torn ; " I wonder imw much they'll !knock* ofT ; tire! Ye month at._ Ist, eb P addrcssing the marker

div.p: "OUR OLD NOBli ITY:
[Published by 111 r. E. J. Kibbleichite, 31, Tavistock-strcet, London, WC., and reprinted by pernzission.] THE ZETLANDS.

There are several branches of this fortunate family, two of which possess peerages. The Earl of Zetland owns in Yorkshire. 9,623 acres; in Fife, Stirling, Clackmannan, and .Durabarton, 13,110 acres; in Orkney and• Shetland, or Zetland, 43 446 acres. With regard to the latter, Sir Water Scott, in a note on Magnus Troil, one of the cha- racters in "The Pirate," !says :—" The [Mailers are the allodial possessors of Zetland, who. hod their possessions under the old Norwegian law, ins'ead of the feudal tenures introduced among 'them from Scotland." The introduction of feudal tenures was nothing more or less than a permanent robbery of the landowners and their descendants. The land was theirs absolutely till the abominable feudal tenures were introduced. In 1643 the islands were granted to the Earl of Morton, and this grant was confirmed in 1707, and made absolute in 1742. Twenty-five years after the Earl of Morton sold his rights (?) to 'Sir Lawrence : Dundas, ancestor of the Earl of Zetland, who had made a great fortune as an army contractor. Army contractors in those days made immense ,fortunes with astonishing rapidity. Apparently the Dundas'es of this branch have still further advanced their fortunes by marriages into the Fita-widiam and other landed families. But I must not dwell upon the House of Zetland, my purpose rather teing, to show of what stuff peers were made at the begiuning of the present centory. • The first Lord Melville obtained a peerage in 1802. For many years he had been the confidant and coadjutor of Pitt. He was a sorb of a Lord President of the Court of Session, and, as Fox said, "ever showed an eagerness to heap up emoluments and to systematise corruption." In 1775 he was appointed Lord-Advocate of Scotland, and for A period of thirty years he held a succession of rich offices, sometimes three or four together. When he held one of the chief offices in the Cabinet he was appointed Privy Seat of Scot- land, and at the same time his wife obtained a pension of £1.500 a year. He also had a grant of the Stewardship of Fife, with arrears of pay amounting to £3,000, arrears which the very persons who signed the warrant declared they were unacquainted with. Sir Erskine May rightly says, in regard to that period, that, with free institutions, the people were governed according to the principles of despotism.' One of the Bills passed at that time empowered the Crown ta secure and detain persons suspected of conspiring against the King's person and government; another provided that a prisoner, on the evidence of a single witness, and undefended by counsel, might be sentenced to capital punishment; another provided that if a meeting of twelve or more persons remainel together for one hour after being ordered to dis- perse, the offenders should suffer death. Well might Fox declare that "every man who talked freely might be, and would he, in the hands and at the mercy of Ministers." Such Was Toryism in its palmiest days. For all these things, neat to Pitt, Dundas was responsible.. I think of the true and brave men whom he hunted down, caused to rot in gaol, or to be transported beyond the se ,s ; and then it is with a stern satisfaction that I proceed to describe the disgraee,ancl downfall of their persecutor. Lord Melville. who had held various lucrative offices for thirty yearsawas a p'uralist who was at the same time Minister of War, President of the Board of Control, and Treasurer of the Navy. The latter office was practically a sinecure, the work being done by a deputy. Former Treasurers had made much gain by keeping large balances in their hands—dirty profits which the elder Pitk proudly refused to touch—hut on Melville's appointment, at his own suggestion. this evil custom was made illegal, and his salary was raised from £2,000 to £4,000; and yet, in 1803, it was discovered by a Committee of Inquiry that Alexander Trotter, the deputy of Lord Melviile, contrived for several years to have balances in his hands deposited with Coutts, the banl:er—one of Trotter's relatives—ranging from £40,000 to nearly half a million. For some years these balances constantly exceeded £lOO,OOO, and with this Money Trotter habitually discounted bills and speculated in stocks.

Trotter entered the Navy Office as a junior clerk at £5O a year, with a slowly rising increment. After at ime he was appointed deputy by Melville, at a salary of £5OO, which was afterwards increased to £BOO. In 1791 this man's dividends from stock in his possession were only £80; in 1802, they were £11,308, and he had purclpsed considerable landed property. Even according to his own statement, Trotter's property derived by marriage and inheritance did not exceed £lO,OOO ; and yet he estimated that he was worth £05,000 when he was examined before the House of Lords.. If this latter statement was correct, somebody else must have Made considerable gains beside Trotter hirnsel, and the question at once arises whether Lord Melvide was a partner in his fraud. This it is impossible to determine with certainty, because the precious pair burnt the docu- ments that might have incriminated them. I quote the statement made by the Cort Committee and signed by its chairman, the late Rev. Dr. Booth, a statement which is fully borne out by the proneedings leading up to Lord Mel- ville's trial :—" When. in 1803, Parliament had appointed a Commission of Naval Inquiry to examine the irregularities of th,e Treasurer, Lord Melville, and his paymaster, Alexan- der Trotter. t- Mutually agreed, a few weeks before the sitting of the Commission, by ft joint release exhibited on the subsequent impeachment of Lord Melville, to burn, and accordingly did burn, their accounts for £134,000,000 of public money, which had passed tfirough their hands." The very last thing which an honest man, with an inquiry peicling over his head, would have done, would blvc becn to burn the documents which he knew would be called for. In the face such conduct Lord Melville's personal denials go for nothing.

, . .Lord Met-Ine, however, admitted that he had a general 1,- ' ...lowledge of Trotter's practices. But that was not all. Trotter, when examined before the Commission of Inquiry, refused to answer whether his chief had shai ed in his unlawful gains. But that was not alt. It was shown that when Lord Melville left office for a short time that he was a defaulter to the extent of £13,000, and that when he came into office again £7,000 of the deficiency was still upaid. It was shown, further, that when he had promo'ed this junior clerk with a paltry salary to the office of paymaster that he had borrowed £lO,OOO and L'20,900 of him at a time; and that, in all, so far as could be ascertained, Trotter had advanced to his chief £40,000, partly with interest, but much of it without any interest. Further, it was shown that with some of these sums Trotter had purchased stock on Lord Melville's account. It would be easy to quote a multitude of damning facts-which came out at the trial, but my space forbids. I have, however, quoted quite enough to justify the deelarit- tion of William W'ilberforce that he could not find words sufficiently strong to express his utter detestation of Lord Melville's conduct; and I must add that, after his lordship had been heard in hisamivn defence at the bar of the House of Commons, the same eminent man protested that "he con- sidered his defence an aggravation of his guilt." Lord Mel- ville had, of course, to resign the places that he held, and his name was s,ruck off the Privy Council. Ultimately he was tried by the House of Lords on ten counts, and acquitted by majorities ranging from 27 to 135; but, as Miss Martin au says, "it was felt at the time, and has been felt since, im- possible that many, if any, should believe him actually innocent of the charges brought against him." I cannot forbear contrasting the treatment of Lord Mel- ville and Henry Cort. Cort was an inventor who had made most important discoveries in the manufacture of iron, on which he spent £20,000. In 1789 Mr. Adam Jellicoe, Deputy-Paymaster of the Navy, with the consent of his superiors, advanced Cort £27,000, and entered into partner- ship with him. WlrenJellicoe died a few years after, it was iscovcred that he had stolen this money and other sums from the office. The ironworks were seized, but, instead of being retained or sold by the Government, they were actually banded over to Jollicoe's son—Cort, who was probably innocent, being turned out. Now, let us turn to Lord Mell, ville. Cort died in 1800, and a few days after Lord Melville I presented a memorial to the Lords of the Treasury, setting forth the value of Cart's inventions and asking on that ac- count a release of £25,000, the amount for which he was 'responsible owing to Jellicoe's defalcations, his own defi- ciency at the time being £190,000. He obtained the release. And what did Cort get? A few years after, Lord Melville's own son was First Lord of the Admiralty, and reported that Cores merits had been sufficiently recognised by the pensions conferred on Cort, his widow, and children, namely, 100 a year to Cort, received for six years ; £lOO to his widow, received for sixteen .yea* ; and £2O to her children after her death., ' ' • A - "' . On 'Monday the whole of the miners employed at the New British Iron Company's Wynnstay Colliery at Ruabon, to the numb..r of five hundred, refused to work, and returned horde. Up to the time of the North Wales strike many of the Welsh collieries stocked their coal when the sale was slack. This the miners objected to, and refused to load into stock, as during the strike several coalowners were enabled to supply customers from their accumulated stocks. •
To be continued.

. • The miners at the Ituabon Colliery, one of the most ex- tensive in North Wales, who struck work at the beginnirae of the wok owing to coal owners stacking the coal, resumed labour on Tharsclay morning. While trade is slack they have resolved to work only three days par week, so that th.e employers will he unable to accumulate coal stocks. This wiil not average more than ten shihiogs per week for miners' wages.

THE WEA.THER AND THE CORN TEADE.—The Ma,k-lane Express says :—" The weather in the nerth was unsettled during the early part of last week, but in the English coun- ties for the most part line and hot. Harves,ing of wheat has been much more general than could have been expected a fortnight ago, the grain having ripeteed very rapidly; and if the weather holds good larger proportions of wheat will be in shed in the current week. A sample of new wheat, weighing 62-.llba. per bushel, was sold on Wednesday for 583 per quarter in Chicheeter markei, and one or two samples have been also sold in Canterbury and Cambridge. New black Tartarian oats in Cork fetched 22s per quarter of 320 lbs , and several samples of new winter oats sold at Mahlon at 22s to 24s per quarter. The value of old Englieh wheat in the provineial markets declined Is to 3s per quarter, and ii London few sales were reported at slightly reduced prices. Country flour is too scarce to be quoted cheaper, but all descriptions of breadstuffs were dull, with slow sale throughout the week. Trade for foreign wheat in London was aff,cled by the fine weather, and foreign flour dull, but not chcaper.7 Txre'LAßoun MARKET.—The labour market remaias on the whole in a satiefactory condition, and recent returns of pauperism show that, with the exception of a slight increase in the metropolis, there is a decrease of registered paupers throughout the United Kningdom. Railway construction works are now specially busy, and several important under- takings recently sanctioned by Parliament will shortly make further demands on strong Unskilled labour. At Birming- ham the hardware branches again ebow sornewbat increased activity, though most of the war orders given to the town are now executed. At all the leading northern ports shipbuild- ing remains very active, and the returns of the Amiga- mated Engineers'. Society show that there is an exceptional amount of employment for men in the engineering trades. The Master Builders' Association, however, report that throughont the country building is somewhat slack, and the supply of labour is, as .a rule, ample. In the North of Eng- land, ironworkers under recent award get an increase of Vl- prr cent in wages, a further similar advance taking place later on in the year. At Barrow-in-Furness more furnaces have been blown in, and prospects are good. In North Wales a strike of quarrymen has been averted, and throughout the principality employment is generally good. The letter- carriers in London are still unsettled, and a demonstration of the auxiliaries has taken place. Harvesting has now corn- tnenced in many districts, and no great scarccey of labour is reported. Advices from the United States indicate that the ironworkers' strike at Piteburg is virtually over. An out- break of yellow fever is reported from Texas. In Montana, owing the the progress of the Northern Pacific Railway, great development is taking place.—Laboue sews.

THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES: MANCHES- TER, WEDNESDAY.—The iron market here has shown but little movement during the past week. There are still only limited inquiries coming in from buyers, but makers are not in any way pressing sales, and prices all round are firm. For Lancashire pig iron the prices quoted for delivery equal to Manchester remain at 4Gs less 21 for forge and foundry qualities, but only a small business is I”..ing done; district brands range from 47s 6d up to 40e anti 50s less 2-1-- for forge and foundry Lincolnshire and Derbyshire iron, and 51s lOd to 52s 10d net cash for Middlesborough delivered equal to Manchester. Finished iron makers are generally well em- ployed on specifications, and prices are steady at about V 78 CI to V 103 for bars delivered into the Manchester dis- tria, lower figures than these toing only quoted in excep- tional cases. The condition of the engineering trades is with- out material change, worLs b.ling still kept well engaged on old orders, but new business is not coming in very freely. The coal trade of this district continues very quiet. Old sales to Clear off stocks continue to 1)5 made at low figures, and actual selling p:ices are very irregular. House-fire coals still move off very slowly, whilst supplies of other classes of fuel for iron-making and steam purposes continue in excess of reqnirements, and pits throughout the district are not being kept going more than four days a week. At the pit mouth the average prices remain at about 83 to Sc 6d for best coals, tie to Gs Gd for sreonds, 4s 9d to 5s Cd for common, 4s 3d to 43 Pa for burgy, 3s Gd to 4s for good slack, and 2s 9d to 3s 3d for inferior sorts. There has keen rather more business stirring for shipment coastwise, bat orders are still scarce, rnd low prices continue to be taken, steam coal delivered at Liverpool or Garston being offered at from Gs to Cs 6d, and :rouse-fire coals at 83 3d to 8s 6d per ton. The St. Helens strike centinues, and shows no sign of early settlement.

div.p: MINISTERS Al' THE MANSION HOUSE.'

The Lord Mayor entertained her Majesty's Minietere on Wednesday night at Guildhall. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were proposed from the chair. In reply, Lord Northbrook eulogised the achievemerns of the fleet and of the Marines in the recent engagements, and spoke of the important services rendered by the mercantile marine in transporting the army to Egypt. Without such a marine the expedition could not have been despatched. Mr. Childers spoke of the great difficulty of the task in Egypt at this season of the year, but said he believed all difficulties would be triumphantly- 0170.1',:)riO. He claimed for the Government that the crisis did not find them unprepared. for within a fortnight from taking the Vote of Credit a force of 15,000 to 113,000 men had been despatched from our shores to the East. The Lord Chancellor; responding fur the House of Lords, said these were times of anxiety. At this moment there were echoes lingering of sharp, hard c nflicts in bath HOLIEIOS of Parlia- ment. We lived at a moment at which it might be possible that serious conflicts between the two Houses might occur, althougfi he hoped it was not the case that they were still impending. Previenslfgood sense, moderation, and wisdlrn on both sids had cansed them to pass away, and on the whole the welfare of the country had been a predominant consideration in both Houses, and had prevailed. So he trusted it would be in times to come. Mr. Gladetone spoke at some length. He said he was so sanguine as to Jbelieve that we had now passed the moment of danger with reference to the possible conflict be- tween the two Houses, and that wisdom and harmony might mark what yet remained of the deliberations of Parliament jot the present year. Referring to the Egyptian c he said we had embarked upon it in the interests of this great empire; but it should be well known and understood that the interests in nnestion were not ours aloae, but com- mon to us with every state of Europe and of the civilised world. • We did not go to Egypt to make war with its peo- ple, but to rescue them from military tyranny. We did not go there to make war with the Mahornmedan religion, or to repress the growth of Egyptian liberty, as we had no interest so great there as that Egypt should be truly free and prosper- 011S. England went toEgppt with clean hands, honestpurposes and no secret aims. Referring nest to the state of Ireland, he said that there did not exist one who could now rise in his place in Parliament to say that the Land Act had been a distnel failure. Its operation was spreadirae, and in the train of the Land Courts come peace and security, where disturb- ance and outrage had formerly prevailed. From month to month, and almost from week to week, there was a steady diminution of outrages which, formidable as they were in themselves, were still more formidable as symbols of a powerful conspiracy for the purpose of breaking up the foundation of social order. He regretted the melancholy confession of.the barrenness of the session, and _emphatic- ally called upon enlightened public opinion to assist the Government in inducing the House of Commons to relieve itself of its present state of incompetence and incapacity for the discharge of. its duties.

THE MEMSMTGI OF DEUTERONOMY.—Tbe fifth book of the Pentateuch is called Deuteronomy, "The Repetition of the Law," arid iasometimes so styled by the Jews themselves, who understand by the words of Chap. xvii. 18, rendered in our version "a copy of this law," tho Book of Deuteronomy itself, the Hebrew literally signifying a duplicate, or second publication of anything. Our translation is probably the right one 1, hut it was a common view of the Fatber!,. founded upon the words of Ezek. xx. 11, 25, that God first gave the Israelites, at Mount Sinai; a spiritual law, of which the ten commandments were the central portion; and that it was only upon their cohstant violation of every moral precept, coupled with the neglect of the Sabbath day, that the burdensome ceremonial or sacrifices and legal purifica, tions and festivals was added, partly as punishment, but chiefly because they were not capable of any thing better than this veiled teaching, in which the spiritual meaning was wrapped up in a cover of type and mysticism. This view is, no doubt, an exaggerated one, though certainl., mach. of the Law was so arranged as to snit the low moral state of the people on leaving Egypt. Tint ARREARS BILL.—Lord CARLINGFORD moved that the House should agree to the first of the Commons' amend- ments to their lordships amendments to the Arrears Bill. —Lord SALISBURY said it appeared to him that all the Com- mons had done was simply to disagree with the amendments on the subject of option. His views on that subject were unaltered. His Lord- ship protested that he would not have any respon- sibility for "any jot or tittle of this bill," which without the alteration making the consent of the landlord necessary, was a measure of simple robbery, a bill which would bear the gravest fruits as a legislative precedent for the future ; but in a conference that morning with the Peers who passed the amendment he found an overwhelming mijority averse to throwing out the bill in the present state of affairs in Ireland and Egypt, and finding himself thus in a small minority he should not divide the House.— The ainendmentq of the Commons were, after some oppoii- tion from the Marquis of Waterford, the Earl of Limerick, and the Earl. of Dunraven, agreed to, with the exception that a verbal amendment, proposed by the Duke of Abercorn, was insertEd, as also one proposed by the Government. and in this final shape the Arrears Bill goes back to the House of Commons.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TaunsDAy.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TaunsDAy.

TURRET: ARABI PASHA: THE MILITARY CONTENTION. —Sir C. DILKE, replying to a question pat by Mr. Arnold, said that all the Powers were agreed in -advising the Porte to issue a proclamation against Arabi. The draft proclama- tion had been submitted to Her Majesty's Government. The proclamation supported the Khedive and declared Arabi, by name, a rebel. A military convention had not yet been agreed upon, but the Porte bad expressed its readiness to conclude one.

DIE PnEMIEn ON ENGLAND'S POLICY.—Lord ELCHO moved the adjournment of the House in order to appeel to the Government that before engaging in military operations other than such as might be necessary for the defence of Alexandria, the protection of the Khedive, and the s-curity of the Suez Canal, they would endeavour to ascertain the true state of feeling on the part of the people of Egypt.— Sir II D. WoLIT seconded the motion.—Mr. GitikusroNE, in opposing the motion, said he must decline to enter at this moment into a definition of the objects of our military occu- pation of Egypt. He admitted, however, that he had said we had something to deal with hi Egypt beyond the military party. There was, he maintained, the strongest .evidence that Ourabi and his confederates did not in the smallest degree represent the national movement. The Government were not making war upon the people of Egypt, but were putting down an uprising which, in their opinion, tvas not only being conducted with unlawful authority and was engaged in machinations against liberty, but which had also for its certain result the revival of that terrible oppression which formerly dominated Egypt.—The motion for adjournment was negatived. On the motion for going into Committee of Supply, Mr. Cowurfs motion in reference to the suspension of the Irish members on the lst July was negatived without a division. —Brief discussions on several subjects of limited interest were raised, and it was not until nearly nine o'clock that the business of Supply was actually reached.

div.head: CE EATAYo•s MOVEMENTS.
div.p: CE EATAYo•s MOVEMENTS.

Cetewayo, accompanied by his suite and his interpreter, Mr_ Dunn, visited the Zoological Gardens on Saturday morn- ing, travelling thither in two carriages. They were received by Mr. Bartlett, the superintendent, and appeared much amused with the visit. The party afterwards returned to M el bury -road. On Sunday, the house at present occupied by the ex-Zulu king and his three counsellors was the object of unabated interest. A large crowd assembled at an early hour, and until nightfall three policemen were required to keep the spectators "moving on." Cetewayo, however, remained within doors throughout the day. He was much amused at the sight of the throngs so anxious to see him. . On Monday afternoon Cetewayo, accompanied by three chiefs, visited the House of Commons, and occupied a seat in the distinguished strangers' gallery. On the termination of questions the ex-King proceeded to the House of Lords, where Lord Enfield was speaking. Mr. Shepstone and Mr. Dunn were present and explained the order of business. When Cetewayo and his suite were leaving Palace Yard they were surrounded by some hundreds of holiday-makers, who cheered them heartily. The ex-King, with his chiefs, was in a closed carriage, the attendants following in open carriages. On Tuesday afternoon Cetewayo was mainly occupied in receiving visitors, among those who had interviews with him being Sir Wilfrid Lawson Mr. Justin M•Carthy, Mr. Alderman Fowler, Mr. Firth, Mr. Pease, Mr. Jesse Collings, and other members of Parliament. The King and his com- panions continue in excellent health. Cetywayo visited Mr. Gladstone, in Downing-street, at 12 o'clock noon on Wednes.lay. A large crowd assembled to witness his arrival. The interview lasted half an hour, and the ex-King smiled good humouredly as he left. Large numbers of persons flocked to the Crystal Palace on Thursday afternoon and evening in anticipation of seeing Cetewayo, who was announced to visit that place. The ex- iting was, however, unable to be prese.nt owing to indisposi- tion, and the , following notice was posted throughout the building:—' A telegram has been received from the Colonial Office that Cetewayo is under medical treatment, and cannot possibly visit the palace this day."

div.head: TITLE STATE oF IRELAND.
div.p: TITLE STATE oF IRELAND.

The little differences that existed between Dr. Davitt and some of his colleagues in the Land League have been in some measure smobthed by the financial success of his visit to America. From various sources Mr. Davitt has brought back nearly £4,000 for the Land League funds. The first newspaper prosecution under the Crime Preven- tion Act was -begun at Tamil on Saturday, when the pro- prietor of a local paper was committed for trial, charged with publishing a letter from Mr. Redpath on the assassina- tion of the late Mr. Walter Bourke.

..„.. A supplEment to the Dublin Gazette, issued on Monday night, contained proclamations and orders of the Lord Lieu- tenant and Privy Council as to the possession of arms in certain baronies of Monaghan; the service of notices and proceduro of magistrates in probibitint and suppressing meetings; service of notices of suppression of newspapers; and fixing general sessions of the peace, to be held at 41 places throughout the country in September, October, and November, for hearing appeals under the 22nd section of the crime Act.

Lawrence Cotter, who was, at the late Cork Assivs, sentenced to be hanged on the 22nd instant, for the murder in May of his employer, an old woman named Margaret Kelleher, has had his sentence commuted to penal servitude for life. Prisoner i 3 of weak mind.--Li the case of Thomas Haynes, sentenced to death at the same assizes for the murd,r of his wife, a reply has been received to the memo- rial forwarded on his behalf that the law must take its course. He will be hanged on the 22nd instant.

div.head: IRISH POLICE FORCE.
div.p: THE IRISH POLICE FORCE.

The agitation which has recently commcnc.d amongst the Royal Irish Constabulary, with the view of calling official attention to certain grievances alleged to exist, is assuming serious proportions. Assurances of co-operation and sym- pathy have been received by the Limerick police, who first broached the subject, from almost every detachment of con- stabulary in the island. The visit of Colonel Bruce, Inspector General, to the head-quarters of disaffection on Saturday resulted in no amicable arrangement of the dis- pute, and, so far as may be judgFd from reports of the proceedings, the interview between that officer and the men only served to further embitter their already strained re- lations. The police have addressed a memorial to the Chief Secretary, asking for a favourable consideration of their complaints, and have intimated their intention of resigning en masse should no amelioration of their condition follow. The demands made by the men are—(l) promotion from the ranks; (2) increased pay, say one shilling a day each man; (3) equalisation of pensions; (4) compulsory retirement of all head and other constable S at thirty years' service, leaving if optional to retire at twenty-five years; (5) lodging allowance to married men. Colonel Bruce, has addressed an official circular to the men, in which he notes the "grave discredit" that has been "thrown upon the character and discipline of:the force " by the Limerick circular. Some of the matters mentioned in the circular, he says, have for some time engaged the atten- tion of the Executive, but the course which the men are taking will tend to retard rather than to improve the con- dition of the force.

The Press Association says :—For some time past some of the Fenian agents in Ireland from America have been encouraging the agitation among the Irish Constabulary for an increase of pay, with the view, if possible, of inducing the men to strike. A more systematic attempt is now about to be made, by holding out to the men who will leave the force the guarantee of employment in America of equal value to that they may have in Ireland. The Limerick County Inspector on Thursday morning received an official letter directing him to inform the men that the Government would grant their request, and would appoint a special commission to erquire into their griev- ances,.and that a grant of £lBO,OOO for special services would be distributed forthwith; The men expressed themselves perfectly satisfied.

The total collections for Oldham Hospital Saturday re £985, which is more than last year. After payment of, expenses, over .£9OO will be handed to the Infirniary. Thel institution is receiving considerable support, the last dsna-1 tion being £2(10 by a lady. At present the building is in course of being considerably enlarged. A SWEET SPIRIT.—There is a sweet spirit—not to be found every hens in the day, nor, indeed, every day in the year, but it is sometimes to be met with--a spirit of forbear- ance, kindness, and charity, that delights to speak well of the absent, and to represent favourably what to others may appear doubtful. "She has a high way with her," said an iriela maiden when speaking of her absent mistress, who was considered proud; "people do not understand her. She has a high way with her; but she is like the lilies, that are so gentle and mild when you come to know them." Oh that we all bad more of the spirit of this lady; that all our seem- ing high-mindedness and pride could be explained in as satis- factory a manner; and that we were enabled to say of our- selves with perfect sincerity and truth, whatever may be our' outward bearing, "Lord, my heart is not haughty, nor mine eyes lofty; neither do I exercise myself in great mat- tors, or in things too high for me."

B House of Commons on Tuesday 'b'iLre the House adjourns he may It is statedp wa that tik the opportunity of again raising the question of his right to take his seat. Birkenhead, which a few days ago was granted a Court of Quarter Sessions by Royal letters patent, has now received a recorder. A communication received from the Home Office by the Corporation announcing the appointment of Mr. Clement Higgins to the office. The Press Association learns that Lord Tavistock, who has represented Bedfordshire since April, 1875, will not seek re-eleetiou, and that Mr. Theodore Harris, banker, of Leighton Buzzard, will offer himself as a candidate in the Liberal interest.

Lord Derby, in declining to become a vice-president of the associ :tion recently formed for bringing about the re- peal of all acts relating to blasphemy and heresy, writes : " I agree with the object you have in view, and will support it in Parliament.__ _ _

As all possibility of proceeding with private members' motions this year is at an end, Mr. Hugh Mason has with- drawn from the order-book his resolution in favour of female suffrage, but has given notice that he will proceed with it as early as possible next session. At Chorley, on Tuesday, four colliers were sentenced by the Magistrates in petty sessions to long terms of imprison- ment for night poaching and assaulting policemen and game watchers. In one case, should the prisoner be unable to find sureties for "good behaviour," he will remain in prison for 18 months. Patrick Pacificos Wade, a priest, of Darlington, was sen- tenced at the Liverpool Assizes, the other day, to two years' imprisonment with hard labour for committing a very horrible offence in Prince's Park, Liverpool. The learned judge stated that this was the heaviest punishment which the law permitted him to inflict. Mr. G. W. Palmer, M.P., has been fined by the local magis- trates.£lo 10s., including costs, for polluting the Thames at Earley, near Reading. The Thames Conservators prose- cuted. Messrs. Huntley and Palmer have also been fined 10s., including costs, for infringing the Reading new Cor- poration Act. A Keswick correspondent stated that the Rev. W. A., Pope, Manchester New College, Gordon Square, London, met with his death on the Great Gable, at the head of Ennerdale Valley, on Monday evening. Mr. Edward Tripp, who accompanied the rev, gentleman, suddenly missed him, and on Tuesday morning his body was found shockingly mangled at the foot of the cliff. In the division on the Peers' amendments to the Arrears I Bill, in the House of Commons, on Tuesday night, several Conservatives left the house without voting. Sir Joseph Pease paired in favour of the Government with Mr. Bulwer against. Sir A. Bass paired with the Hon. Thomas Bruce. Among the Liberals shut out from the division was Mr. Hanbury Tracy. Princes Albert Victor and George of Wales were on Tuesday confirmed at Whippingham Church, East Cowes, by • the Archbishop of Canterbury, assisted by the Bishop of Winchester. Amongst those present to witness the rite were the Queen, the Prince and Princess of Wales, and other members of the Royal Family, with a number of officers of the Royal yachts and the guardship. Mr. Clarke Aspinall bad 139 prisoners brought before him ' on Tuesday, the majority being charged with drunkenness. , The number shows a considerable diminution compared with last year, and is not large when it is remembered that the preceding day was a general holiday, when many thousands of visitors flocked to Liverpool and thousands of citizens made holiday. SALVATION ARMY SQUABBLES.—A few days ago, Captain Gibsy Smith, leader of the Salvation Army Corps in Han- ley, accepted a gold watch and testimonial as a token of I respect on his leaving the district. On receiving these the 'captain was discharged from the Salvation Army by Gene- ral Booth, as were also two lieutenants who bad likewise received watches. Captain Smith will only be reinstated on Igiving up the watch to the Army. The circumstance has caused much comment._

A coroner's jury on Tuesday inquired into the death of Samuel Leach, who, hut state of intoxication, attempted on Sunday night to enter a house at Hest Bank, near Lan- caster, and was shot dead by a boy of.twelye, named Steven- son, who had been left in charge of the premises, and viewed Leach as a burglar. A verdict of "justifiable homi- cide" was returned; but the county magistrates have re- manded the boy in custody on a charge of killing Leach. Several melancholy cases of drowning have occurred within the past few days. On Monday afternoon a young gentleman named Scott, whilst bathing in a dangerous part of Loch Lee, Forforshire, was observed to sink, and his body was not recovered for some Hours. Two young ladies, bathing in the river Endrich, near Glasgow, were drowned the same afternoon, a third lady narrowly escaping a similar fate. The loss of three lives is also reported owing to the capsizing of a pleasure boat on the Thames. Some idea of the enormous ferry traffic on the Mersey may be gathered from the fact that 208,055 persons were carried by the Birkenhead and Wallasey ferries on Monday, exclusive of contractors. This enormous total leaves out of reckoning the other ferries higher up the river, which were all glutted with excursionists. The most satisfactory feature is that the traffic was entirely conducted without. accident.

THE COMPOSITION or OUR Artmv.—lt appears from the official statements just published that amount our recruits of last year the proportion of those born in England or Wales was higher than that of the previous year by .21 per 1,000; while of those'born in Scotland the proportion was on the contrary, 15 per 1,000; and of those born in Ireland, 8 per 1,000 less. The natives of England and Wales represent 702 per 1,000 of the entire number. Ireland stands next for 202 per 1,000; while Scotland furnished only 82 per 1,000. At Birmingham on Tuesday, a man named Albert New- brook, who has only recently completed a term of imprison- ment for cattle stealing, was committed for trial on a remarkably audacious attempt to rob a jeweller's shop. He entered the establishment as an ordinary customer, and, having selected a gold watch and chain, dealt the shopman a savage blow on the head with a stone that he had tied up in a handkerchief. He then attempted to make off with his plunder, but in this, fortunately, he was foiled. THE WORKINGMEN AND THE CHANNEL TUNNEL—A. con- ference of the Trades Union organizations of the West of England and South Wales was held on Tuesday night in Bristol. Over 100 delegates, representing nearly 100,000 workmen, attended. Mr. G. Shipton, secretary of the London Trades Council, presided. A resolution was passed, regretting the opposition manifested to the construction of the Channel Tunnel, and expressed a belief that the increased facilities for social intercourse which it would afford between the two countries must result in increased good-will and mutual ad- vantage.

AN EXCURSIONIST KILLED AT LYTHAM.—A sad accident occurred at Lytham railway station on Saturday night. Just before eleven o'clock an excursion train from Black- pool. to Bolton ha& drawn up, when the station-master observed a man Under the wheels of the van. The train was backed slightly, one wheel being upon the man's body, and he was taken into the waiting-room, where he expired in two minutes. He was unknown. Ho was aged about 25. was of pale complexion, five feet seven in height, and had on brown Tam-o'-Shanter cap, brown cloth coat and vest, small plaid-cloth trousers, white silk handkerchief, silk scarf, and gold pin. He had a Bolton return ticket, and was supposed to have been getting out whilst the train was in motion.

Lord Cranbrook addressed A Conservative demonstration at Wandsworth on Saturday, and strongly Criticised the policy of the Government in regard to colonial and Irish affairs. The bringing of Cetewayo to this country, he thought, was a mistake, as tending to raise unduly the ex- pectations of the ex-King and his supporters, and running the risk of tumult and bloodshed in Zululand. In Ireland the same policy of " sacrificing the interests of loyal and patriotic men to the clamour of the disloyal and criminal " had been pursued. He condemned the Arrears Bill, being of opinion that though a temporary relief might be given to burdened tenants, the arrears were certain to accumulate again, anp he asked, Why should the English people throw their money into the sea ? It was the duty of the House of Loris to see that the British public was not robbed. ACCIDENT TO A TOURIST COACH. A serious accident has occurred to one of the tourist coaches running between Callander and the Trossachs. The 3.10 p.m. coach was driving through Coilintogle, about two miles from Callan- der, wben one of the four horses yoked to the brake shied at some object in its path, and, rearing amongst the other animas, caused them to swerve, with the result that the coach was overturned and several of the occupants thrown to the ground. The €lriver, Duncan Keir, was severely injured about the body, and had one of his legs broken. Mr. M‘Michael, solicitor, Callander, with his wife and son, were sitting on the dickey beside the driver, and also received serious injuries, Mr. M'Michael having one of his legs broken. The other passengers, beyond receiving a severe shaking and some slight scratches, escaped uninjured. The injured persons were driven back to Callander, where medical aid was procured. After having their wounds dressed they were each sent home. -

THE FORESTERS' HIGH COURT MEETING—The Foresters' High Court meeting was opened on Monday in the Burdon Rooms, Weymouth. Chief Ranger Hounsell presided, and there were _over 500 delegates present. The Mayor, Mr. Howard, and Mr. Edwards, one of the borough members, were present, and were most cordially received. Both highly commended the objects and the influence of the society, and dweit upon the great benefits it conferred upon the indus- trial classes. Mr. Edwards incidentally observed that he liked to encourage prudence and thrift, as he was desirous, now the working classes commanded the political situation, that they should also become possessed of property. If the wealth of the nation were restricted to a few he feared there would be very little stability. for the institutions of the country. The High Chief Ranger, in the course of his in- augural address, said the Order increased last year over 8,000 members, and many of the suspended districts, by which 8,000 members left the Order, were applying to be reinstated. THE RATEABILITY Or MARRIED WOMEN.—The incapacity of a married woman to be rated even in respect of her own house in which she lives with her husband is due to the fact that, except to the very limited extent allowed by the Married Women's Property Act, a wife is still linable to hold property, without the intervention of trustees. The owners of a house settled to the wife's separate nse are, in contemplation of law, not the wife nor the husband, but the trustees, who allow the husband and wife to live in it. The effect of this permission is to constitute the husband legal occupier. Such occupation as the wife has is, in law, the occupation of the husband; and although the trustees hold for her, yet when, with their sanction, she and her hus- band live in the house, the effect is the same as if the trus- tees were strangers to her. The wife is thus excluded from offices for which rating is a qualification, but under soul() eumstances the parish might seriously be embarrassed. The husband being the ratepayer, the wife's furniture cannot be seized for the rates, although it is in the house rated ; so that if the husband has no property, the only way open to the parish of enforcing the rates is-to put the husband in gaol until the wife pave them. (Such are the anornAlies which arise from retaining the shadowy of the old rule by which husband and wife are one, and that one the husband, while the substance has long departed. All that is required is a simple enactment making married women capable of holding property.—Lan journal.

the Reform and Codification of the Law of Nations, which was opened at Liverpool on Tuesday, the law of affreight- ment and bills of lading came under discussion. It was agreed that it was desirable to have a common form bill of lading, and prior to considering the details of a bill drafted by an influential Liverpool committee, the Conferenc3 ex- pressed approval of the general principle that while the shipowner should b 3 liable for the faults of his s?rvants in all matters relating to the ordinary course of the voyage, such as stowage and the right delivery of the cargo, .he should be exempted from liability for everything which came under the head of "accidents of navigation," even though the loss ,for these might be indirectly attributable to some fault or neglect of the crew. In the course of Wed- nesday a rather animated discussion took place as to whether the expression "the act of God " should be retained in the form, Professor Peabody suggesting that it was the 'Act of God which carried vessels to their destination as well as caused disastrous storms. Mr. Dudley Field thought the phrase" superhuman cause" would answer all purposes, and M. Clunet was strongly of opinion that the old formula. casusforeuitzts, would be enough. Oa a division the wards "Act of G-t,d " were retained by 27 votes to 12. Some other amendments, intended to impose upon -shipown.rs responsibility for accident or damage through the neglect of their servants, were proposed, but, as on the previous dav, they met with no success, and the proposed common form, as modified in the course of the proceedings, was finally adopted unanimously. At Thursday's sitting of the Con- ference, papers were read on the commercial growth of Liverpool, and conflict of the marriage laws in various countries, international arbitrati.on, and war indemnities. Resolutions were adopted bearing on some of these subjects. The conference met again yesterday. THE SUN AS FIIEL.—If the Paris correspondent of the Times is not too sanguine, a discovery has just been made likely to be of the utmost importance to the world. This is an apparatus for the concentration and utilisation of solar heat. At a popular fete in the Tuileries Gardens on Sun- day, although the sun was not very brilliant, he saw the apparatus in action. The sun's rays are, it seems, concen- trated in a reflector, which, moving at the same rate as the sun, heats a vertical boiler and sets a steam-engine at work. On Sunday a printing machine was thus set in motion, and several thousand copies of a sPecimen newspaper were printed off for the amusement of the spectators. What chiefly struck the Times correspondent was the adaptability of the process for military purposes. Under our northern skies it could not, of course, be always depended on; but in a land of uninterrupted sunshine, such as India or Egypt, it would be of inestimable value. A portable apparatus, easily carried on a man's back, might, we are assured, have its boiler heated by the solar rays in thirty or forty minutes, and could boil two and a half quarts an hour, or four gal- lons a day, thus supplying the culinary needs of six or eight men. What fuel does in common use the caloric action of the sun does here. The advantages for military purposes are the cardinal consideration of the correspondent, who suggests that for once red tape should be disregarded, and a competent commission be at once sent over to Paris to examine and report. But we shall be surprised if the in- vention, admitted to be at present only imperfect, will not hereafter be of avail in other and more surprising ways than in cooking the food of our soldiers in India or Egypt. The iaea of utilising the solar rays has suggested itself for ages, and, as we are reminded, savage tribes still exist who use no other mode of combustion. Still, to use the sun, that centre of all power, as fuel, will be an achievement for the future hardly less great than that of Prometheus.
