Sir 11. Macpherson embarked at Bombay on Thursday. MISCELLANEOUS ITEMS. It is reported that British troops have been landed at Ismailia. The water supply at Alexandria is steadily decreasing, and the city has been put on short allowance. The Egyptian troops are in full passession of Port Said, but the place continues outwardly quiet. Twenty Bedouins were arrested on Sunday night at Ramleh while pilfering, and are now in prison. The Suez Colal authorities in Paris have published a protest against the action of England. Three of the marines wounded in Saturday's encounter died on Tuesday morning. All the other wounded are'doing well. The Queen has sent a message to Admiral Seymour in- quiring after the condition of the men wounded in Saturday's encounter. On Tuesday, the Superb shelled the Bedouins who were engaged in constructing earthworks to the south of Ramleb at a distance of 2,200 yards from the sea. The enemy abandoned the works after a few shots had been fired. The losses of the Arabs in the skirmish of Saturday are placed at between 200 and 300 men. The prisoners who were taken state that Arabi's force at Kafrdowar amounts to 16,000 men. It had previously been estimated as high as 50,000. All accounts agree- in stating that Arabi is rapidly in- creasing his strength between Alexandria and Kafrciowar, but there not much prob`ability of an attack being made until the arrival of the Commander-in-Chief and the numer- ous regiments now on the way to Egypt. An Alexandria correspondent telegraphs that the Arabs have reappeared in their old positions, full of military form and precaution, with sentries and vedettes along the line, as of yore. It is said by the prisoners that food is very scarce in the enemy's camp, and that the Bedouins are deserting for want of pay. A letter has been addressed by the Khedive to Ragbeb Pacha expressing the desire that the Egyptian Government
should declare ha readiness to indemnify in an equitable manner coinpatible with the resources of the country all those Neho have siilorsd by the massacres, pillage, and burning of AlixandriA. _ _

Large numbers of middle and lower class Greeks, Italians, and Maltese are arriving at Alex ,ndria daily, the majority of whom have no means of sub-sistence and will find no em- ployment. At least 1,000 arrived on Saturday. Admiral Seymour has requested tke authorities at Malta not to assist in giving passages. The Porte having corns to the conOusion that no aid is , likely to be given by Germany seems disposed to turn to- wards Russia, ad it is stated that steps have been taken to sound the Oz tr. as to whether his help may not be purchased. Our (Daily 21-eies-, correspondent says there can be-no doubt that the co-operation of the Turkish troops in restoring order in Egypt will be highly dangerous unless merely nominal er under European guidance. A European °Oda( who bat arrived from Cairo reports that all was quiet when he left. Great anxiety was, however,- felt among the Europeans. The respectable natives believed that if Arabi were beatew and retreat,d on Cairo, all the European Houses would be' fired, an& thlt much native pro- perty would aTho suffer. The clerks at the various Minis- tries attended regularly, and the SuMinisters were at their posts. Two great councils bad been held—one on the 17th aad one on the 23th July. At the later it was resolved , that all the Khedive's orders should he considered null and void.

Alexandria, a correspondent says, is rapidly resuming its business aspect. Already many of the streets are cleared of rubbish; and many tottering houses have been pulled down. There is still some doubts as to the water supply, but food is plentiful; the shops are re-opening, and confidence is nearly re-es'ablished. The great square looks like some country fair, with its crowd of wooden huts, run up as temporary places of business, and carria,es and donkeys are plying for hire as noisily as if nothing had happened. A ,special correspondent in Alexandria telegraphs that there was much excitement there on Tueaday, in conse- quence of the strong reinforcements which had been seen to- arrive at the enemy's advanced line. The report that he would attack us at Rimleh was again circulated, and the foreign merchants were half inclined to take refuge on board ship in the harbour. The correspondent went out to our lines, but instead of witnessing an attack upon them, found the enemy working in swarms to entrench the sandy ridge where he resisted us on Saturday. The Admiralty have given instructiens ordering her Majesty's Indian troopship Crocodile to be ready • for cona- mission on the Ist proximo, and adding that the work of , the Indian reliefs for the season 1852-83 will be borne en- tirely by the troopships Crocodile and Seraphis, the remain- ing three usually engaged in the service, vile, the Malabar, Jumna, and Euphrates, being at present too busily engaged in transporting troops for active service in Egypt to be spared for the regular trooping service. A summary of the forces now or shortly to be on their way to Egypt shows that the total strength of the "Army of Egypt" sent from England, exclusive of seamen and marines, is 15,239 officers and men. For this farce 5,741 horses have been shipped from England, and others, toeether with mules' will be forwarded to Egypt from abroad. To this force the Indian contingent must be aided, numbering in all about 10,000 men. To comply with the requisitions ' of the War Office, 43 transports have been chartered to con- vey 740 officers, 54 warrant officers, 14,445, noncom- missioned officers and men, and 5,741 horses. The Cavalry unmher 15 squadrons, the Artillery eight batteries, the Infantry ten battalions, the Royal Engineers four companies, one pontoon train, one telegraph troop, one field park, the Commissariat and Transport ten companies, bearer com- panies four, and field hospitals ten, besides General Divis- ional, Brigade, and Regimental Staffs. The Army and .Navy Gazette is greatly concerned as to what may happen to the Duke of Teck, who sailed from the Mersey on Saturday with the members of Sir Garnet Wolseley's staff. Our con- temporary "yields to no one in its devotion to the Throne," but it protests against tLis "senseless excursion " on the part of his Serene Highness, apparently from the fear that the most serious results may follow, " not to individuals only, but also to the expedition with which the Duke of Teck will he associated."
PROCLAMATION BY THE KHEDIVE AGAINST ARABI.

The Khedive has issued a proclamation declaring Arabi and his followers rebels. Arabi is said to have " committed odious acts prejudicial to country and population—acts which are viewed with horror by the powers, and which have induced them to consider the country and inhabitants as savages." He is accused of the massacres and pillage of the 11th June, and of being the cause of the destruction of Alexandria. "Ills insolence and his calumnies have become notorious," and he is consequently declaied a rebel, and every man who follows him and assists in his rebellion will be culpable towards God, and vrill be regarded as much a rebel as Arabi himself. AN EGYPTIAN PROTEST. . The Porte has received from the Central Committee in Cairo a long telegram, of which the following summary is given in a Times telegram :—" By a previous telegraphic despatch we related Cow the English had taken possession of Sucz, and how the Arab population had emigrated. Orders had been given to the commander of the town to retire, lest the English, in view of the strategical importance of the place, should bombard it as they bombarded Alexandria. The English likewise took possession of Ismalia, without paving any attention to the correspondence which had taken place concerning the neutrality of the Canal, and they ,I issued a proclamation enjoining the inhltkants to attend to I their ordinary avocations and obey the Khedive, as being in accord with England. Since that time English war vessels have remained at Suez, Ismailia, and Port Said. English troops have been lanced on the western bank of the Canal, and small boats passing to and fro in the Canal make demonstrations with mitrailleuses and electric lights. Notwithstanding the Sultan is Sovereign of Egypt, the. Khedive has joined the English, and thereby provoked disasters which it will require years to repair. Since the secret designs of England are now apparent, it is the duty of the Imperial Government to protect the general interests of the Empire, while it is our duty to protect the internal interests of Egypt and to ward off the evils of war and oppression which have no parallel in 'history: As they attempt to advance into the country, Rashid Husni-Pasha, „commanding tbc 3rd Division, is instructed to prevent them, and for this purpose he has occupied the necessary strategical position. The Canal has been hitherto regarded as a com- mercial highway, and the Egyptians, considering it to be their duty to respect this belief, made no fortifications on its bank. We are astonished to see that the English act in a way calculated to injure this highway .which they have described as the road to India. As it is the sacred duty of every nation to resist to the uttermost all kinds of foreign aggression, the responsibility for any injury done to the Canal in consequence of any defensive measures being taken Gannet justly fall on the Egyptians."

div.head: BRITISH EIGHTS IN THE SUEZ CANAL.
div.p: BRITISH EIGHTS IN THE SUEZ CANAL.

A correspondent writs to a London evening paper :—ln one of the clauses (No. 10) of the contract between M. de Lesseps and Ismail Pasha, dated February 22ad, 1866, Egypt reserves for herself the right to lake all necessary measures for the protection of the Canal by erecting military posts within the 200 metres of the Canal territory, on both sides. The contract was confirmed by an imperial firman on the 10th of March following, It will thus be seen that the Government of Egypt holds by contract with M. de Lesseps, and under the authority of an imperial fir- man the unrestricted right of preserving the freedom of the Canal. It appears, therefore, plain that the Powers who are now trying to interfere with the Canal are virtually and directly interfering with the status quo ante which it is the object of Her Majesty's Government to restore. When our work for that object is completed, we will then have re-established the legitimate power for the protection of this important waterway. What right, therefore, have the continental Powers under these circumstances to interfere, as they . are now attempting to do, in the matter? It follows from the facts I have men- tioned that the Khedive has an absolute right to authorise one or more of the Powers to protect the Canal, and that neither the Sultan nor anyone else can legally object to such authorisation. If the report, then, is true that His Highness has already given Admiral Seymour carte bla.ache to do this, the meddling of the Powers about the future condition of the Canal appears to your correspondent too barefaced an attempt to upset the status quo, and to escape the attention of Her Majesty's Government, who: may perhaps, when the right time comes, boldly and success- fully meet it ARABI TO BE PROCLAIMED A REBEL.

A Morning Post telegram from Constantinople, Of Wed- nesday's date, says: The Imperial Irade authorising the proclamation by the Porte of Arabi Pasha as a rebel has been issued, and also a second Imperial Icade commanding the despatch of Turkish troops to Egypt, where they will be placed under the orders of the Kiredive.

AN IMPORTANT ARREST. An important arrest was made on Wednesday in the per- son of Hajzi Moussa, one of the Alexan4rian mustafegin, most deeply implicated in the events of the 11th of J une. When arrested he was actu illy doing duty as a policeman. According to the evidence forthcoming, he is alleged to have Laken an important put in plundering, to have robbed many women, and to have murdered the liavass of the French Contulate.

THE WATER AT ALEXANDRLk. An analysis of the water by M. Ludvig, chemist, states that sample I, before filtering, 'was very turbid, and after standing one hour formed a deposit ol brown, earthy matter, 165 grains per gallon. The water had a disagreeable smell and taste, and turned red testpap3r blue. It contained car- bonate of ammonia, resulting from putrid fermentation of organic matter. One gallon of water contained 101 grains of organic matter and 21.8 grains of mineral salts, chiefly carbonate of lime and chloride of soaium. Sample 2, after passing through filter beds, was only slightly turbid, formed hardly any deposit, and was otherwise unchanged. THE ENEMY IN WANT OF COAL. The Arabs are still kusy strengthening their earthworks about the village of Sheik Ibrahim Pasha. They are still said to be much distressed for food in the camp at Kafr lldwar; but this is not very probable, as all the resources of Egypt are open behind them.. One thing which the enemy i Cannot get is coal, and he s In more danger of running out of this necessary article than the English are of running out of vr :ter at Alexandria. The Arabs cannot continue to run train .1 to Cairo very much longer.

The Press Association learns that no data has yet been definately fixed for the visit of Her Majesty to Drumlanrig Castle, the Nithsdale residence of the Duke of Buccleuc?, but extensive preparations are in progress at that place m anticipation of the event.

1 RUNCORN Bunten BOARD. —The vice-chairman, Mr. Caleburn, occupied the chair at the monthly meeting held on Wednesday, and there were present Messrs. Mellor, Little, and Salkeld (secretary.) The secret rry reported that the interments to July 25th were 100, corresponding Period last year 91; increase nine. The fees received to the same date amounted to £92 is. 81., corresponding period last year £B5 Is. 4d.; increase£7 Os. 4d. nil was all the business. CHARGE OF WOUNDING AT WIDNES.—An Irishman named Patrick Lynch, was on Wednesday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, charged with wounding his sister, Ellen White, whom he lived with at 14, Catherine-street. A Constible stated that about a quarter to nine on Saturday night the prosecrutrix called him into her house at 14, Catherine- street. When he got in he found that she was bleeding freely from a wound on the top of her head which she alleged had been inflicted with a piece of iron by the prisoner. The constable afterwards found the piece of iron—which was produced—in the coal hole, besmeared with blood. The woman also stated that her arm was broken, it being swollen considerably. Ihe prisoner was in the house at the time, an) was at once taken into custody. Inspector Barker said that the prosecutrix would not appear, and he applied for.a warrant to be issued for her apprehension, which was granted, and the case was remanded for a week. RUNCORN Y. M. C. A. SCIENCE CLASSES --The following are the results of the examinations of these classes by the Science Pepartment, South Kensington, and the City and Guilds of the London Institute held in May last.— Building, construction, and drawing, (elementary stage,) Ist class and Queen's prize, J. M. Frith, Thomas Holmes; 2nd class, R. Birkett, T. Bradshaw, Wm. Cropper, J. Farrell, J. Gandy, Israel Hayes, T. J. Holt, A. Killcross, E. Rhodes, R. Robinson, J. Wilson, H. West.—Mathematics, (Ist stage), Ist class and Queen's prize, W. Jukes; 2nd class, B. Crosby, W. Comes, J. J. Halton.—lnorganic chemistry, (advanced stage), Ist class, Walter Millington. (elementary stage), Ist class and Quben's prize, A. E. Pierpoint ; 2nd class, Samuel Abrams, J. M. Frith, H. A. Hankinsons J. Holford, J. Marton, G. J. Percival, W. Williamson.—Gas manufac- ture, (ordinary stage), let class and sth prize, bronze medal, J. M. Frith.—Alktli manufacture, (ordinary stage), Ist class, E. khodes, T. Jimkin, G. G. Tomlinson.— Mechanical Engineering, (ordinary stage), 2nd class, F. W. Lowe. The prizes for the class work of the session were awarded by the teachers as below :—Building con- structions, Ist, J. M. Frith; 2nd, T B?adshaw ; 3rd, H. West.—Mathematics, Ist, IV. Comes; 2nd, J. Williamson. —lnorganic chemistry, (old students' prize). J. M. Frith. Special prize, A. E. Pierpoint ; Ist, Samuel Abratns ; 2nd, H. A. Hankinson. Over 130 specimens of the drawings of the building construction class were forwarded to South Kensington for examination, on which the department made an extra grant to the teacher Mr. T. Jimkin. The next session of the classes will probably commence early in October next.

SWINE FEVER AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., and W. L. Evans, Patrick Hughes was summoned for having two pigs in his possession affected with swine fever, and- with neglecting to report the same to the police.— Superintendent Barker stated that recently there had been a great deal of swine fever in Widnes, and there had been several cases in which people had neglected to report it to the police, as required by the Contagious Di3eases (Animals) Act of 1878.—Inspector Barnett, inspector under the Act, said that he went to the defendant's house on the 2nd inst and ascertained that two of his pigs had died from swine fever. Defendant informed him that Mr. Dickson, sanitary inspeptor, had ordered them to be remeved to the slaughter house, Widnes. belonging to the Local Board. He went to the slaughter house in company with Mr. Barker and Mr Welsby, a veterinary surgeon. The latter gentleman said he examined the pigs,and found they were affected with swine fever, and gave a certificate for them to be destroyed. Mr. Dickson stated that a neighbour of defendant's informed him of the disease which the pigs had been affected with, and he had them removed to an outbuilding near the market to prevent them getting into the hands of sausage makers.-- The Chairman observed that it was a very extraordinary proceeding en the part of a public official to remove affected pigs to a public neighbourhood, and it seemed to him to be a very obvious way of spreading the disease in the district —Superintendent Barker said there was no more effectual way of spreading the disease.—The Chairman said that he was sure the Local Board would not approve of what the Sanitary Inspector bad done. The Bench did not at all approve of him taking diseased animals through the public streets to public buildings. He then went on to quote the. section of the Act which, says that any person having in his possession, or under his charge, an animal affected with disease shall, as far as practicable, keep that animal separate from ! other animals and shall give notice of the fact of the animal being so affected to the police.--e The chairman, pro- ceeding, said that the act was very clear, and that the Inspector of Nuisances ought to have known the law.—Mr. Dickson said he would know the law in future.—Superin- tendent Barker observed that information given to a con- stable in the street was quite sufficient.—James Collins, Patrick Horan, Robert Kerley, Henry George Seddon, and Mary Helsby were all summoned for a like offence, and after hearing the evidence of Inspector Barnett and Mr. Welsby, veterinary surgeon, the chairmen said that James Collins, Patrick Horan, and Robert Kerley would have to pay a fine of 20s. and costs each. Mrs. Kelley bad acted very improperly, for she carried her pig and buried it simply under six inches of soil, not at all sedicient to prevent the spread of infection The law said it must be buried six feet deep and cavered with quick lime. They would, however, reduce the fine to ss. and costs in the case of Mrs. Ilelsby. They thought Patrick Hughes and H. G. Seddon seemed to have intended to do what was quite right in sendiag infor- mation to the public authorities; but they sent information to the wrong authority. They informed the Inspector of Nuisances, thinking they were doing what was right. It was not so, and those cases Would be a warning to them and others that the Inspector of Nuisances was not the right authority. They ought to have given information to the 'inspector of Police, but as they did give information the Bench were disposed not to inflict a fine provided they, would pay the costs. They had broken the law by not giv- ing information to the police, as the law required them to do. Thera was a great deal of swine fever in the district, and all those who kept swine ought to be careful when their swine benra2 5!: to send word to the pollee at once.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 12, 1882.

HORRIBLE IMMORALITY AT WI:MISS.—Wm. WaltoL was indicted at the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, before Mr. Justice North, for having committed a criminal assault upon Hannah Nixon, on the 18th December, 1881, the complainant being under 12 years of age. Dr. O'Feeley prosecuted: The prisoner had seduced the child when only ten years of age, and had, according to her account, con- tinued evil practices with her ever since. He was found guilty, and sentenced to seven years' penal servitude.

THE LONDON AND NORTH -WESTERN DIVIDEND.— We have received the following circular horn Mr. Stephen Reay, secretary of the London and North-Western Railway Company :—" With a view of making the public aware, a the earliest period practicable, of the dividend likely to be declared by the London and North-Western Railway Corn- Company at the ensuing general meeting, the secretary is authorised to state, that the accounts for the past half-year, though not yet finally audited or approved by the board of directors, show a balance sufficient to admit of a dividend at the rate of 7 per cent. per annum. The dividend for the same period in 1880 was 61 per cent. per annum, and in 18816 i per cent."

ODDFELLOIV'S ANNIVERSARY AT HOUGHTON GREEN.—The anniversary of the Sir Gilbert Greenall Lodge of the Loyal Oddfellow's Friendly Society, was celebrated at the Plough Inn, Houghton Green, on Monday. The members met in the lodgeroom about ten o'clock, and a procession was formed which was headed by. the secretary, Mr. Joha Ryder, and six members on horseback. The banner of the lodge preceded the band of the 49th L.R.V. (Golborne), which was followed by the members on foot in full regalia. The route was by Middleton, calling at Mr. James Hattons, Southworth, the Horse Shoe, Joiner's Arms, and General Elliott Inns, Croft, afterwards past the church to the New and Old Noggin Inns, Culcheth, by Risley where a call was made at the Farmer's Arms Inn, Fearnhead, a return being then made to the lodge. After an excellent dinner had been served and disposed off, the band played for dancing, proceedings coming to a conclusion about half-past nine o'clock.

LEADING "THE LIPP. OF A DOG" AT NOETON.—On Monday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr. Wm. Bankes and Mr. Henry Reynolds, Thomas Nixon Roscoe, a young man, 19 years of age, was charged with assaulting his mother, Charlotte Roscoe, on the 29th ult.—He pleaded guilty.—The complainant said the defendant livea with her at Norton, and on the date named he struck her on the breast with his fist, and knocked her to the ground. He then dragged her about the house and kicked her.-1n defence, the defendant stated his mother was drunk, and with a knife in her hand tkreatened to cut his threat. During the past week she had seized articles in the house. He led the life of a dog with her.—Complainant admitted shehad a " little drink."—Mr. Bankes rematked that the great provocation the defendant had received did not justify him in assaulting his mother in the way he had, but taking all the circumstances into cansideratien, the Bench would deal leniently with him and fine him 10s, and 10s. 6! cos.

Goss ASSAULT AT RUNCollll.—Margant Wilelam, a young woman, was brought up at Runcorn Police Court on Monday, on a charge of unlawfully and maliciously Wounding Ann Swan, who lives in Grinlrod-square, Run- corn. The charge was ulti.nately reduced to on of common assault. From the evidence of the prosecutor, it appeared that her husband is a man of colour, and the prisoner win lived in the same street, was in the habit of making use of this fact to annoy her. About midnight on Saturday the prosecutrix Was "sitting at her own door," when the prisoner went to her and callal her bad names. Afterwards she struck her on the forehead, and seizing her hair, pulled her to the ground and knocked her head upon the pavement. She also received a wound on the thigh, but she was unable to say whether it was made by an instrument or by a kick. Cor- roborative evidence was given by Mts. E. Webb, and Dr. McDougall, who had examined the prosecutrix, informed the Bet ch that the would was not at all dangerous. It had, however, not been caused by a kick, but by some sharp in strurnent.—The 13,uch characterised the assault as a gross one, and fined the prisoner 10s. aud costs, or in default 14 days' bard labour.

ROBBERY 1,201 i THE PERSON AT WIDNES.—On Wed- nesday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, a young female named Ellen Sullivan, aged 10, was charged with having, on the sth inst., stolen Loin a basket in charge of a little girl named Margaret Quinn, aged 10 years, one sovereiun and two half-crowns, the monies of John Fallon, of 103, Midwood-street. John Fallen was the first witness called, and he said the girl Margaret Quinn lived with him, and she came to the alkali works about two o'clock on Saturday afternoon with his dinner. When he had finished his din- ner he gave the girl a sovereign and two half-crowns to give to his wife. He wrapped the money up in a cloth and pat it into the basket, and the girl went on her way. Mir- garet Quinn stated that as she was going home, in company with another girl named Catherine Loftus, she met the pri- soner in Aune-street. Sullivan asked to be allowed to carry the basket, which Quinn allowed her to do. Prisoner carried it as far as the King's Arms, in Anne-street West, when she gave the basket back again to Quinn, but the cloth and money were gone. The prisoner then went into the King's Arms, but when Quinn went to look for heroshe could not find her. Subsequently witness gave information te the police, which resulted in the prisoner being arrested about an hour afterwards. On being seirched no money was found upon her. The girl attleiine Loftus gave confirma- tory evidence. The prisoner erongly urged her innocence of the theft, but the Bench oansidered the case proved, and sent her to gaol for two mouths with hard labour.

A:VIOLENT CrrAnecrEu AT SIITTON.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Messrs. Wm. Bankes and Hy. Reynolds, a young man named Abram Bough, was brought up under a warrant charged with assaulting P.C. Davies, of Frodsham. The Prisoner lives at Sutton, and on the 22nd ult, the constable went to his house to serve a commitment warrant upon him, in default of paying a tine for drunkenness. He was informed that if he did not pay the money he would be conveyed to Knutsford gaol, and tie then deliberately struck the constable in the face. A struggle on the ground ensued, and Davies eventually succeeded in getting the prisoner outside. About 40 yards from the house the prisoner again assaulted the officer in a violent manner, kicking him on the legs and body, and he was obliged to use his staff. This had a somewhat quietening effect, ad the prisoner walked along the road, but he threatened to smash in the head of the constable with the handctiffs •i which were upon his wrists. The prisoner was drunk at the time, but knew perfectly well what he was doing.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and said he did not know what he was doing at the time.—lnspector Holling- worth said the prisoner wfo one of a gang of notorious bad characters which frequented Frodsham Bridge, and had been previously convicted.—The Bench committed him to gaol for a month with hard labour.

TUE RECENT ROW AT WIDNES.—At the Liverpool I Assizes yesterday week, before Mr. Justice North, Peter Quinn (33), labourer; John Lane (29), watchman; Wm. M'Namara ,23), labourer; and Mary Mannion (23), fustian cutter, were indicted for haying at Widnes, on the 25th Jnne, seriously injured John Norton. Mr. Heywood prose- cuted, and the prisoners were defended by Mr. Cooper, Mr. , Segar, and Er. Commins.--It was Atated that on ty night in question the prosecutor was at the Commercial Inn in Widnes, situated in a district where most of the residents were Irish, and the probability was (Mr. Heywool said) that the question was one of nationality. Norton left the house about eight o'clock in the evening, but returned in a short time. There Was then present a man named John Hannen, who was not in custody. Hannen used abusive language. I and a row being likely to result the landlord got Norton out ' of the house by tl.e back door, He, however, had to come round to pass the front door, and there be met all the pri- soners, who assailed hint, and set iously assaulted him. The wife of the prosecutt,r said there were from twenty-five to thirty persons present when the fracas °courted —lt was stated in defence that the prosecutor was in a combative mood, and was armed with a bar of iron, which he used in a threatening manner, and all that resulted was brought on by himself.—Lane was acquitted, and the other prisoners were found guilty of unlawfully wounding. On Baturday Quinn and M•Namara were each sentenced to three weeks' imprisonment, and Mary Mannion to a month's imprison- ment.

FUNERAL OF A VOLUNTEER AT WIDNES. The remains of James Clunie, whose death was raeorded in our last issue, were committed to the grave on Sunday afternoon at Widnes Parish Church. The deceased, who had snved in the army in India, was a prominent Oraneeman in Widnes, a teacher at the Parish Church Sunday-school, and a member of the. local volunteer corps, and the esteem in which he was held was testified to by the demonstrations at his funeral, which was attended with military honours. It was of a most imposing character. The funeral cortege was formed at the residence of the deceased, and was headed by the Star of Temperance Brass Band, which played the "Dead March " in Saul. A firing party, under the command of Sergeant Coltbrook, came next, followed by the coffin, which was borne on the shoulders of eight volunteers; while on each side walked the scholars of the deceased's Sunday class. They were in charge of Mr. Balmer and Mr. J. Williams. Walking immediately behind were the rela- tives and frlends of the deceased; *then marched a detach- ment of about 60 members of the volunteer corps, under the command of Captain Waring. Following were about 60 scholars from the Waterloo-road Sunday-school, and the members of the young mons' and adult classes. The pro- cession ended with about 40 Orangemen who did not wear their regalia. Hundreds of spectators lined tKe route of the procession along Cholmondeley•street, Irwell-street, and Mersey-road, to the Parish Church, which was crowded to excess, it being computed that about 650 people were pre- sent. The solemn and impressive service was conducted by the vicar, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, and the choir chanted the 901 h Psalm. The usual service at the grave side was also gone threugh, and after a few remarks from the vicar, the firing party discharged three volleys over the grave. Beautiful wreaths given by teachers and friends, and one by Mrs. Wright-Williams, were placed noon the coffin. The numerous spectators dispersed in an orderly and reverent manner at the conclusion of the ceremony. The widow and family of the deceased are left unprovided for, and a movement, in which the Rev. J. Wright-Williams and Mr. W. Crabtree (a manager of the West-bank School) are the prime mover!, ie On foot to raise: 51.1b9cripti!)1g tinar behalf. •

Three houses erected on the side, it is believed when the canal was opened, have been pulled down, and the aspect ef the neighbourhood has been somewhat changed. ROBBERY FRO7i A bwELLING-lIOUSH AT WIDNES.—OH Thursday at the Widnes Police Court, Sarah Devereaux, and Elizabeth Harper, were each charged with stealing 7s. I the money of a labourer named Wrn. Murray, from the dwelling-honee 44, Margaret-street. It appeared that on Wednesday afternoon Mrs. Murray had Occasion to leave i the house for about an hour. Before doing 80 she locked all the doors of the house, and- saw that 7s. in a glass jar on a shelf in the front kitchen was safe. When outside she met the prisoner Devereaux, who inquired where she was , going, and if she had loched the door. Mrs. Murray replied in the affirmative to the last question, and went on her I way. Subsequently Mrs. McKenna, who lives next door to prosecutor, saw Devereammx climb over the prosecutor's back- yard wall, stating she wee in search of a chicken. However, ' I on Mrs. Murray returning home she discovered the back- Yard door and the beck-door of the house had been opened, and the 7s abstracted from the jar. Information of the ! robbery tires given to P.C. McMester, who apprehended in , an entry in Margaret-street, Devereaux who said " Oh sir, don't take me and I will tell yon where we bid it." ehe officer went with her to a water-closet behind the house wheie Harper lived, where in a s nail 'hole in the wall he I found 33. 711. Devereaux alleged that eirerper had hidden it, and the officer brought them both to the Police-station, when they were formally charged. Devereaux replied that Harper went in the house and stole the money, and Harper answered "I never saw no money."—The Bench tined Devereaux 10. s. and costs, and ordered Harper to be dis- charged. .A 'ARMING FIRE AT NORTON PRIORY.—A tire, which caused considerable destruction of property, occurred at Manor Farm, Norton Priory, on Tuesday evening. The I farm is built in the form of a rectangle, and enclosed a sp mcious yard. About half-past nine it was discovered that a fire had broken out in the range of buildings nearest the highway. These consist of shippone. stables, and a barn, which contained a quantity of old hay, end this material, beins. very inflemmable, the fire spread with great rapidity. Messengers were sent to Riancorn, where information of the occurrence was received at hal f-p mot ten. The tire bell was at once rune, and with admirable and praiseworthy celerity the Fire Brigade got out the engine, which, drawn by three powerful horses. arrived at the ecene of the disaster in half an hour after the receipt of the information of the fire. By that time the ti-e hed gained a great hold unon the building, and efforts were immediately niacin to get it under. Water was poured upon the burning mice in great quanti- ties, but the roof at length fell in, and it was not until about three o'clock on Wedneaday rnornine that the dames were extinguished. The labours of the brigade were, however, far from being barren of result. The stable in the block of buildings was saved from injury, but the other portion, with the exception of the onter walls, was completely des- troyed. The adjoining buildings remained intact. Fortu- nately there were neither cattle nor horses in the building, and the olds- produce stored up, we understand, was the old hay previously mentioned. It is supposed that the fire originated in the hay, and this indeed is time most probable explanation of the coeffegration. The damage is stated to be about £350, but it is fully covered by insurance in the Pecenix Company. Thl farm is in the occupation of Sir Richard Brooke, Bert. .inspector Ifelliagsworth and two other officers were on the spot, and meintaiaed order.

RUNCORN MERSEY MISSION TO SEAMEN.—The anniver- sary services in connection with this mission were held in the Public Hall on Sunday last. There were large congrega- tions. Mr. 11. A. Pear,on, of Liverpool, preached a sermon in the afternoon and evening with much acceptance. Mr. W. P. Roberts had been announced to sing several solos in the afternoon but was unable to be present, but he arrived late in the evening, and his performance was greatly enjoyed. The collections amounted to 19s. On -Wednesday the annual excursion excursion to Liverpool took place, and was conducted by Mr. Shaw. with great success. The journey was made by water in the steamer Fairy Queen, which left Dukes Pier about eight o'clock, taking up a few more excursionists at Weston I'oint. Passengers by the trip had several advantages, and (Indira; the day had the pleasure of inspecting the training ship. Indefatigable lying in the sloyne, the White Star Line steamer Germanic, Itatton Garden fire engine station, and the Sailor's Home. The witnessing novel sights thus afforded, combined with the many other attractions which the great seaport possesses, passed the time pleasantly until half past three, when the company adjourned to the Excelsior Dining-rooms, Castle -street, for tea. Afterwards a meeting at which were present a number of missionaries, was held and short addresses were delivered. The return journey was accomplished in safety and in good time, the participators in the popular excursion having thoroughly enjoyed themselves. The fife and drum band in connection with the mission accompanied the trip.

WARRINGTON UNION SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. —The usual monthly meeting of the School Attendance Committee for the Warrington Union was held in the Board-room, in the Workhouse, on Wednesday afternoon The Rev. WARRINGTON ROUGHS AND THE POLICE. Thomas IGarretty and James McKenzie, both mere youths, were i charged at the Police Court, on Monday, with resisting P.C. I Donald NlcLaren whilst engaged in tho. execution of his duty.—P.C. McLaren, it appeared from the rividence, was i ithe previous night on duty shortly after eleven in Winwick- , street. He heard a disturbance going on in George-street, I where it had been noisy for some time past on a Sunday ; night, and on proceeding to the place he found a lot of War- rington" hopefuls" shouting, cursing, and swearing "all over the street." Ile did not know what was the cause of , it, but there had been a row going on oppesite the roadway from about half-past ten that night. When he spoke to ii them they began to shove him abaut, and finally when he ,laid hold of one of them, they knocked him down, kicked him and performed the various other feats of bravery and daring, which lads of their class do when they get a man, especially a peliceman, on the ground. He lost his lamp in the affiir and had not seen it since. The two prisoners distinguished themselves by the able manner in which they kicked the , constable when he was down. When P.C. Taylor Came to i his aid, it was of course, "every man for himself, and the 'bobbies' take the hindmost." The police, however, had marked their "men," and secured ;both the prisoners—as ; being in a measure ringleaders—after a sharp race along : Bewsey-street, just at the top of Frogliall-lane. Both ; prisoners denied all knowledge of the matter, Garretty, an old offender, despite the fact that he was still in his 'teens, acting in a very insolent manner while in the dock. Sem- , tence of one month's imprisonment in Garretty's case, and 14 days in that of McKenzie, was paased. ASSAULT BY A SOLDIER: A COMPLICATED CASE.—At the Warrington Pelle,: Court, on Monday,—the Mayor (Alderman Pickmere) in the chair, Councillor Fairclough ' and Alderman Chandley on the Bencle,—James Peel, a !soldier recently on the reserve forces, was charged with being drunk and crsorderly in Buttermarket-street, on the previous night, and also with assaulting P.C. Evans whilst in the due execution of his duty. In answer to the charge prisoner said he was drunk, and he did not know that Evans was a police constable, while he did not strike him wilfully. P.C. Evans, whose face bore signs of rough usage, said he had been in his house in Buttermarket-street when lie heard a row in the street. He ran out and saw the prisoner fighting with a man whom he had got on the ground. The constable got him off, and P.S. Spinks coming up at that moment they advised the prisoner to go home quietly. Ile ! refused, and became very outrageous aiming a blow at Sergeant Spinks, but instead hitting outrageous, on the mouth, land cutting his lip. They took him in custody, another , police-constable, Shaw, having come up; and at the seal, n i when Evans charged him with the assault, he said " You I will have something worth being charged for," and ! struck Evans a severe blow in the eye.—P.C. Shaw cor- roborated, as did Mr. Brown, assistant rnagiatrates' who stated that he happened to be in the office at the time ! and saw Evans struck.—Prisoner said that the real Cause of the whole aff dr was that he, in company with a friend from 1" the other side of Glasgow," were together a short time be- fore, when a woman, whom he did not know, came up and snatched a handkerchief from his friend's breast pocket, which at the time contained 17s. Peel ran after the woman and was remonstrating with her when some men came IID and engaged in a fight with him, so as to enable the woman to get off. He was engaged with one of these men whet' the policeman came up,—The Chief Constable made a state- ment which went to show that there might be some truth in the prisoner's story, especially as it was corroborated by his , Glasgow friend. *The Mayor, while he expressed strong dis- approbation of the prisoner's conduct, said that under the eireurnstarepa lie would roily be fined 10s. and costs, with the alternative of 14 days imprisonment.

THE WELSH WESLEYAN'S IN WIDNES. GRAND BAZAAR. Followers of the great John Wesley have always been in very considerable strength in Widnee, and the Welsh section of the persuasion have not been bshind, at any time, in influence, if not in numbers. The Welsh Wesleyan cause has existed in Widnes for over a aiarter of a century, in fact ever since the town showed signs of its pre3ent pros- perity. With the exception of the Victoria-road Chapel, it was the first cause in Widnes. About 25 years ago, the first 1 Welsh Wesleyan community was formed in Widnes, and after four or five years of work and worship in a temporary building, a chapel was erected in Cromwell-street, which then had all the signs of ta coming the main thoroughfare of the town, :end on this account was more specially selected by the founders of the church. The frieride, liewever, were disappointed in this, traffic having taken more the line of Victolia-road, thus leaving the chapel in a side street as it were. Owing to this and to the neighbourhood becoming occupied by a chase of people who do not pay mueli respect to buildings either secred or a cider, 00 chanel nom very inconveniently situated, while in allition is a very dilapidated appearance. After duly considering the subject, a decision was arrived at about two years ago that the time had come when a new chap?l, and one more conveniently situated, was in Urgent request, and immediate rMeasuees were talon to procure hue v;.l-v im- portant wherewithal. A number of the leading manufacturers promised their help, and concerts were given and lectures delivered, with the ()hied of aiding in the movement. It was also decided to hold a bazaar, and the ladies of the congregation set their hands to the work of • preparing those fancy articles whichavhile forming the staple goods at all bazaars, seem to be in such constant demand. The latter effort culminated in the announcement of a grand " Weis bazaar" to be held in the Volunteer Hall. The congregation is composed, to a large extent of the poorer classes of the poorer classes, and as the chapel is expected to cost about £l,OOO a bazaar formed as usual the readiest means of raising the money. On Monday afternoon the bazaar was opened in the Volun- teer Hell, which had been metamorphosed throughout by the bazar committee. Its usual lack-of-paint appearance be- came instead one of varied and bright colouring, from the tints of the banners which draped the walls to the warm hues of the articles on the well-filled stalls. Four stalls occupied the body of the hall, three of which had side while to the right of the entrance was an enclosure containing the museum of curiosities and scientific iustru- menta which no bazaar is now complete Without. At the far end of the ball a platform was enclosed, with a frontage strongly recalling pantomime transformations, and set out as a luncheon buffet. As might ho expected, special promi- nence was given to all matters appertaining to the land of the Cvnary. A unique feature, even in these days of " Fancie Fayres," German towns, and other artistic developements of the bazaar idea, was the appearance of the stall holders in full national costume, high crowned hat • enclusive. Not a few of the fair amateurs 'at stall keeping had a right as teal daughters of Wales to the quaint old dress and we are sure that many of our readers, who went to the :bazaar, would be made aware how difficult it was to say "nay " when wooed to buy by a fair dame whose speech still bore "the accents‘f the mountain tongue." The etalls were all got up in a ver- attractive manner. One of the side stalls was worthy of paiticular attention, it censisting almost solely of fancy model work in brass, iron, and wood, made and presented by Mr. Edward Roberts, whore dausliter Mrs. Crawford most fittingly looked mite" the dis- posal of the articles. The Liverpool still, as the lady, Mrs. R. W. Relents, who almost wholly presented it. likes to designate it, was also well got up, end arranged in a capital manner, the display of china, p:caliarly patterned, being much admired.

The opening ceremony was performed on Wednesday by Mr. George Davies, of Liverpool. There was a fair atten- dance, amongst those. present being the Rev. T. Hughes, pastor of the congregation, the Rev. J. Tessevmsn, Mrs. Tesseyman, the Rev. T. Peters., Mr. and Mrs. Benjamin Brown, Mr. and Mrs. R. W. Roberts, Mrs. G. Davies and Miss Davies, of Liverpool, Mr. and Mrs. Peter Davies, Mr. John Jones, of Liverpool, Mrs. Lord, Widnes, Mr. and Mrs. Williams, of Wasston, Mr. and Mrs. O. Stiller. Mr. and Mrs. Giffith Mrs. Morris, of Runcorn, Mr. R. Roberts, of Moore-lane, &c., &c. The Rev. T. lluoirEs, briefly iotroduced Mr. Davies, and cslled on him to open the b iza Mr. GEORGE Davies assured them that he was very proud to have the honour of opening that baz tar. He theught the Weis!' friends in Widnes had really worked hard for years and years and were deserving of every success. He had been in the Liverpool circuit for some 29 years and he remembered that at first there were only two chapels. In Widnes, he understood, that the first place of worship was in a saleroom, kindly lent them by as auctioneer. During the winter and when the weather bccarne cold, the gentleman, who'had procured them the use of the seleroom, invited them to his kitchen and there in any meetings were held. There was a story told of In old min at one of those inset- ings who called out that he felt the gospel coins in at the key-hole—(laughter)—but the meetings were otherwise very earnest. As the worshippers increased a chapel was built, which was the sne at present occupied.* From what he could understand this chapel was in a roughish neighbour- hood, and the friends wanted to get one outside the town a little bit and have it built slightly grander than the present one was. (Hear, hear.) He did not suppose that the old chapel would realize much over the ground rent. sod as th is new one was to cost somewhere about £l,OOO heip was needed. One usually could not help many but in ny cou'd help one, and he was sure that 311 would be done en that occasion to help on the work. ( Appl3us-.) He referred to the progress that the cause was making in Liverpeol.and the differeoce between the chapels which were now belonging to the denomination and those in which it first worshipped. and stated that they were thistly to build a chapel in Liverpool which should cast about £ll,OOO. One gentleman was giving £5„000 himself, and he (the speaker) only wished that there was someone like him in Widnes. (Hear, hear.) He concluded by im- pressing upon those present the value of the sanctuary, and he especially urged the advantages of the attendance at a Sunday school when young. He quoted an old Welsh motto " lob dainty bet) ddim, dnw a digon "—with God, everything; without God, nothing—which he had read on a carriage or panel, and held that its trutli was apparent. He declared the bazaar duly opened. (Applause.) The whole of the troop.; siationed at Chatham under orders for Egypt have now left the garrison. A great amount of activity prevailed in Portsmouth Dockyard yesterday morning, when, in addition to three transports busily engaged in embarking troops, the Malablr, Indian troopship, was cleared of the wives and families of the regiments which proceeded from Malta to Egypt.. The women and childred were deep aci:ed to various parts of the country in Cases where they bad fiends to go to, and the remainder were transferred t) various barracks in the garri- son. Yesterday a i'arliarnalt try return was issued showing that the total agrarian outrages committed in Ireland dui lug July was 231, of which two were murders. During June there were 233 outrages, of which five were mutders. Among the parliamentary papeTs issued yesterd.ly was a list of persons now in prison under the Coercion Act. The total number is 170, of whom 83 are rea-onably suspected of murder. The numbers were 182 in July, 263 in June, 276 in May, 511 in April, 687 iu March, and 512 in February. At Blackburn Polka Court yestercla2., morning, Mary Ann Garnett, milliner and dressmaker, was summoned for em- ploying two assistants beyond the time allowed by the Factory and Workshops Act. Inspector Maitland found the msistants at work at 20 minutes past five on Satnrday week, though they should have ceased wen k at four o'clock. A fine of 10s. and costs was imposed in each case, tlie total bAng £2 53. Mr. Henry George, authar of " ProT4r ss and Poverty," who was re-arrested at Adenry on Thursday, just as he was entering a tram for Galway, was discharged at Nudude, after over ten hour's detention. Mr. George was first brought before Major Lobden, who refused to hear the Case, and then before Mr. Byrne, of Longhrea, who eventually directed his role:age. Sub-Inspector Bell said he arrested the prisoner because of his associating with suspicious characters, and called evidence to prove be was seen in the Old Abbey grave- yard with Mr. Joyns and Father Mcrhilipin, and had entered the shops of three suspects. Mr. Lieorge explained be went to the graveyard to view the ruins, at d to the shops to buy a collar button.
THE E 'IDEMIC AT ACCRINGTON. 22 DEATHS.

No fewer than 22 deaths have occurred from the 4th to the 10th inst., 16 being under eight years of age, most of them being victims to scarlet fever. In three different houses there have been two deaths in each, Mr. Nall, veteri- nary surgeon, Edgar-street, being amongst thosie who have lost two children. The effect of the hot weather of the last few days en the afflicted cannot yet be spoken to.

div.head: ROD FISHING IN THE RIVER DEE.
div.p: ROD FISHING IN THE RIVER DEE.

An immense number of salmon have now gone. into the upper waters, the recent floods having enabled them to clear the obstacles at Coester. The waters are in splendid condi- tion. Many anglers have arrived at Chester, and will fish up stream to Bangor Bridge. The river is low at the present moment. Draft and trammel net fishing in the lower waters has been unsuccessful this week.
EXTRAORDINALY CHARGE AGAINST A PAUPER.

Samuel Morrison, a one-leggid pauper, for some years an inmate of Stoke-on-Trent Workhouse, was charged before the Potteries stitsendia.ry, yesterday, wdh disposing of a new wooden leg, the property of the Board of Guardians. On the 5.11 instant, he left the WorkLousa wearing the wooden leg, which a short time before cost £3. Wien out he sold it for half-a-crown, and returned on crutches. He was sent to gad l for one month with hard lahout. FATAL FALL OVER A PRECIPICE.

On Thursday, at Whitesvell Bottom, Rossendale, an in- gniry was held into the circumstances attending the death of Charles Gill, aged 31, woollen printer, Leeds. Gill, who had recently obtained work at IVhitewell Bittam, went ftr a walk cver the hills on Sunday night. and, being un- acquainted with the lucality, he fell ov,r a precipice, receiving injuries which terminated fatally on Tuesday night. Deceased's wife and children, who were ignorant of the accident, arrived with their fu-niture at Whitewell Bottom a few hours before h 2 died.

_ " ANGLO-SCOTUS " DISCOURSES ON ANTS. a Sir,—ln my last letter I left off at "cats." My reason for • eluding to a second version of the story about the Kilkenny Csts was jest this: Some of my good-natured critics seem ' to think that I am attacking or doubting the origin or derivation of the word "catch," whereas I have merely drawn Z attention to the fact of its (-irruption, or substitution for a 1'" ward of a different meaning, but with a similar sound, each - Similarity of sound being increased when the words "first" and "thatch "or "case " are spoken hurriedly. Now as to els Cat and-its connection with entomology, it is just this: It is well known that cats will at times eat grass, Sec.; and this habit has led to the saying, "As necessary as clover is to cats "—another corruetion, as the words "cats" and 'clover" should be tiansposed, thus: "As necessary, &c., as cats are to clover." The following brief explanation of the correct phrase is from Darwin's "Origin of Species" (will my critics please take note that I, where possible, endeavour to give my authority for any statement I may make?) :—" Red clover is fertilised in this country by humble-bees; field-mice keep down humble-bees by destroy- ing their comb.s and nests ; field-mice in their turn are preyed upon by cats and owls; and so, to a certain extent, the existence of red clover depends upon these carnivorous animals." (Br the way, has any one ever tried a dish of roasted field-mice, the cleanest feeders of the whole sedent race ; or the efficacy of the contents of an owl's eggin making the hair enrl; or the yolk beat up in castor oil to increase the growth of the hair?) Again, surely my critic has not forgotten that to test the so-called intelligence of the bees, ~1 Sir John Lubbock put some in transparent glass bottles, with their honom or closed ends towards the light, and their necks or open ends towards the dirk ; and that they had not the sense to find their way out of their open prison. Again, tn. as to the so- called intelligence and ingenuity of the ant, the same eminen t authority has proved to demonstration that they were incapable of extemporising a bridge, or jumping a cletana,—in fact, of being incapable in a major number of •. instances of shortening dietance or economising labour. In ' Brazil the ants were excommunicated. In the "Nova Fioresta " of Father Manoel Bernardes, it is recorded how the Friars Minors of the province of Sietrade arraigned the ants before the "Tribunal of Divine Providence " tor steal- ing the grain laid up for their daily consumption and undermining the foentation of the convent. Lawyers argued the case pro. and con., and the decision—that a large field •- shoubt be set apart by the monks for the insects, and that the lattsr should vactte the convent and ceaee to annoy the monks—was pronounced on January 17th, 1713. According to Manoel Bernardes, the records are to be found in the Monastery of St. Anthony. The Peruvians also excommuni- cated the ants for destroying a great number of books. In Cornwall the ant is called by the peasantry a muryan, and it is consilered unlucky to destroy them. In fact, in some , parts of tie county it is believed that if you place a piece of tin in a tank of tnuryans at a certain age of the moon it will he turned into silver. So it will be seen that neither the ant nor the bee are perfect or reliable exemplars. And some of the dicta and customs of Solomen's time would not . scan in these 'natter-of-fact days. And although lam a widower I shall object to take Solomon as an exemplar in the matter of wives. In conclusion for the present, I hope my Newton friends will give me credit for haying no desire to unnecessarily interfere with their prejudices or wound their feelings. At some future time, should opportunity or time permit, I may have the pleasure of again communi- • eating with them by means of prirter's ink. But that will depend, as hitherto, upon the courtesy and good feeling of the editor, whom I again thank for the space he has already So kindly accorded me.—l am, sir, k.C:c , ANGLO-SCOTUS.

div.head: OPENING THE PARK ON SUNDAYS.
div.p: OPENING THE PARK ON SUNDAYS.

Sir,—"Attalue," in your last issue of the Examiner, re- commends the opening Bank Park on Sunday mornings. On this question there are two opinions expreesed by thepub- lic, SOFTIe for and some against. If open on Sunday morning, some additional strength would be required to keep order. If the gardener is absent some one must be on the premises in his place, for when glass houses are filled with plants, watering and ventilation must be attended to. " Attains " says "There is no fear of any one running away with the gardens, and I have too much faith in the respectability of the Warrington working classes to believe that they would be guilty of abusing any privilege that may be offered them." I can bear testimony that a large portion of the working class do appreciate the works • of nature, and that they deserve every refined pleasure that can be afforded. There is a great number of Leah this and the middle data who take daily walks through the gardens and some to enjoy what little there is to be seen there. But lam sorry to say there are others who are the very reverse, more particularly on a Sunday afternoon; and though there may be "no fear of any one running away with the gardens," there is scarcely a Sunday but someone takes something away. Some young men take a delight in annoying resprct- able visitors, while females reCeive above their share of insults. And some would play games on the Sunday more 20 than on the week thy. The unruly ones watch the police like a cat, as the grouad is laid out in such a manner that you cannot have your eye far away from where you stand. Though the park is visited by thousands on a Sunday, I am assured many people will not come in through the annoy- ance by the class referred to. List Sunday hut one, in the afternoon, I visited three narks in Salford. I there read one a the rules, which is as follows :—" No person shall on a Sunday use any play ground or play any genie, or play any musical instrument in the park." Special watchmen are numerous, each having a radius allotted to him over which he can see from one peint. Each has a whistle to use if scything is wrong. There are four parks in Salford, and three are well stocked with flowering plants kept in the neatest order. Three are %bent the size of Bank Park ; one. double the area. D-1,425 is allowed to maintain them for the present year, eseiuFive of the museum in Peel Park. Though Bank Park is insignificant compared with those of Salford as well as of many other towns, yet I know the committee wish it to be kept as well as circum- stances will aPow, and everything made comfortable for the respectable portion cf, the people of Warrington. Though there is the drawback I refer to, She privileges such as they ore are very much taken advantage of ; and I have no doubt if the committee are approached in a pro- per manner on way question of improvement they will carefully consider any reasonable suggestion.—Yours truly, E. GREEN.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS.
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS.
FRODSHAM.

CATrLE SALE—Messrs. liarrop and Mosscrop held their usual fortnightly cattle sale at the Auction Mart, on Tues- day, when competition was brisk, and there was a good attendance of buyers. Seven fat beasts were offered, which realised from £l4 to £25 each. There were also 100 sheep and lambs which sold remarkably well. CROSFIELD SUNDAY SCHOOL.—The annual treat to the scholars attending this Sunday school took place on Thurs- day, at Mersey View, and, as on previous occasions, an ex- cellent tea was provided for the children and teachers, and every provision made for their enjoyment. Mr. Barrow's drnm and five band attended by invitation. VOLUNTEER INSPECTION. The annual inspection of volunteers was made on Thursday, at Chester, by General Tyacke. The Frodsham corps mustered 60 men, and were under the command of Lieut.-Cohinel Ashton.

BANS HOLIDAY.—The splendid weather on Monday con- tributed in no small degree to the enjoyment of pleasure- seekers, and Sir John Lubbock's festival appears to have been generally observed, judging from the immense number of excursionists who came to and passed through Frod- sham. The natural attractions of our pleasant rural neigh- bourhood are always sufficient to draw the crowd who have been "long in populous city pent," and for quiet enjoyment it is deservedly popular. The visitors on Monday were more numerous than ever, and seemed to have spent a happy day. We should think that the cottagers who exhibited the notice to supply hot water bad a busy time of it, as it was clearly evident that "the cups that cheer but not inebriate" had been partaken of, the bacchanalian crew being conspicuous by their absence. The Salvation Army Band brought a large contingent, and it is needless to add that they returned home at a respectable hour in the early part of the evening. INDEPENDENT ORDER OF REOHABITES : ANNUAL FES- TIVAL.—The annual festival of the Delight of Frodsham Tent and the Hope of Frodsham Tent (Juveniles) of the above Order was held at Frodsham on Monday, and was very successful. The members paraded the town, to the number of 70, during the afternoon, decorated with the regalia of the Order, some wearing the neat badge of the Blue Ribbon Army. The procession was headed by the Weston brass band, and accompanied by the banner and the official charter, presenting quite an interesting sight, especially when it is borne in mini! that the principle demonstrated was total abstinence fr,tru intoxicating drink. The patrons of the society were waited upon, and we ob- served from the financial report, prepared by Mr. William Lockett, the secretary, and audited by Messrs. Samuel Sharp and William Jones, that the sum of £5 15s. was given by the patrons on the previous festival day. It also appeared that £29 Bs. bad hoer. paid to sick members during the year, and £l2 13s. to the district funeral fund, the total worth of the tent being as under, on the 31st December, 1881, viz.:—Money invested, £l5O ; money in savings' bank, £l7 4s. id.; sick fund with treasurer, £l2 las 3d.; management fund with treasurer, £3 12s. 4P.; total, £lB3 12s. sp., or an increase of £l9 9s. sp. over the previousyear. The tent numbers at the present time 105 members, of whom 70 are adults and 35 juveniles. A public tea was provided in the Primitive Methodist schoolroom, and in the evening a public meetiog was held in the chapel, when excellent addresses were delivered by Mr. Councillor Roper, H.D.R., Mr. Ellis, Mr. E. D. King, agent for the Chester Christian Temperance Society, and Mr. William Lockett, the local secretary. The Vicar, Rev. H. B. Blogg—who is a strong temperance advocate—had promised to take the chair, but in ' his absence Mr. Councillor Roper presided, and in the course of a capital speech dealt with the statistical and financial condition of the Order, from which we gathered that the Order numbers 40,000 members, although it has only been in existence about 50 years. The death rate was suprisingly low, being one in 41, whei eas in other societies the death rate was one la 144.—Mr. Ellis followed, and in a vigorous speech advocated the moral and higher claims of the Order, • while Mr. Ellis in the short time at his disposal showed that he was a fluent speaker, and had a store of anecdotes which, while amusing the audience, showed the bright side of temperance and the fearful evils arising from intemper- ance. The usual vote ot thanks to the speakers brought the m :,eting to a close.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

BANK HOLIDAY—Monday last was one of the few "Bank holidays" of the year, but was not generally observed by the tradesmen of the district. The mills were running, and the only perceptible observance of the holiday was in connection with the post-office, which closed at twelve o'clock, the afternoon delivery being "knocked off." A large number of the local Conservatives, however, paid a visit to Rufford Park, and a short account of the " out " is given elsewhere. THE SERIOUS ACCIDENT IN A COTTON MILL—The young man named Benjamin Roberts, who recently had his fingers severely crushed at the mill of Messrs. S. Brewis and Co., is still sultfe:ing severely. Two of the fingers on his left hand were amputlted at the first joint, and one of the fingers on his right hand was so badly injured that Dr. Worsley recently had to amputate it at the root, as putrefaction had set in. The young man is still being attended by Dr. Worslev.

GOLBOnNn COICSEnVATivES AT RUFFORD PARK.—A num- ber of the Conservatives of Go!borne and district spent a very pleasant and enjoyable day at Raiford Park, the seat of Sir Trevor Hesketh, Bart., on. Monday last. It was arranged some time ago that a Conservative demonstration on a large scale should be held at the place named, and the committee of the local Conservative club decided to have a kind of pic-nic on the occasion. The party, who numbered 68, left Go!borne about quarter to nine, . being conveyed in three waggdnettes and one omnibus belonging to Messrs. Dearden and Middleton, of Leigh. The route lay through Abram, Wigan, Standish, Shevington Moor, Longton, &c., and their destination was reached about one o'clock. The afternoon was spent in various ways, several attending the meetindto bear addresses . from Lord Sandon and others, while many enjoyed themcelves in strolling about the beautiful park. The return journey was commenced about six o'clock. On arriving at St mdisli, the party partook of an excellent tea at the White Dog Inn, it then being about eight o'clock. The journey was again resumed, and Gel- borne was reaclied about ball-past eleven. Fortunately the weather was very fine, and all were well pleasedand satisfied with their day's out.

div.head: LYM M .
div.p: LYM M .

BANK HOLIDAY.—The village presented a very animated appearance on Monday, Bank Holiday, although the day was not kept by the inhabitants in general. A large number of visitors from Warrington, Manchester, and various other places, found their way to the village du:inz the day. Ttip weather was capital, and the different pic-nic parties, &c., had. full opportunity to visit the places of interest in the district.

" SERIOUS ACCIDENT AT LYMM.—On Wednesday morning an accident which very barely escaped proving a fatal one, occurred at Whitbarrow Bridge. It appears that one of Messrs. Greenall's drays was conveying some barrels of beer to Bunce's at the Bridgewater Arms, when suddenly the horse backed against the rails, causing them, together with the wall, to fall into the road. Happily no one was hurt, but a boy on his way home from school, very narrowly escaped injury. If he had been half a minute later the stones and rails would have been upon him. The road was partially blocked for some time, but thanks to Mr. Brazen- dale and his moo, the debris was soon cleared off. „ THE HARVEST IN VIE DISTRICT.—Cutting was com- menced at the beginning of this week in this part of Cheshire in a field belonging to Mr. Plinston. The crop seems to be a good one, despite the fact that oats in the district generally are ripening very irregularly. Farmers do not speak with great confidence of the other cereals, but a fair crop should be obtained if the, present good weather continues.

RIISH-DEARINO AT LYMM.—Just now tymrn is presenting a very animated appearance. The preparations for next week have been carried out with great vigour. All. the available space near the Old Cross is covered with swings, merry-go-rounds, Sic., those already fixed seeming to do good business, although the fpstive week has not yet arrived. On Monday next the Lymm Sunday schools have a trip to Llandudno. Oughtrington and district propose going to Liverpool and New Brighton. Altogether, there is every appearance of there being quite as much in this usually quiet village as in former years. TEMPERANCE MEETING IN THE PAROCHIAL SCHOOLS, LT/431.—A meeting, presided over by the Rector, was held in the Parochial Schotils on Tuesday evening, in connection with the Lymm branch of tte Churc's of England Temper- anco Society. There was a fair. attendance. After songs, recitations, Arc., had been given by the members (chiefly juveniles), the Rector kindly gave a reacting, which seemed to interest the younger portion of the assembly immensely. The singing of a hymn brought the evening's entertainment to a close. Mr. J. Smith, Jun , was kind enough to officiate at the harmonium, doing ample justica to the duty he had undertaken. This meeting was held strictly for juveniles, but at a meeting of the executive committee, held about a week ago, it was resolved to inaugurate an adult branch in Lymm. OVER.

On Friday and Saturday the annual show of the Over and District Floral and Horticultural Society was held at Over. The weather was fine. The show both as to quality and held. quantity was considered superior to any previously

, OVER FLORAL AND HORTIOrLTURAL SOCIETY. —Ttlis year's show, which was of a superior character, was held at Over, on Friday and Saturday last, in a field in Delamere- street. A great many of the neighbouring gentry attenthd, and some of them were exhibitors. The gardeners of Captain Turner and T. Knowles, Esqs , came out especially strong The cottagers had a fine array, and Mr. Errington had a splended exhibition of farm produce. The show of bees excited much interest, especially the transferring from One hive to another. The judges were Mr. Lee, of Tiroperley, and Mr. Toll, of Manchester, and Mr. Gee, of Nantwich, for bees. Mr. Beeton's commodious tents were used, and he and Mr. Chambers provided refreshments. The rifle band gave
Of

to the accident. It appeared that in March last, as the plaintiff's husband was assending the shaft, a stone fell from the roof of the mouthing of an old air•way, and struck the deceased when in the cage, inflicting injuries which resulted in his death. At the coroner's inquest the jury returned a verdict of accidental death, but recommended that the mouthing shou!d be bricked or timbered, and this had since been done. The roof was rock, and one witness admitted that it was not usual to timber it. Mr. M'Connell contended that there was no case for him to answer, as no negligence had been proved. Mr. Wharton maintained that the fact of the defendants having since timbered the roof of the mouth- ing showed previous negligence, for if this had been done before, the accident might not have happened. His Honour ruled that the mere happening of the accident was no proof of negligence, and that the fall of the stone did not neces- sarily arise from want of precaution on the part of the com- pany. He did not think there was any evidence at all of negligence, and gave a verdict for the defendants. WINSFORD. LOCAL GOVERNMENT ENQUIRY. The Winsford Local Board requiring to borrow £7OO for street improvement and sewerage, Major Tulloch held an enquiry at the Local Board Offices, where the members and officers met him. Being satisfied with the representat;ons made he sanctioned the application and early closed the enquiry. The Primitive Methodists of Station-road, Winsford, held their anniversary services on Sunday, Monday, and Tues- day last. The preacher was Mr. Nicholas, from the Potteries, who, being a great favourite at Winsford, drew good congregations on each occasion. ORGAN SERVICES.—The annual services for expenses con- nected with the organ were held in the United Free Methodist Chapel, Winsford, on Sunday last. The choir as usual did their part extremely well, especially in the anthems " Twas glad," "Exalt Him all ye people." "The earth is the Lord's," and "Lard, what is man." Miss Buckly, from "The Academy," presided at the organ. The collections amounted to £6 14s. 9d., and as both organist and choir gave their services, this will form a nice addition to the fund for incidental expenses. The preacher was Mr. Samuel Wright, from Norley, who spoke from "There is no discharge from .this war" and "Prepare to meet your Odd." THE SALT TRADE. The scarcity of ships and other Iminor causes have reduced the export below last year's figures. More works are stopped. The Association is firm and indissolubly attached to its present policy. Higher prices must he the result, anyhow they are for freights, which to America range as follows : To Charleston ss, Baltimore (steam) 8s 6d, New York (steam) 7s 6d, Boston (steam) 7s Gd, St. John's N.B. 45, Halifax Bs, Quebec Os, Montreal (steam) 10s, while to Calcutta it is 163, and to Australia and Melbourne 27s 6d, Sydney the same. To the Baltic ports they run 7s GI to Os, to Pillan and within a few pence the same to Riga, Cronstradt, Copenhagen, and other chief ports. Even across the North Sea to Bruges it is Bs, Harlingen 8s 9d, and so on to the rest. The prices are pretty much as quoted last month, and the amounts exported run for July 1882: To United S'ates 24,106, which is in excess of any July for years back; to British North America 13,553, likewise in excess; to West Indies and South America 2,473, Africa 2200, both 'above last July; but to Calcutta only 21,074, against 47,047 of last year, which ' furnishes the leading and chief decrease, except such as Chittagong, to which nothing was sent in July. But Ran- goon has risen from 834 to 3,822. Melbourne is only 200 tons against 1,118 last year, but Queensland and New Zea- land 580 are in excess. The Baltic ports are somewhat under, being 1,122 against 2,092; and the Russian ports 4,718 against 5,270: North Sea ports 3,931 against 1,941 ; France 125; British Coasts 4,173 against 5,224; Holland is ten tons in excess, and Belgium 626, the two reaching 6,900 tons. The total tonage from the Mersey is 124,203.
