The Canturaraer : Yes. Major CARTwEIGHT : If you carry on in this way it will be like Thompson's will, take more to prove it than it is worth. (Laughter.) Mr. BROWN said he thought the title from 1839 till then was quite sufficient for them. . Major CARTWRIGHT asked what course was open for the Board to adopt. The CHAIRMAN said that was in the hands of the Board. Major Calerwßidarr said they should deal with it at once. The CLERK thought that if they passed a resolution stat- ing that they would be satisfied with the title from 1839 to now it:would settle the matter. Mr. BROWN moved that such title do satisfy the Board. Major CARTWRIGHT seconded, and the motion was carried. THE INCREASE IN WARRINGTON PAUPERISM. Mr. COOPER said that if the Chairman would allow him he should like to ask the Clerk to explain to the Board why and wherefore the unusually high rate presently demanded by the Board was being levied. A great number of rate- payers, particularly out his way, had asked him the question as to why it should be so at this time of the year. . He was afraid that many were putting it down to the building at Padgate, and on that account it would be as well while the tax collector was going his rounds to ask the cause of the high rate. It was better that the public should know why it was being demanded. The CLERK said that he was not aware that Mr. Cooper was going to ask this question but he had prepared in reply to a request a statement on Mr. Cane's tables, more especially because of a statement made at their last meeting. He had - then said that for some reason or other pauperism had grown in this Union, and that he could not give any reason why it should be so. If they had paupers, and they became chargeable there must be the expense of providing for them in whatever institution they might be placed by the Board. The Board had all the cost of maintenance of those people who became chargeable to pay, but to remove any doubt as to the cost of the children he might re-state what he bad said before, that with rent, clothing, food, education, and all the rest necessary to keep it up it would not affect the poor- rate to the extent of id. in the £. The Clerk, proceeding, read the statement he referred to, which was to the effeet that he last week intimated to the Board his regret to find that the number of paupers had, in the year ending Ist January, 1881, increased as compared with the corresponding previous year, and the cost of pauperise) to have increased in the year ending March, 1832, compared with the corres- ponding previous year, and that was the more to be regretted because throughout the country a different result was general. It was also a matter for surprise because Mr. Cane's figures, an additional number of copies of which had been sent to him, were based on the population of 1882, and the increase for this Union compared favourably on exami- nation with other unions. The per centage of pauperism on population throughout Mr. Cane's district had fallen. In Lancashire the fall was from 2 2 to 21. In the previous returns Warrington, though less favourably placed than it used to be, stood at le9 compared with the average for Lancashire 2 2. In the present Warrington rose to 2 2 though the average for Lancashire had fallen to 2.1. In the previousreturn the per centage in 12 Lancashire Unions was below, and in 16 above, in the present return 20 are below, and 8 only are above. As to the cost of relief the total for the county fell from £105,348 for the year ending Lady Day, 1881, to £386.376 in the year ending Lady Day, 1882. The cost in this Union rose from £7,849 to £8,468. The per centage of pauperism in the Preston and Prestwich Unions is 1.1, Lancaster, Haslingden, and the Fylde 13, Barton-upon-Irwell 1.4, Barrow and Aehton-under-Lyne 1.5. Upon comparison to the few Lancashire Unions in which the per centage of pauperism is higher than in the previous year, and which Unions include Barrow and Barton-upon-Irwell, Warrington holds an unfavourable position in the fact of the proportion of increase being hieher than that of any other Union. The subject was one worthy of serious considera- tion. Major CARTWRTGIIT said that the question was how did the Clerk account for the increase; Was it that the paupers were more liberally dealt with, or that pauperism was really on the increase ? He did not think the statement of the Clerk was very satisfactory. Mr. Derbyshire had some time ago brought forward a series of statistics which were very startling. They showed, if he remembered rightly, that Warrington 'e as the 6th highest on the list of the Unions as regards pauperism. They should make inquiries into the matter. There was no doubt that the Board had spent a great deal of money lately, and he was not surprised at the ratepayers grumbling at the heavy calls made upon them. They should get to the bettorn of the matter. Trade was better than it had been for the last twelve months, and they were better off in that respect. If the Clerk could point out where he thought the increase war, he (the speaker) thought it would 'be very beneficial to the Board. Mr. COOPER said he had noticed a great increase in the cost of maintenance in the house, but why it should be so, when all provisions were so touch cheaper than they were ten years ago, he could not underetand. He remembered when it never exceeded 3s. Per person, and provisions were much dearer than now. (Hear, hear.) Mr. BURNS sail he thought it was a question most cer- tainly worth all consideration. He thought, however, that if s me of the gentlemen were to .go through the house they would find that there was nothing wasi-ed. He lead never been in a Workhouse where there were so many old and sickly people—people in fact who had only come there to die. Mr. COOpER: That will account for the high diet. Mr. BURNS : Yes. Then there was the large number of children ei,ho had been deseeed and left in the Workhouse. Major CARTwnreurr said the Barracks were costing them £l,OOO more per year than it ought to have done ever since they were put up. Mr. BROWN: Not that much, .2500 a year would be sufficient. Major CARTWRIGHT: You will find that it is as I say. The CLERK said that they would find that the schools were cheap compared with other places. In Salford they bad cost £B,OOO, and they must look at them as compared with other places. Referring to the statistics mentioned by Major Cartwright he said that they were defective in respedt to Warrington. Mr. DARBYSTHRE said that one reason why the rate was higher that year than before was that the annual value of the property in the Union had been reduced. (Hear, hear.) If this reduction took place on the right hand and the left it would make a great deal of difference. In Havdock alone there was £2,000 taken off. They must naturally raise the rate upon the smaller assessment just in proportion as the assessment was reduced. There was another reason. The school fees did not used to be granted, but now they amounted to between £3OO and £4OO a year of which had to come out of the rate. They also had an excess of paupers in the house, which was full when the children were taken away, and it was now getting filled up with adult paupers. There were 100 more paupers than before, and he should like it to be understood thoroughly that the schools at Pad- gate had nothing to do with the increase in the rate. , Major CARTWRIGHT : I beg your pardon; they have. Mr. DARBysIHRE (continuing said the money had been borrowed, and they had not paid anything from the rates save a trifling interest. He did not see how they ceuld affect the rates at the present time. He hoped that the schools at Padgate when they became inhabited would turn out well and Tulfil the views of those members of the Board of Guardians who desired that they should be built; and that they would ultimately lead to the recdction of rates and the lessening of the number of paupers. (Hear, hear.) Major CARTWRIGHT asked the Clerk how much had been paid back. The CLERK said that the interest and part of the principal had been paid back. Major CARTWEINIIT: Yes. As soon as the money was got they had to begin and pay interest on it, and also to lessen the principal every year. Mr. Burns: That will not be much. Major Carawracarcr: It is still something. Mr. DensaysmßE said he allowed that there had been money paid back. Two instalments he thought been paid. The CLERK: £470. Major CARTWRIGHT : That is nearly £l,OOO a year. The CLERK: You are mixing up two half years, which you should not do. The CHAIRMAN said he was very glad that Mr. Cooper had brought that question before the Board. Ever since those schools were built a general idea had been going through the place to the effect that the schools were the cause of the increase. The Clerk had told them, however, that the increase for the schools did not amount to id. in the A and that indeed was net an ad- vance, but was much about the regular cost. That was

saying very plainly that the schools were not liable for the advance. They must also remember that there were a great many rates collected under the title of. poor rate, such as the county rate, dzc. The CLERK called attention to the fact that they were losing sight of the main object of the discussion, which was why the percentage of payers should be increased in that Union. He held that the whole question lay in the fact that they could not maintain 100 paupers at the cost of 50. Mr. HALL said that they were bound to have an increase in the rates from the fact of those schools being built, what- ever might be said at that Board to the contrary. Mr. BROWN held that the previous Board was a too liberal minded one. ‘(Hear, hear, and laughter.) He took his cue from the people who came before the Board for relief. It had been a very liberal-minded Board, but it had not been a just one. It was all very well to be charitable, but they should be just first. It was not fair to take the money from the working people to give it away in unnecessarily liberal pauper relief. They had also been too liberal in the indoor relief. If there was better control, better management in looking after things, and people round about who would use time and diligence in the matter, many things could be reduced. It was extravagance both outside and inside that i was causing the increase n the rate. He did not think that the Padgate schools would add much to it. (Hear, hear.) He considered that if Padgate was rightly managed it could be, to the greatest extent, self-sustaining. (Hear, hear.) Mr. LONGSHAW was pleased that that subject had been brought up. When the ratepayers considered the rate, he hoped they would remember that the children were driven out of the Workhouse. He alleged, however, that things were not properly looked after, and that there was more liberality than should be. Major CARTWRIGHT said it was very amusing to listen to those gentlemen. He was surprised that if they had seen anything they did not immediately put their hands upon it, and let the committee know. When a gentleman came before them and said there had been reckless extravagance, he should be the first to point it out -- Mr. BROWN (interrupting) : I have already pointed it out. Major CARTWRIGHT : So that there may be a check put upon it. Those gentlemen had the power of visiting that institution, and it was for them to point out where extra extravagance had existed. He as the chairman of that committee, insisted that there had been no extravagance, and he was surprised that if they bad met with it they had not acquainted the Board with it. Do not let the public be gone to with a story that the last Board was a very liberal one. He did not see the difference lAween it and the present one. The CHAIRMAN: I have been told that there is a great' difference between the relief granted outdoors last year and that granted this year. Major CARTWRIGHT : They say so. But were they to make a hard and fast line in the matter? He failed still to see any difference in the Boards. The CHAIRMAN: The outdoor relief is considerably less this time than last year. Mr. WOOLFALL said Mr. Brown was not speaking about the house; it was about the schools. .

Mr. BROWN said that it was the management of the schools be referred to. Mr. LONGSHAW said that outdoor relief was given on a more liberal scale last year. Mr. BURNS was not aware of any extravagance, but thought that if any member of the Board knew anything about.it he should point it out. The CLERK again called attention to the fact that they were losing sight of the subject under discussion. Mr. COOPER hoped that the Board would not lose sight of Mr. Darbyshire's remarks as to the reduction of the assess- ment. The reduction at Haydock was a very great blow to them, especially as they got more paupers from there than from any other district in the Union, with the exception of Warrington. The assessment was reduced, as it was claimed that they were not paving the same rent as formerly. The rent fixed by Mr. Legh was 61. per ton of coal, and when they considered that those enormous collieries, scarcely second to any in the world, were only assessed at £7,000, they must consider that it was very nearly time that they be revalued. •
The CHAIRMAN : That is a question for the Assessment Committee.
Mr. COOPER ssAid'that waq so, but he wished to call the attention of the Board to the fact. He stated that at Burton- wood a small colliery compared to Haydock was assessed at £1,500.

Mr. BROWN : There is something wrong. Either the one is assessed to high or the other too low. The CLERK said that it would not do to assess collieries upon their profits, as often there would be nothing to assess on at all. The assessment of the Haydock collieries was effected by a compromise,. and it was but right that the Board should abide honourably by the award given when that assessment was made.
The CHAIRMAN said that they were still losing sight of the question at issue, and after a few further remarks from several of the members the matter dropped.
THE KYRLE SOCIETY.

The CLERK read some extracts from a letter which be had received from Mr. Thurnham, the bon. secretary of the Kyrle Society, propounding certain enquiries to the Board with reference to some remarks made at its last meeting. Principal of these was the question as to whether the Boird disapproved of the society ia tote, and if it objected to the monthly concert.

Major CARTWRIGHT said that had arisen from a remark ' of a member of the Board, which reflected on the gool of. the society. It was said that the concerts were got up for the benefit of the offldials inside, and that they were very poor. It was more than two years ago since leave W 33 given to hold those concerts, and he did not see why the Board should object to a society like the " Kyrle." The concerts were given to people who never heard anything of the sort from one year's end to the other. They should rather be thank- ful to the society for giving the concerts. The Cw.kritmAN thought that it was as little as the society could do to ask leave to hold their concerts.

The CLERK said that at times Warrington had a great preponderance of paupers because so much attention was shown them. They knew which was the best house to step at as well as commercial travellers could do. The CILUR3INN : Do you think that the music is wi attraction ? (Laughter.) The CLERK: Perhaps 60.
After some further 'remarks the Clerk was instructed to inform Mr. Thurnharn that the Beard was obliged to the society for its attentions, and that it hoped they would be continued.
do TIIE APPOINTMENT OF SURVEYOR.. Mr. Owen's appointment as borough surveyor was formally confirmed by the Board.
THE BUILDING COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the Building Committee, Mr. Thompson, surveyor to the Highway Board, submitted a plan of sup- posed alterations in Green-lane, Padgate, and applied to the Building Committee for a plot of land at the east end of front boundary-line, containing 107 square yatds of land, for the purpose of straightening the road and raising same to a new level. Resolved, that ;I`.lr. J. C. Sutton and Mr. Pier - point be appointed to confer with the surveyor to the Highway Board as to the above application. Resolved, that permission from the Board of Guardians be obtained to offer for s de by auction the crop of oats now growing in the Industrial School land at Padgate. In consuquence of the supply of wate^ in the well at Padgate being found insuffi- cient the committee advise that Mr. Pierpoint see Mr. Tim- mins, of Runcorn, as to the desirableness of boring the well or otherwise, so as to obtain a better supply. The committee arc of opinion that it is desirable the Board should authorise the architect and some members of the Board to wait upon the officials at the Local Government Board offices, White- hall, with a view to getting the plans of stores, warehouses, &c., passed, so as to avoid building operations being thrown into winter. The plans were forwarded to London on the 14th June, and as yet nothing has been heard of them. Mr. DARBYSIIIRE moved that the minutes be passed. He referred to the deputation to London, and explained that the plans had been sent up two months ago, and were not passed yet. If they were not passed at once the best of the weather would be passed for building operations. The minutes were adopted. OFFICIALS AND THEIR HOLIDAYS,

In the minutes of the House Committee was one to the effect that the master had asked for 10 days' lea-7e of absence, and the nurst for 14, which had been granted. In reply to a question, Mr. DARBYSHIRE said they had been for their holidays. The CHAIRMAN: That is the way they do business in this house.

Major CARTWRIGHT : That is the way they do business in the barracks. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN': It is very wrong. Major CARTWRIGHT : Ido not see anything wrong. I never heard of any objection to it. - Mr. HALL: Have the parties asking leave of absence had it or are they to have it ? The CHAIRMAN: They have had it in this case. Mr. HALL: It is quite ridiculous then; and very irregular They take their holidays and then ask the Board to allow them to go. Major CARTWRIGHT: Well, really, really. I gave Mr. Hall for much greater sense than he has. These are the committee minutes and, the committee ask the sanction of the Board to their transactions. They are granted leave of absence With the expectation that the Board would pass their minutes. If you like to get up now and pass a resolation that in future all the Union shall make application to the committee subject to the sanction of the Board it will be right. The proceedinc, as it is is not irregular. The CHAIRMAN: 11" us committee is but carrying out its duties. •

Mr. HALL said that Major C trtwright need not have been surprised at what ho said. If they had already had leave what was the good of bringing it before the Board at all. The CHAIRMAN : You don't require a resolution. It is simply common sense to require people to ask leave. What is the good of asking leave to do a thing after it has been done. (Laughter.) Mr. BROWN, after some discussion had taken plice, made a strong:,' protest against a resolution commenting on the matter being passed. It was an insult to the committee,and if it was passed he would not sit on it again. (Hear, hear.) Major CARTWRIGHT : It is a very trifling matter. Mr. HALL said be had no object in throwing discredit on the people for going away. • He just wished to comment on its irregularity. , Mr. LONGSIIAW said there was no reason for the people to have gone away. He objected especially to Mr. Mackey going away. What if a fire had taken place—(laughter)— or anything happened. Mr. BURNS: There's animus. Mr. HALL did not object in the case of Mr. Mackey. He considered he highly deserved his holidays.

Mr. BenNs said the nurse also deserrt.d hers, for she had bad some very heavy work. Major CARTWRIGHT : I think the eammf;tee is almost in- sulted by this dinussion. The nurse decideth!y deserved her 14 days' holiday, although it is longer than usual. (flear, hear.)
Some furthur discussion having taken place, Mr. BROWN said they did not want the Board to grant leave of absence. They only wanted the minutes con- firmed.
The minutes were 01'2n: carried. The CHLIRMAN : You are declared not guilty this time, but do not do it again. (Laughter.)

THE SCHOOL COMMITTEE. The minutes of the School Committee stated that Miss Wood's application for .extension of absence from 10 to 14 days was refused, on the ground that 10 days has always been the terms allowed, except in very exceptional cases. The doctor reports only one case of scabies, and all cases now in hospital are fit to be returned to school. Mrs. Wil- liams having been appointed assistant matron at Tendring Union, near Colchester, tendered her resignation as indus- trial trainer. Her resignation was accepted, and a favour- able testimonial was granted as to character. The committee decided that advertis3ments for candidates to supply the vacancy be issued at once. Through the kind invitation of Mr. Prse4er, a slumber of the children attended his concert at the Co-operative Hall yesterday evening; the music of which they seemed to thoroughly enjoy. They were provided with refreshments during the interval by Mrs. Praeger. Mr. BROWN moved the adoption of the minutes. Mr. DARBYSIIIIIE seconded, and the motion was carried.
THE WASHING AGAIN!

The Crmut read a letter, which the 'reporters were not furnished with, as to the washing in the House, which he had prepared for sending to the Local Government Board. Major CARTWRIGHT contended that it was One aided, and did not explain the circumstances of the case properly. A short discussion took place, and Mr. DARBYSISIRE proposed that the letter be forwarded to the Local Government Board. Mr. BROWN seconded, and the motion was carried. This concluded the business of interest, and the Board proceeded to the relief cases.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUAPDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUAPDIANS.

Mr. J. Mclntyre presided at the fortnightly meeting held on Tuesday at Dutton Workhouse. There were present:— The Revs. J. IV. N. Tanner, J. Lookwood, Mes,ns. T. Nor- man, John Highfield, NV. Fisher, J. Weir, W. Jackson, Geo. Whitlow, James Darbyslaire, Henry Lowe, G.S. Haz!ehurst, E. A. Wallington, John Smith, senior, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk.)
MR, LOWE AND THE MASTER: THE RECENT APPOINTMENT.

After the minutes of the last meeting had been read, Mr. LOWE said he thought before an appointment like that of the Master's son to be assistant bookkeeper, the Guardians should have received notice. .
Rev. J. LOCKWOOD : .Was that. necessary.
The CLERK was not aware that it 1,149. The Board simply complied with a suggestion of the Local'Government Board.

Mr. LOWE said it was usual to give notice when anything ISarticular was going on. The appointment only seemed a I trivia: matter, but it would entail an annual expen,liture of £3O. If Jones was unable to perform the duties with- out assistance, he thought it would have been the better plan to give him his pension instead of adding another official to the staff of the house. Let them give 'Mr. Jones his pension, and then he could go and live with his famity where he liked.
Mr. N_onmAN enquired what Mr. Jones's pension would amount to.

The CLERK replied that that 'depended upon the Guardians. Mr. LOWE : Mr. Jones has other perquisites Iy:sides ; but what I complain of is the appointment of a fresh officer without giving the Gru trdians notice. The CIIAIRMAN : Are you going to move a resolution, Mr. Lowe.
The DEPUTY CLERK: The question is whether these minutes are a correct record of what took place at the last meeting.

Mr. EowE : There tire other people who would have ob- jected to the manner in which the appointment has been made had they been here. • The CumnmAx: I don't think this is the proper time. Mr. LOWE : Proper time! We didn't know he was going to be appointed. When is the proper time? NORM&N pointed out-that the proper course would be for Mr. Lowe to move the resolution that the appointment be rescinded. TO* matter was fully discussed at the last meeting. Mr. LOWE : There were no members here to discuss it. The DEPUTY-CLERK: There were twelve Guardians pre- sent.

Mr. Low: If a man is not capable of doing his work, I say let us give him his pension. Mr. Lowe hinted that Mr. Norman had been in favour of such a proceeding. Mr. NORMAN said he would never eat any words he had said or intended to say. He had always said this : that Mr. Jones was feeble; and they were all aware that for the past four years Mr. Jones had suffered very much, and could not perform the work he formerly cou7d. The DEPUTY-CLERK: Only the bookkeeping. Mr. NORMAN went on to say that he considered the appointment of an assistant bookkeeper the best proceeding under the circumstances, for it must be plain to everyone that after Mr. Jones' long and faithful service, the Board could not offer him less than would keep him, should he be compelled to apply for superannuation. The discussion then ceased and the minutes were con- firmed.

div.head: ASYLUM.
div.p: THE ASYLUM.

Mr. T. NORMAN moved that the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner Messrs. Ashton, W. Fisher, Henry Lowe, T. Norman, and the Clerk be appointed a committee to pay the annual visit to the Couaty Lunatic Asylum and report on the condition of the lunatics from the Union.

1%.1r. LOWE proposed that Mr. E. A. Wallington should take his place. , This was agreed tq, and the committee was appointed. The Finance Committee rocommended that accounts amounting to £329 19s. 4d. be paid. ---

div.head: COST OF PAUPERS.
div.p: THE COST OF PAUPERS.

The Clerk placed on the table a statement of pauperism and expenditure for Mr. Dansey's district. Common charges, lunatics in asylums, and vagrants were not in- cluded. The Runcorn Union was stated to cover an area of 40,598 acres, contain a population of 33,960, and had a rate dale value of proper'y of £201.480 up to Lady Day, 1882. The number of paupers relieved Jan. Ist, 1882, was indoor 200, outdoor 634, total 834; an increase of 25 on the previous year. The expenditure for the half-year ended Lady Day, 1882, amounted to £641 for in maintenance, and .£1,609 for out-relief; making a total of £2250, which is a decrease of £lO compared with the sime period the year previous. The amount paid for school fees for non-pauper children during the half-year ended Lady Day, 1882, was £7l.
• -.- This concluded the business of public interest.

div.head: SONS OF TEMPERANCE, RUNCORN.
div.p: SONS OF TEMPERANCE, RUNCORN.
ANNUAL DEMONSTRATION.

The members of the Runcorn Life Boat Crew division of the above order, celebrated its establishment on Sunday and Monday last; and on each day the proceedings passed off with gratifying success. On the former day the members gathered in Devonshire Square, about two o'clock, and after hearing a short address from Mr. Withington (the presiding officer of the division), they proceeded to Bethesda Congre- gational Chapel, which had been kindly lent for the occasion. The Rev. D. t4chofield, of Frodsham, preached an appro- priate sermon to the brethren. In the evening another ser- vice was held in the same edifice, the preacher on this occasion being the Rev. J. D. Thomas. The choir' under the conductorship of Mr. F. Fairhurst, rendered in good style a number of special hymns, and at the conclusion .of the service sang in an excellent manner, the Hallelujah Chorus. Mr. John Ravenscroft presided at the organ. Monday's proceedings commenced at 1-30, when the Members assem- bled in Regent-street schoolroom, with the intention of walk- ing in procession through the main thoroughfares of .the town. The weather was very favourable for the event, and as the day was somewhat of a holiday, the immediate neigh- bourhood was crowded with spectators. Leading the pro- cession, mounted On two fine horses, were Mr. J. 'Withinu,ton and Mr. T. Ileesom, immediately following being the Mill Brow Wesley-an Sunday School Brass Band, while next in order was the handsome two-poled banner of the division. Then came the adult members (numbering I 10), who wore their badges. The juvenile members or cadets, who num- bered 63, held the next position, headed by Weston Sons of Temperance Band, and after these was a symbol of the order in the shape of a ship's boat, manned by a crew of youths in sailor costume, and captained by Mr. Henderson. It was fixed on a lurry, and decocated with ivy leaves and illuminated with temperance texts, and was a most interes- ting of the pageant. Mr. John Jones, who was on horseblck, brought up the rear. At frequent intervals in the ranks of the processionists, flags fluttered in the breeze, and added considerably to the effect of the demonstration. The route taken was over Savages Bridge along Lowlands- road, down Waterloo-road, iShridge, Lord, and Church- streets to Dr, Robinson's, veere selections of music were played by the band. Proceeiling alonr, Halton-road another stoppage was made at the residence or the Rev. Geo. Hack, where the band again discoursed music, afterwards retiring to a field near the Grange, which had been kindly lent by Mr. Charles Hazlehurst. Messrs. Jeffrey, T. Cooke, James Jones, William Faulkner, J. Faulkner, and Abraham Goodier acted as Marshalls. Several hours were pleasantly spent in the field. When returning to the school about five o'clock, the procession gathered in front of the Temperance Hotel, High-street, kept by Mrs. Lees, where the band played a number of pieces of music. Tea was provided in the school- room, and it was very numerously attended, between two and three hundred persons partaking of it. In the evening a public meeting was held in the school- room, which was crowded. Mr. F. Fairhurst occupied the chair, and amongst those present were the Rev. Geo. Hack; Messrsi. James Withington, William Ince, J. W. Boyle, T. lleesom, T. Cooke (grand scribe of the Cheshire district), John Jones, James Bisbrown, Charles Littler, &c.

The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, said he felt somewhat bashful in taking the chair on an occasion like the present. and when his, good friend Mr. Cooke waited upon him and asked him to take that position, he at,once refused; because he was of opinion that a pledged teetotaler could do' it with greater propriety. He did not wish there to be any misunderstanding as to his position that night; he was not a pledged teetotaller, but he took the chair because he had much sympathy with the movement. (Hear, hear.) He , could give his reasons to that meeting why he was not a , pledged teetotaller, but he_deemed it was unnecessary to do so, as he had given them to the satisfaction of Mr. Cooke. Therefore it was not because he had no.sympathy with the temperance cause that he at first refused to take the chair, for he•bad worked in it, and after a little persuasim and with a perfect understanding with Mr. Cooke and he be- lieved the committee, he consented. to fill ;he position. (Apnlause). Mr. J. WITHINGTON said various thoughts passed through his mind that, afternoon whilst they were in proceAsion. He looked around and saw a company of respectably dressed men ; and he thought these men were in the position they were that day through becoming total abstainers. (Hear, hear.) But not only were the men partakers of the blessings resulting from total abstinence, but their families also. (Hear, bear.) He contrasted the happiness and comfort of a sober man's home, with the misery and wretchedness of the drunkard's; and remarked that the majority of those who took part in that day's demonstration were followers of the Lord Jesus Christ. (Hear, hear.) He then gave some facts with regard to the society, which was one of the largest in Cheshire. In their division they had about 160 or. 170 members ; and he was proud of the number. (Hear, hear.) Those persons who joked their society had many advan- tages over those who were members at a society held at a publichouse. In the first place, by joining the Sons of Temperance they were in a great measure free from the temptations to which others were exposed by plying their contributions at a publichouse. He knew Christian men, who belonged to societies held at publichouses, who scrupled at taking their own contributions to their lodge—were in fact ashamed to go, bz,cause they considered it not a right and proper place for them to frequent. And what did they do? Ashamed to go themselves they send, perhaps, their children or wives, forgetting that they were exposing them to the temptations, and causing them to witness sights and scenes of a disgraceful nature. (Hear, hear.) If there were any persons present who scrupled at taking their contribu- tions to the publichouse, he urged them to join the Sons of Temperance. (Applause.) The contribution was 6d. per week. The payments were 10s. per week in sickness, and £l2 at death ' • while on the death of his wife a member would receive £lO, and on the death of his child V.. The scale was about to be altered, and he trusted when it was made public, they would have scores crowding into' their divisions and becoming sober men. There was also a Cadet Section for the boys of members, the entrance fee for which was is. and the contribution 2d. per week. In case of sick- ness they received 3s. per week, and £3 at death. He con- cluded by making a stirring appeal on behalf of temperance. _ _ _ _ _

Ttc Ifev. GEO:HACK then .aildressed the meeting,-observ- that he always felt a delight in temperance work, for, in one sense, it was proclaiming the Gosptl—it was proclaiming liberty to those who were enslaved. He remarked on the imposing demonstration held that afternoon, and related several apposite and interesting incidents. Mr. CHAS. LirrcEn proposed a vote of thanks to the chair- man, speakers, the tea makers, and to all who had contri- buted tl that day's entertainment; also to the committee of Bethesda Chapel. Mr. J. INcF, seconded, and Mr. D. BISBROWN supported the resolution which was carried with acclamation.

During the evening the Mill Brow Wesleyan Sunday School band played several selections in good style. Miss Booth contributed a song, which was greatly appreciated ; Mr. T. Faulkner, the recitation "Bashful man"; Mr. J. W. Boyle, the recitation "The labourer's evening song." A trio was excellently sung by Miss Booth, Mr. Beswick, and Master Yates, and they received an encore.

div.head: SINGULAR AFFAIR IN A WARRINGTON TRAIN. AN ALLEGED IMITATOR OF LEFROY.
div.p: SINGULAR AFFAIR IN A WARRING- TON TRAIN. AN ALLEGED IMITATOR OF LEFROY.

On Saturday night the railway officials at Bank Quay Station, Warrington, were informed by a gentleman, who jave his name as Thomas Davies, Foundry-lane, Warring- ton, and presented his business card, which was to the same effect, of a somewhat exciting occurrence which had taken place in a train running between Widnes and Warrimtton. He travelled from Widnes by the 9-20 train on the London and North-Western Railway to Warrington, and stated that soon after leaving Widnes statfon a man opened the carriage door, and, stepping into the compartment, struck the lamp a violent blow, which shattered it, and pushed it out of the roof, leaving the compartment in darkness. The intruder then commenced a violent attack upon Mr. Davies, as if the object of his proceedings was that of robbery, and a struggle took place, which lasted some minutes. During the struggle Mr. Davies alleged he obtained the upper hand of his antagonist, and threw him through the carriage window on to the six foot way. " ANGLO-SCOTUS" -AND lIIS

We can assure Anglo-Scotus that his letters to the Examiner never fail to interest and amuse us. He evidently 11.4 s the happy faculty of telling a good story pleasantly and with what used to be called a moral, when we read igiop's Fables (or what passed by that name), and his latest savours very much of one of tbose Folk Lore tales. Whether original or not it makes us laugh, and that is said to be as good as physic for the melancholy or misanthropic. We co: t drily shall not get across if we can possibly avoid it, and so far the exchange has only been " Tokay "- for " Yam," or a" Rowland " for an " Oliver." We do sincerely hope and trust some day to meet " Anglo-Scotus " in the flesh, and enjoy the " calinna of peace," whether with mild tobacco or not, for unfortunately for us, or as some may think fortunately, we do not often smoke, and when we do we feel quite obfuscated and squeamish, so it will have to be a very mild cigarette, not but what we enjoy the emetic when not too, too strong. Far be it from us to abuse any habit or proclivity of others, as many do, denouncing all • such habits as filthy, &c., &c., for our own 'paternal " was an inveterate smoker, and often gave us a benefit till he could smoke no longer, and, mark the irony of excess, had to have medicated tobacco prescribed at last, Our first essay in smoking WaS disastrous for an elder brother intro- duced us to a very, very ill-flavoured, ill-flavoured " cutty," which effectually cut short our career as a smoker for ever. Perhaps " Anglo-Scotus will not credit it, but we once met a man who smoked all day and night, or, to he exact, from nine in the morning till ten at night without intermission. Now he will be ready to make an exclama- tion, bat we vouch for the fact, as we were cooped up with him in a railway carriage on a long journey. He had cigar cases in every coat be had with him, and was never at a loss for a cigar, and often apologised for his seeming slavery to tobacco, and so we left him smoking. He bad also a bottle of rye spirits, which he tried to persuade us was quite innocent, but after making some slight inroad upon his store he began to look a little fishy about the eyes, but he said that was the effect of the tobacco; so it might have been, or perhaps a little of both. Returning one day from the Blue Alsatian Nleuntains, we arrived in a certain large city, and incau- tiously took up our abode in a hotel at a very early hour, and was about to retire to rest, when on turning • down the bed clothes we beheld some dozen of the blood-thirsty tribe ' mentioned by " Auglo-Scotus," which decided us to sleep on a sofa, but this too was seamed with the aforesaid cimex, which finally determined us to sleep on the floor, but a glance at that showed myriads, so we finally took to flight to the next and biggest hotel, an experience almost equal to that of " Anglo Scotus," but we cannot hope to vie with him in story-telling, and we look forward with interest to his story of the cat and the humble bee, whether original or select.
CKING BATHING ACCIDENT IN THE CANAL AT EARLEiTOWN.

The report that a man had been drowned in the canal created the utmost excitement and commotion in Earlestown on Tuesday evening. The rumour gained credence just as the works were stopping for the day, about half-past five, and iri a few minutes the bare fact was known almost all over the town. Hundreds of persons made their way to the point at which it was said the man had met with his death, and it was found that the statemsnt was but too true. The canal, which runs along the south or bottom side of the Common and thence along the similar side of the Viaduct Works, is known as the Sankey and St. Helens Canal, and belongs to the London and North-Western Baal Nay Com- pany. It has been ascertained that the name of the un- fortunate man who was drowned therein was John Melntyre,37 years of-age, that he was a glass maker and lodged at the Flying Dutchman Inn, St. Helens. Owing to his ill-health lie had been out of work for some time past, and on Tuesday lso came over to Earlestown and Newton on a visit. In the forenoon he met a companion named JAI). Coyle, another glass maker and also residing at St. Helens, ' and together they visited several public houses an partook of clink pretty freely. The deceased is stated to have prevailed upon Coyle to walk back to St. Helens along the canal bank, but when passing.by the common,the d2ceased undressed him- self and said he was going to bathe in a pool of water there. Coyle prevented him from going in and the man re-dressed himself. They called at the Ship Inn, near to the lock and bridge across the canal, and were there served with some mere drink. On leaving the latter place Mclntyre told his companion that he intended having a swim in the " cut," but Coyle attempted to prevent him from so doing, saying that he,conld not swim owing to the drink he had bad. The deceased, however, who is said to have been a powerful and noted swimmer, persisted in entering the water, and after pulling h;s clothes off several times he did. so. Coyle again attempted to prevent him, but the deceased sail he . would have his own way, and accordingly jumped into the canal. He swam_ on his back, side, and breast for about three minutes, when he commenced to struggle, and sang beneath the water. Seeing the precarious position of his companion Coyle, with all his clothes and clogs on, jumped into the water alter him, and made a grab at his body. but could not catch it. The body did not again return to the top, and a lad named Shallcross, who witnessed the occurrence, ran to the Earlestown police station, and gave information that a man had been drowned. The news quickly Tread and in a short time croavds of people gathered ! on the banks of the canal. The water was dragged with hooks and rakes, and several men entered the water and dived after the body. This was continued for About three and a half hours without any avail. Shortly before nine o'clock, a collier named James Andrews, residing at Collin's- , . green, touched the body with his foot and it was afterwArds brought to the side, and immediately conveyed to the Ship Inn, occupied by Mrs. Jane Hayes. It was found that the • head had been slightly injured with one of the hooks. It is ' stated that the man, who appears to be a powerfully built one leaves a wife and three children, who are at present living at Glasgow. Up to a few years ago he was a soldier, and had served in that famous regiment the " Black Watch." An inquest on the body was held .on Thursday, before Mr. C. E. Driffield, coroner, at the Ship Inn. Several witnesses ' were called, and their evidence bore out the facts contained in the narrative given above. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased met with his death accidentaßy through bathing in the canal while under the influence of drink. Several of the jurors afterwards expressed the opinion that there ought to be better hooks and rakes kept at hand in case of another similar accident, which, it was ! said, might occur at any time.

STEALING A PIECE OF GLASS AT ST. HEL7S . —On Thursday at the St. Helens Police Court, a boy named Thompson was brought up charged with baying stolen from Messrs. Pilkington's glass works a piece of glass, valued at appeared that Sergeant Sherriff had seen the prisoner that morning near Ravenhead. He was on the canal bank, and the officer noticed something under his jacket and told him to come down or he would bring him. The lad came towards him, but on the way be dropped the piece of glass produced, which he said had been given him bv the fore- man. Sherriff went to the foreman, who said he bad not given it to him. The priscavr then admitted that be had told a story, and said he had found it on the railway. Super- intendent Johnston asked for a remand until Monday, width was granted.
