div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The usuil monthly meeting of Widnes Local Board was held in the Board offices on Tuesday afternoon. There were present Messrs. Gossige (in the chair), S. Webster, Dr. Booth, Sadler, Kershaw, J. Midwood, D. Wright, T. bland- ley, F. H. Pank burst, Shuttloworth, Allen (clerk), Higgicson (surveyor), Roberts (engineer), and Dickson (inspector).
THE MINUTES. The minutes of the last meeting of the Board were passed.

THE NEVI BYE-LAWS Mr. KERSHIW suggested that, as the chairman of the committee was absent, the consideration of the new bye-laws should be deferred for one month. Mr. HANDLEY seconded, and the motion was carried. cuII3II7NICATIONS.

A. number of circulars from the Local Government Board was laid on the table, the Clerk explaining that they referred to slaughter-houses, Sic. THE BOARD AND THE LIVERPOOL WATER SCHEME. The CLERK read the following communication which had been received from the clerk to the Liverpool Corporation: Town Clerk's Office, Dale-street, Liverpool, 25th July, 1832. —ear sir,—ln the agreemert between yor Local Board and the Corporation of Liverpool for a supply of water from the Vyrawy aqueduct, It is provided "that the Corporation shall within three yeas. 4 app.y for and use the:r best endeavours to obtain, and the Local Board shall consent to, an Act of Parliament ti ratify and confirm this agreement." lam directed by the water commlttee to communicate with you with reference to t'ais provision, and to ask whether your Board avi I have any objection to extend the period for the application to Parliament to five years. As it will not be practical to supply any water unier the agreerreat at all events before the Ist July, 1885, it may be more convenient for the Corporation to postpone the application in order that they 'nay include in it matters in which they may require furtker provisions in clunenion with their waterworks, and under these circumstances the committee hope your clients will make no objection. I shill be glad to hear from you at your earliest conveni.enc and to discuss the matter with you if you consider it necessary to see me.—Yours truly, J. RATNnIi.

_ The CHAIRMAN said he thought they had better refer that to the Gas and Water Committee as knowing more about it than the Board in general, and especially so as there was no absolute hurry about the matter. They would see into it And say whether the revest could be acceded to. He saw ao objecllon to it himself, but still it would be putting it through the usual course. Mr. MIDWOOD said he should like to know what sizree- snent there was between the Liverpool Corporation and the Local Board. If sent to the committee he should not know anything about it. The CHAIRMAN said that the agreement was made when the Board opposed the Liverpool Water Bill in Parliament. It was agreed that the Board should have a supply of water at a fixed price as a compensation for the works under the Act pasaing through the district the Board commanded as the suppliers of water. He was not quite clear as to what was the exact price, but thought it was 6d. per thousand gallons. They as a Board, when they opposed the scheme, simply did so in a friendly manner, so as to enable them to get water, if they should require it, at a cheaper rate. He thought that was the position of the Board at present with the Liverpool Corporation. They were not alone in that, because Runcorn and Warrington had also made special agreements. Mr. MIDWOOD said that was what he wanted to know. Still he should like to know if they had signed an agreement with the Corporation, and, if so, what alteration was required to be made. The Cleetamax said that they had a signed agreement. Mr. HANDLEY explained that it was only wanted to ex- tend the time of application to Parliament from three to five years. The subject dropped.

div.head: WHOLESALE GAS SL-PPLY.
div.p: A WHOLESALE GAS SL-PPLY.

A. letter was also read from the Wigan Coal Company to the following effect : The Wigan and Whiston Coal Co. (Limited) Praseot sth August, 1832, F. H. Gossage, Esq.. Chairman to the Local Board, Withal!. Dear 81r,—We shall feel obliged If you will bring this communication before your Gas end Water Corn- nsittee et their next meeting We are desirous of knowing whether your Board will entertain an effer from th's company to supply your di. trict with gas at the rate of 7d., say seven pence, per I.ooocubie feet, delivered into your mains to be laid toour Whlston colliery, which, Ina di, ect line, is four miles from your Dl'eton gasholder. The Illuminating* power of the gas we should offer would be equal to 17 candles, London referee's standard. We might be disposed to make al5 years' contract subject, if you wish it, to a bre .k by either side on giving one or two yeses' notice. Before entering into the contract we should satisfy your Board as to our capability of producing the quantity you may require. We are quite aware that it Ls an unusual circumstance for colliery proprietors to become gas manuf icturers. and to apply the same to Local B .ards. We, however, con.ider th's a step in the right direction, as it will enable gas to he sold at a very much less rate than at preient, and at the Fame time w.ll not only avoid further outlay on plant at the B. ard's works, but will enable gas to be sold at such a price as will warrant a day consumption for nomesLie pm poses, for whieh there is a great future, awl as you will in'er this additional day consumption will ultimately become very large, and will produce a profitable revenue, as no further outlay will be required t, the present mains except the extension to our Colliery. If you will work out your sale quantity with a pro- bable increa.se from day consumption.. to _which add_ your .di

tributing and other expenses. we think that you will find that much larger profits will be obtained by busing than manu- facturing gss at Widnes. If this cries.inn is entertained we shall be Wad to aton.'. your committee meeting to further discuss tbis.—Your? &c., for the Company. ED. W. FIDY.E2. the Managing Director.

tin PANKnutasr sahl that in reply to the letter it might be stated that the matter had not been lost sight of, as the Chairman, when on the Gas and Water Committee, had brought the matter More them, and it was now under con- siderAtion. The CHAIRMAN stated that the letter was received after

the committee meeting. He explained that the method used by Mr. Fidler was that ofusing:a grea quantity of coal and getting a larger and better supply of coke, so that gas was to a great extent produced as a by-product. It would be quite possible for the Board to follow the process in the same way—waking gas of a greater illuminating power, and thus procuring more coke, ammonia, and coal tar. Ai to the price, he thought that exces3ive. However, he would be very glad to give the committee oil the help which lay in his power in regard to the matter. The matter then dropped.

div.head: TIIE HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.
div.p: TIIE HIGHWAY COMMITTEE.

An ordinary meeting of this committee was held at Alfordo Chambers on the 27th July, when accounts amounting to £73 10s. N. were examined and passed for payment. A letter was read referring to the Moss Brook Bridge Approaches, from Mr. H. Mather, asking for contract plan for the purpose of measuring up, and stating that the contract was broken. The Surveyor denied any deviation from the plan. A letter was read dated, the 15th July, from the L. di N.-W. R. Co, acknowledging letter asking their engineer to visit the Waterloo Lz:vel Crossing with the committee. A letter was read, dated 15th Julr, from Mr. James Taylor, referring to Peel House-lane, and it was recommended that the original minute as regards his own land be carried out, and that as to land for which he is a trustee that his proposition be not entertained. The Committee, however, would be glad, if thought necessary, to see him. The Runcorn Property Co. wrote approving of sample brick for paving Lower House. lane, and it was recommendea that the parapet be made so as to suit the present formation of the road. With regard to the New-road, Lugsdale, a letter was read from the L. di N.-W. R. Co. as to discrepancy between the Board's plan and the signed Parliamentary plan, and asking that the deviation from the latter be approved by the Board and Mr. Robinson. it was recommended that the plan of road, as laid out by the Surveyor, be approved and sealed. The Surveyor reported that Nos. 10 and 12, Travis-street, Mr. C. C. Woodcock's property, unoccupied at present, are in a dangerous condition and the committee recommended that he be instructed to take the usual proceedings to have the same remedied.

div.head: W.I.TERLOO LEVEL CROSSING.
div.p: THE W.I.TERLOO LEVEL CROSSING.

Mr. KERSHAW moved the passing of these minutes. There was no matter calling for special attention. He c4uld only say that if the railway cotnpany did not reply to the letter, as to the above crossing they should have te act on the resolution passed by the Board. Mr. MIDIVOOD seconded. Mr. WEBSTER referred to the recommendation as to the paving of Lowerhouse-lane, and asked what was the precise meaning of it. Mr. MARTLEY asked of what nature the deviation in the plans for New-road, Lugsdale consisted.

div.head: DIRTY STREETS ON SUNDAY.
div.p: THE DIRTY STREETS ON SUNDAY.

Mr. PexxnuasT asked if the committee could devise any means by which the streets could be kept cleaner on a Sun- day, than was at present the case. They were usually dirtier on a Sunday than on any other day. Mr. KEnelrew said in reply to Mr. Webster, that the Board were bound to make a parapet in front of the land given up by the Runcorn Land company, and as they wish,d te save expense they put it in a temporary form to suit the present level of the road. As regards New-road, Lugsdale, which Mr. Martley had asked about, he might stite that the matter was only a simple deviation from the Parliamentary plans of an unimportant nature, and was left to the surveyor to arrange with the railway. As to keeping the streets clean on Sunday he could not say much. He thought la:sas that the streets were dirtier on a Sunday than they ought to ba, but still he did not think it was the duty of the Cial- ralttee to call upon the men to sweep the streets on Saturday night or a Sunday morning. It was due to the shopkeepers sweeping out their shops on a Saturday night. They should keep a box and give it to the men on Monday morning. The CHAIRMAN then put the motion, which was carried unanimously. THE GAS AND :WATER. COMMITTER. A meeting of this committee was held on the 20. h July when referring to the Stock's well, the engineer instructed that this station be worked for 24 hours for six days, until the necessary repairs to pump could be made, and Netherley worked 12 Jaunts. Another meeting was held on the 28th of July. The engineer read his report as follows :—Gentlemen, —I have to report the " Cross" engine at Netherley was handed over to our man an the 11th inst., Daglish's man leaving the house on that date. The engine has worked satisfactorily since then, but I consider that one of the tappet cylinders should be taken out by Messrs. Daglisb, and eased a little. The girders and columns for the gearing ta remove the condenser ends are in band. The papering and cleaning of the cottages was completed at the commence- ment of the month. There is the question of insurance on the three new boilers at this station. Consequent on the decision come to by the Committee on the 20th inst., pump- ing at Netherley was reduced to 12 hours per day, to admit of Stock's Well working the 24 hours per der, to reduce the water there. Tne quantity has n:t been much affected yet. Daring this forenoon a fall of 51ft. was still registered to eftect the necessary repairs, the level of the water now being close on the same as on Saturday evening last." The pro-

posed meters at Pax Hill for fixing on the I4in. and 161 n. outlet mains from the reservoirs, were estimated to cost— for the 13in. titian, £l5B 15s. 61; for the I6in., £lB5 165. sd, Including all appurtenances and fixtures. The engineer, continuing, stated that he had written to Mr. Deacon, Liverpool, on the 25th ult., with referesce to the Vyrnwy Main Branch, asking what had been done in regard to this, and have a reply on the 26th July. Notice to remove the present instruments at the end of September was given to Mr. Marr, Liverpool, on the 30th ult. On the 12th instant I wrote the Lancashire and Cheshire Telephone Company, stating that theirs of the 15th June bad been considered by the committee, when it was decided that the matter should remain over; since then there has not been any further letter from them. An account, dated 30th June, had been received from Messrs. Welsh for balance due on the Netherly contract, and is submitted. The water in stock on the 19th July was 10,558,661 gallons, and the illuminating power of the gas during the month has averaged 16 45 candles." It was re- commended that inquiry be made from the neighbouring towns as to the rate per 1,000 gallons for supply per meter. It was recommended that the usual inspector's uniform be supplied. Mr. PANKIIIIRST moved that the minutes be adopted.

Mr. MOISTER seconded. The CHAIRILLN desired some explanation with regard to the engine, as the minute referring to it was not quite clear. Mr. MIDWOOD asked what was meant by spending £l5B 15s. 61. for meters, valves, &a. There was also a large sum placed against the extension scheme at Netherly. Mr. MARTLEY complained of the manner in which the charges for water had been laid, which he contended were most unequal. Mr. PANKEITTIIST, in reply, said that the engine at the Stock Well had been out of repair, and in order to reduce the quantity of water they had to set the engine working the extra time. The water was now much reduced. As to Mr. Midwood's question, the large ampunt was the balance of account due to Mr. Daglish for the engine. Mr. MIDWOOD: I wish we had it back again. Mr. PANKIIIIRST, continuing, said that with regard to the meters they wished to ascertain how to charge as compared with other towns. The assessment was at fault in the case in which Mr. Martley had complained, and the remedy lay with the people themselves. THE INSPF.CTOR'S 'UNIFORM._

Mr. Minwoon : There is another thing—this "Inspector's uniform." Every month since I came here there has been something Lout enthes or uniforms of some sort. Mr. PANIKIIIIRST: That is an antutal affair, and there is a good many men in uniform. Mr. MIDWOOD It has happened every month since I came here.
The minutes were passed unanimously. TITR "JAMES CROSS" ERGINR.
Mr. PLNICHIIIIST moved that the engine " James Cross" be completed, the balance paid, and it taken over by the Board.
In reply to a question the ENGINEER said it was now com- plete.

Mr. HANDLEY seconded. Mr. Mums!. asked if it still made the annoying noise which had been complained of. The ENGINEER explained that the engine had been altered so that the noise was lessened. It, however, made the engine more liable.to get out of order.
The motioa—was carried. THE lIOSPITAL COMMITTEE. '

At this committee accounts amounting to £l3 17s. Bd. were examined and passed for payment. It was recom- mended that the tender at £6 103. of C. J. Sutcliff, for a copper cylinder fitted complete with empting tap, weighing not less than 941b5., and tested up to 501bs. preesure be accepted. The patients unthr treatment at date of last meeting ware nil ; admitted since, four ; discharged one ; -died one ; under treatment 31st July two. • Mr. SADLBR, seconded by Mr. WEBSTER moved the ad- option of the minutes, which were agreed to.

div.head: HEALTH COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE HEALTH COMMITTEE.
. - TLis committee met on the Ist inst., when accounts amounting to DES 19s. 11d, for health, and £9 12s. 91. for market, were examined and passed for payment.
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

This report stated that there had been—births 78-37.4 per 1,000; deaths, (total) 43-20 6 per 1,000; including children under one year, 20-9 6 per 1,000; children between one and five Tears, 5-2.4 per 1,000; zymotic diseases, 7-3 3 per 1,000; inquests, one.

div.head: NU. ISANCR INSPECTOR'S REPORT.
div.p: NU. ISANCR INSPECTOR'S REPORT.

The Nuisance Inspector reported that there bad been " seven deaths from diarrhoea (all children under five years). Several cases of scarlet and typhoid fever have been reported, but none have proved fatal. Disinfection has been attended to. Notice to attend committee had been served on My. Doran, for keeping; pigs in hick yard. Mr. Fitzpatrick, grocer Victoria-road, has called attention to unwholesome bacon for- warded to him from a wholesale house in Liverpool. I seized 19 flitches, weighing about 2cwt., and destroyed it upon a m tgistrate's order. I have also seized a quantity of green pees and fruit at Mr. Turtoes shop, Cholmondeley- street, and have destroyed the same. The usual inspection of butchers' shops has been made; a piece of beef waft for human food was seized at the shop of Mr. James Moss, Ann-atrect, against whom I took proceedings, when he was fined 104. and costs. The surveyor is havinr, the requisite work done at the closets in Irwell-street; he has also served notices in accordance with instruction upon Mr. King for property in Barn and North-streets, and he has arranged a meeting with the owner of the Derby-road property. I have served notices open the occupiers of eight houses in Travis- street to vacate the premises on account of their unsanitary condition as requested by the owner, Mr. C. Woodcock, Leicester. Through the neglect of E. Percy, I have been obliged to get some work done by R. Smithson; and owing to E. Percy's returns of work done having been sent in only yesterday, I have been unable to check and present the usual report. At the request of Mr. Seddon, grocer, Nelson-street, and Mr. Ilughes, labourer, Pitt-street, I have removed the caresses of three pigs which died on their premises, and I have communicated with Mr. Barnett, police inspector, on the matter." With regard to keeping pigs in back yards, Mrs. Doran atterried, and on a promise not to repeat the offence, the committee decided not to take further pre- ceedings. It was recommended that Turton, Cholmondelev- street, be prosecnted for keeping diseased fruit, and the inspector n as i nstructed to take proceedings against the owners the unsanitary houses in Travis-street who had not com- plied with the notice already served. It was recommended that as the damage caused to land in Lacay-street owned by Mr. White was reported by the Surveyor as not caused by the Board, that the owner be written to to that effect. A letter was read from the Schaol Board agreeing to the pro- Ns.l,d alteration of clesets at West Bank Board Schools, the cost not to exceed £32, of which one half was to be borne ty each Board ; the work to be done at the next vacation. The Market Superintendent reported that the receipts for July amounted to £l4 131, a decrease c Livered with last year of £ll 53. .Five shops were still unlet. The tolls from stills and Carts were not so much as last month. The committee did not think it advisable to mike any change in the rent of shops. Several other recommendations were made by the committee of an unimportant nature.
Mr. 15Atts1WILST moved that the minutes be adopted. 51Awncv seconded.

Dr. Boom asked if they were to take any proceedinga in the case of the Lis.-erpoo lliouse for supplying unwholesome food. He als.) referred to the peas and vegetables which had been destroyed. Mr. l'ilinwooD asked if the Inspector had had any com- munication fro:n the owner of Travis-street in regard to the proceedings against him. He objected to the alterations at West Bank Board Schools. It was about every month there was continual changes going on at those schools. He did not see what was the good of the Board paying one-half. It had all to come out of the rates ; they might have paid it all at once. It was a complete waste of money. Mr. Partartunsr said, in reply to Dr. Booth, that they had no power to prosecute anyone outside their own district. The peas and gooseberries were in a very wretched condition, which would be borne out by members of the committee. In answer to Mr. Midwold'e remarks on the Board Schools, he might say that the closets were put up at the express wish of that Board according to their own plans, and it bad since been found that the closets did not answer the purpose so well as those at Sim's Cross. The committee had accordingly asked, from a sanitary point of view, that a new arrangement be put in, and agreed to pay one-half of it. They had got Woodcock's authority in the case of Travis-street. Dr. Boom asked if Mr. Pankhur3t had a legal authority for his statement with reference to the-unwholesome food? • Mr. PANEHUILST said they kept closely to the Public Health Act.

The INSPECTOR explained that they could only prosecute for keeping unwholesome food the party on whole premises it had been seized. In reply to Mr. Sadler he stated that they would stand between this man and the merchant who supplied the bacon, and that he expected to be summoned as a witnegs in a county court case in this very connection. Mr. MIDWOOD. referring to the alterations at the Board schools. said that it had firqt been estimated to cost only £3. He could not understand how it had mounted up to £32. Mr. PANKUURST said he thought it 'must have been a mistake oa Mr. Midwood's pan to have thought the altera- tion would only cost a%out £3. There had been two tenders one of £lO and the other of £32, and they took the latter because it was considered to be the best. Mr. Midwood must have been thinking of some other closets which were altered in West Bank-street.

The CLERK read the minute which referred to the latter, and which set forth that the cost was to he only £3. Mr. MIDWOOD : Things alter awfully; don't they? (Laughter.) The minutes were adopted. THE FINANCE COMMITTEE.

A special meeting of this committee was held on the 27th July, at which Mr. Beasley's accounts were submitted and referred to the Clerk of the Peace for taxation. Another meeting was held on the2nd inst. when it was recommended that unless payment of gas and water accounts now in arrears be made before next committee meeting that pro- ceedings be taken for recovery. In the case of the property improvement accounts it was recommended that proceedings be taken in several cases unless payment is made within seven days. A large number of accounts were renmended for payment. Mr. HANDLEY, in the absence of the chairman of the committee, moved that the minutes be adopted. Mr. WRIGHT seconded.

Mr. Mtuwoou thought there was something wrong with regard to the collection of the accounts. He knew that, so far as he was concerned or those he acted for, Mr. Allen (the clerk) was very pressing when money was owing, and why he should press him (the speaker) and sem. others,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 12, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, AUGUST 12, 1882.

I while he let other parties run on for nine months without bringing them before the committee, he could not under- stand. Mr. KERSHAW asked if the list was there, because he should like to see it. He knew his own name was in.

Mr. MIDWOOD (continuing) said he did not see why some should be prosecuted in seven days, while others were to get off for ever so long without paying a penny. Mr. MARTLEY said many people who would have a chance to be prosecuted were quite willing to pay, but in a reasonable time. Money could not be got just now with property at the low rate it was, and all, especially cottage property, going down. He knew of some, and could give their names if need be, who were told it would be all right if they Came before the committee, but who, when they did come, were denied a hearing. They would pay the rate as soon as it was pos3ible to pay it. Mr. SADLER asked if it was true that one of the parties referred to by Mr. Midwood had been allowed to run up to £2OO.

Mr. HANDLEY said he distinctly recollected that there was a resolution passed at a committee meeting asking those in arrears to come before the Board and explain this matter. They had been apnlied to again and again, but did not seem to take any notice. The clerk then received instructions to take proceedings. With regard to the gas and water accounts, till definite application was made by the committee it was understood they should have the usual grace allowed them. Mr. WEI3STER, as a member of the Gas Committee, explained that till that moment he had not heard tell of anyone being in arrears. Mr. MIDWOOD did not think that Mr: Hanley's reply was satisfactory. He never heard a syllable mentioned of those gentlemen being in arrears till Wednesday last. It was only giving them fair play to give them also up to the next com- mittee meeting to pay up. -He did not think that it was fair that they would not allow him to owe anything to the Board without being on him at once. If he owed 2d. he believed that the Clerk would soon have a man at his place after it. (Laughter.) A vote took place at this stage on tin minutes, when it was understood that the minutes were carried with three dissentients. The CHAIRMAN, however, explained that he had neglected totake the adverse vote, and proceeded to call for a re-show of hands.
Mr. MIDWOOD : Before the minutes ara passed am I to get -a reply or not ? I asked why some people were allowed by the Clerk to run to such a large extent while othcrs are

The CHAIRMAN: Perhaps an explanation from Mr. Handley will satisfy you. Mr. SHIITTLEWORTH said that it was quite possible for Mr. Midwood to have investigated into that matter before he came to the Board.

Mr. HANDLEY • zplained that I me of those were paying off old scores, and were all doing what they could to clear off arrears. Mr. Allen had often great difficulty in getting the money, and had just to go where he would get it readiest. Mr. SatrrLEwormt said that the Clerk was very indus- trious in the matter. He knew his business, and tried to do the best for the Board

On a division, six voted for the minutes and five against, the Chairman decliring them carried by a majority of one. This concluded the business of public interest, and the Board shortly after adjourned.

settled. If there was any truth in that charge the conduct of those members was worthy of the severest condemnation, and, if on the other hand, the charge was unfounded, the members ought to have an opportunity of denying it. It was a charge which had not been made openly, but it was a general rumour. He was told that it had even been made by other members of the Board, and he thought it was only right that the Chairman and other members should have a chance of stating whether there was any truth in the matter at all.

The CHAIRMAN said rumours were very frequent with regard to the members of the Board. Tkings were hinted, implied, but not plainly spoken so that they could be re- futed. Whilst he was away he had received a newspaper, which contained a statement, underlined, that a prominent member of the Board was for the other side. He concluded that the prominent member meant himself, and he thought he ought to state for the satisfaction of the ratepayers that he should have kept clear of the court altogether, only he was subpcened by the other side on the Saturday previous to the trial. He was consequently bound to appear. He should have been very sorry indeed to have done anything which would conpromise the case. _ .

Mr. Sitew said it was opportune that this question had arisen, as far as the Commissioners were concerned, because it answered itself; for if a truthful statement of the case by any members of the Board was against the Commissioners, it followed that on whatever side their evidence was given, it would have had the same result. Some of the Com- missioners, including himself, were subpcened by Mr. Beesley; what they were expected to tell he did not know. He was not asked what he had to say; what he wished to say or anything about it. It might be true that their evidence might settle the matter, but it looked very bad, in his opinion, for the Commissioners to have to touch the cise at all. He rediculed the idea of turning Queen's evidence. The CHAIRMAN proposed that the committee consist of Messrs. Lake, P. Speakman, Shaw, Fisher, and Taylor. Mr. LAKE said as the committee would have to go into the legal aspect of the question, he would not like to be put upon it. Being a solicitor he should not like to discuss the work of the Law Clerk.
The CHAIRMLN, replying to Mr. Briscoe, said he thou gh the Board would receive the accounts soon.

Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN seconded the Chairman's proposition. Dr. McDotreaLL moved an amendment that the commit- tee consist of the whole Board, and explained his reagonsfor doing so. There had been a disposition on the part of some members to deny any part in the action, or even to have any knowledge of it. It seemed to him that whatever had been done was done by the Board—(hear, bear)—or by the authority of the Board, and it would be better that the ques- tion should be dismissed by the whole Board. Mr. MEADOWCROFT tieconded the amendment.

The CHAIRMAN wished to correct a statement made by Dr. McDougall. who said the proceedings were taken by the Board. fie (the chairman) had always contended that they were not taken by the Board, and did still. For himself he must contradict the statement.
Dr. McDoroiLL : Why you actually presided at the Board at the end of the meeting. The CHAIRMAN: Certainly. Mr. SnAW remarked that the subject had never been brought before the Board.
Tlie amendment was then put and carried. lIIGHWAY AND SANITARY COMMITTEE.

At a meeting of the Highway and Sanitary Committee, held on the 13th July, the Surveyor was instructed to ascertain, as far as he could, the nature of the connection between the drains and the main sewer in Ellesmere- street, and if there was any connection with the sewerage and the fouling of the fountain water. —Accounts amounting to £583 us. Ild, were, at a subse- quent meeting, passed for payment. —lt was recommended that 2-1, per cent. be charged for superintendence of new street work; and that permission be given to Mr. Philip Speakman to erect a ternporary boarding in Cooper-street.— The Canal Boats Act Amendment Bill was considered, and the Secretary was instructed to write to the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton to ascertain whether there is any likelihood of the Bill being proceeded with during the present session. The minutes were confirmed, on the motion of Dr. McDouGALL, seconded by Mr. WILLIAMS.

Dr. MCDOUGALL, referring to the question of the erection of new offices, said he should intinately prefer that scheme, and have the Board-room and library in one build- ing, if it were possible. He thought it was possible, and they could have the building in any part of the town, while the cost would•not exceed the sum realised from the free sale of the property which the Beard bad at present on hand. He spoke of the inconvenience of Waterloo House, and spoke strongly in favour of the present Board offices being used solely for the objects of the library as requested by the public meeting of ratepayers, and asked why the Board should deprive the ratepayers of it. . .

The CHAIRMAN here interrtipied and said at present the Library Committee had the room rent free. The Board bad always done everything it could to help the Library. Dr. McDouuALL: You have no right to be interrupting me. You must declare me out of order. The CHAIRMAN: ou are out of order. Dr. McDorciaLL : Then I decline to recognise your authority in the matter. (Cries of " chair.") lam sorry to be obliged to do so. The CHAIRMAN, in the act of putting the motion, sug- gested an alteration, when Dr. McDouGALL said there had been a great amount of tinkering with that resolution. If he (the cha,rman) was going to move a resolution let him draw up one they could understand and vote upon. The CHAIRMAN: I ttink it is clear enough.
Dr. McDouGALL : Ido not think it is. You suggest that it he altered this way and that way, and it has not been read.

Mr. HAZLEHURST said a building on the ground next to Bank Chambers in High-street would be a very much better place than at Waterloo House. He was afraid if they moved to Waterloo House they would stop there. The Board might as well remove to some better premises in the main street, and in his opinion it would be well to defer the matter until the properties of the Board had been advertised for sale, and see whether they could not raise enough money to get the town's offices next to Bank Chambers.
The CHAIRMAN: That has been before the Bcard, and the Board refused to pass it. Dr. McDouGALL moved an amendment that Waterloo House be advertised for Bile.

The CHAIRMAN refused to accept this as an amendment, and the resolution was passed as follows :—" That the busi- ness of the Board demands more accommodation than is afforded by the present office, and that the offices of the Board; including the Free Library, shall be concentrated in one building. With the view to providing such accommo- dation and concentration the committee recommend that the present offices be let at a fair rental. and that, when so let for the time being. put of Waterloo House be occupiel as offices for the Board, part set apart for the Free Public Library, the remainder of the building to be let on a tenancy."
Only Dr. McDougall and Mr. Ilizlehurst voted against the resolution.

Dr. MCDOUGALL said he thought this was a very serious step, and in the very teeth of the ratepayers. A great deal had been said about the ratepayers' resolution, and some members of the Board had alleged that the ratepayers pre- sent were of the nondescript class. The CHAIRMAN: I cannot allow such language to be used. I won't allow it.
Dr. McDounsx.r, said he was g;ving the meaning of the words used. The CH kIRMAN • No one made use of the expression. _ • _

Dr. McDouGau. : It was said that there were people pre- sent at the meeting who were not voters, and I take that to mean that they were nondescript characters. The CHAIRMAN: You take it? But the gentleman didn't say so. You are putting the wards into your own mouth. Dr. McDorGALL: That is what they allege. I move- The CHAIRMAN: So now we are going to get something. Dr. MCDOUGALL moved that the Board Offices be adver- tised for sale six years hence, so that they might be used for the purposes of the Free Library. It was a serious step they were taking, and the ratepayers would have something to say about it. The time might come when they would not come under the category of nondesCript characters. Mr. SHAW objected to any gentleman trying to put words which had never been used into the mouth of somebody else. Dr. McDougall's motion found no seconder, and the Board separated.

div.head: RITNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RITNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The ordinary monthly meeting was held at tbe Town Offices on Wednesday morning, under the presidency of Dr. Steel. There were also present Dr. McDougall, Messrs. Lake, G. S. Hazleburst, J. J. Speakman, Briscoe, Fisher, Meadowcroft, Shaw, Handley, Taylor, Williams, Dr. Monritz (medical officer), W. Brooks (secretary), and Barker (sur- veyor.)

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The MEDICAL OFFICER read his monthly report as fol- lows :—The number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amounted to 31; one death occurred at Halton within Runcorn; total deaths 32. Of the above deaths 6 were due to pulmonary complaints, five to abdomi- nal diseases, five to brain diseases, four to scarlatina, four to senile decay, four to marasinees, diarrhos4, gangrene, measles, and typhiod fever aceount for one each representing a death rate ef 25 per 1,000 per annum. Twenty one deaths occurred amongst children of five years old and under, and of these 15 were one year and under. The CHAIRMAN remarked that the health of the town was not so good as it might be. There were several cases of, scarletina, and he thought the public ought to be made aware of the fact in order that they might take propee pre- caution with their children. The MEDICAL OFFICER said the disease was confined to one particular part of the town. Cross, Regent, Halloway, and Surrey-streets were the places affected.
A DANGEROUS NUISANCE. The CHAIRMAN read the following letter:—

Bold-at-ee', Runcorn, August 3rd, 1882. T. the Runcorn Commissioners. Dear sir.—l am sorry to make complaints. but I think lam in duty bound to do so. On the 20th Juiy I was taken very ill with a very violent pain in my head, and had to send for Dr. Mon. itz at ten o'clock at oight. Though it WAi a late hour, the d ctor was very kind in coming, he said the comp'aint proceeded from the nuisance from the works on the Sprinch, and he said if there was not a stop put to it, the town would be full of gastric fever. I have not been able to work I since, and am still under the doctor's hands.—Yours truly, J. I DODSON.
Mr. HezLEnunsr said the complaint was ganeral, and he proposed that a letter be sent to the glycerine works asking them to abate the nuisance.

Mr. SHAW remarked that he had not smelt the gas yet. It might ba that the wind was in the wrong direction. Mr. IlAzLEwunsT thought it was a smell that could be abated. It arose from the boiling down of the soap lees when they reached a high degree of concentration. Th., smell was or -anic in its nature, and was most horrible; it; effect upon people being much worse than that from alkali works.

The CHAIRMAN suggested that the letter should be re- ferred to the Sanitary Committee. Mr. FISHER said Mr. Sbaw had been very fortunate in not having smelt the nuisance, but if he would go to that part of the town where Mr. Fisher resided he would both taste and smell.

Mr. BRISC,)E remarked that if a memorial was drawn up in favour of the abatement of the nuisance everybody in the neighbourhood would sign it. It could be abated. The letter was eventually referred to the committee. TARPORLEY AGRICULTURAL SHOW.

The CHAIRMAN had received a communication from Mr. Stewart], eecretary to Tarporley Agricultural Society, asking the Board to receive a depatation with reference to holding the autumn show in Runcorn.
Dr. McaorGALL asked what guarantee the society would require._ _ _
the CHAIRMAN s iid be knew nothing furthe: than was c':intained in the letter.
Mr. LAKE: It is a good society.
On the motion of Dr. McDouGALL. seconded by Mr. SPEAKMAN, it was unanimously decided that the Board should receive a deputation on a date to be fixed by the Chairman.
MR. BEASLEY'S ACTION: INTEMISTING DISCUSSION.

The CHAIRMAN said all the members of the Board would know the result of the recent action by Mr. Beasley. In the absence of the Law Clerk he should say nothing more at present; but be thought it best to allude to it. _ _
Mr. SlrAw : I think the best time would be when we hie the taxed bill, so that the whole question may be dis- cussed.

The CHURMAN : That is true; but I think we should know our position thoroughly in the meantime, and in order that this may be done I move that a committee be appointed to consider the qustion, and bring it before the Board. It can do no harm in any way.

. • Mr. Mmanowcnovr : Have we now or not? (Laughter.) I don't think you have said. The CItAIII3fAN : I don't think it is a laughing matter for the ratepayers or any body else. It means a very heavy loss. Mr. SHAW: It will be.
_ Mr. HANDLEY suggested the matter should be specially referred to the Finance Committee.

Mr. SHAW said he could hardly see where the committee were going to start, or of what nature the inquiry would be; because he thought the questions as to how far the Board was responsible was one which the auditor would decide.

Mr. fIAZLEIIIIRST: You mean to say that if the bills are paid from the rates that the auditor may surcharge us. Mr. SHAW: Certainly. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN: We ought to know our position be- fore we pay. We must not be surcharged. Mr. LAKE' asked if the committee was to inquire into the cause of the case being lost. The CHAIRMAN: Yes, everything about it. How we stand, how the ratepayers stand, and arrive at same definite conclusion about it.

Mr. HAZLEHURST suggested that the opinion of the audi- tor should be got. The CHAIRMAN observed that there would not be much time for consideration when the bills came in. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN was of opinion the best course would be to hold a special meeting and appoint a deputation to wait upon the auditor. . Dr. MCDOUGALL was in favour of a committee of the whole Board considering the matter. Mr. &few : I cannot en what you can do. As to the ex- pense we know nothing about it. I have not heard what the defer& was, nor what the action was. Ido not know whether it is information to you, but I don't think the chairman knows what the defence was or what the case really was. The CHAIRMAN: I don't know how the case came to be settled or who authorised the Law Clerk to settle it. I arrived at the assize courts at half-past nine on the morning of the trial, just in time to see the action settled. The barristers were all coming out with their papers. I did not knew what it was ell about and as Chairman of the Board, I was very much surprised. Mr. SHAW: The Board seemed to be in a fog altogether. The CHAIRMAN: Entirely; and that is why I propose that a committee be appointed. Mr. SHAW: I think when we get the bills will be the best time. The CH4IRMAN : I have been away for my holidays, and have not thought over the matter particularly. Mr. LAKE said he should like to ask one question with reference to the case. There were rumours flying about the town directly after the triaVand bad been since, that cer- tain prominent members of the Board bad, as it were, turned "Queen's evidence," and that it was owing to various mem- bers of the Board offering evidence on the other aide, or in some way treating with the appellant that the case was

div.head: ERECTION OF A HOSPITAL.
div.p: ERECTION OF A HOSPITAL.

The minutes of the Canal Boats and Hospital Committee stated the following tenders for the erection of hospital pre- mises had been considered :—W. Statham, 514; H. White, £615; James Wilson, MO; W. Farrell, £7oo.—lt was re- commended "that W. Statham's tender be accepted, and that he be required to complete the work by December 9th next. Mr. HANDLEY moved, ar.d Mr. TAYLOR seconded the con- firmation of the minutes.

Mr. MEADOWCROFT proposed that a clerk of works be appointed at a salary not exceeding £2 per week. Mr. SIIAW Slconded the motion, which was carried, and with this addition the minutes were passed. The CdAIRMIN was authorised to sign and seal the con- tract when completed.

div.head: FINANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: FINANCE COMMITTEE.

The recApts for the month of July, as shown by the minutes of the Finance Committee, were £443 195., which included £29 13i. 7d. received for market rents and tolls, and £365 4s. 7d. from the general district rate Accounts amounting to £354 Bs. Bd. were recommended for payment. It was also recommended that £5O be transferred to the Free Library fund. Instructions were given to the collector to issue notices requiring all rates to be paid by the end of August.
The adoption of the minutes was moved by Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN, seconded by Mr. HANDLEY, and passed.
THE PROPERTIES OF THE BOARD: WATERLOO HOUSE AGAIN.

Mr. LAKE, as chairman of the Properties Committee, sub- mitted the following resolution The recommendation of the committee, dated April 24th last, having been referred by the Beard to the committee for reconsideration it was unanimously agreed, that the business of the Board demands more accommodation than is afforded by the present offices, and that the offices of the Board, including the Free Library, should be concentrated in one building. With a view to providing such accommodation and concentration, the committee recommended that for the present part of Waterloo House be occupied as offices for the Board, part be set apart for the Free Public Library, and that the remainder of the building and the present offices be let." He observed that the recommendation virtually divided itself into three parts, and he suggested that it should be considered as three; and would simply move the first division. The CHAIRMAN said if the Board liked to let the Board offices, and move to other premises, well and good, but let them stay there until they had done so. They would have the expense of moving, painting, cleaning, and many other things to do and then perhaps 'have the building on their hands and save nothing to the ratepayers. Mr. HAZLEHURST thought the divisions of the resolution mentioned by Mr. Lake a wise method. If they attemioted to decide the three in a general discussion they would get into a hopeless muddle. The CHAIRMAN ruled that the resolution must be taken as a whole ; and Mr. Lake concurred. In reply to a question, Mr. LAKE said the Surveyor esti- mated the cast of removing touted fitting up Waterloo House at £llO. Mr. Sway/ remarked that he could not be a consenting party to the Board occupying Waterloo House and still keeping on the present offices. The CHAIRMAN said at present the Board allowed the Library Committee the use of that room without charge, but if the Board removed to Waterloo House the committee would have to pay a part of the rent for their accommoda- tion. .

After a little further discussion as to the desirability of dividing the resolutios, which the Chairman would not allow, Mr. LAKE moved that the resolution, in its entirety, be passed. Mr. Suew seconded.

Mr. HAZLEHURST moved, as an amendment, that the latter part of Ole resolution from the Words " the present offices," be struck out. They would then get an opinion from the Board which had not been elicited hitherto.

Dr, McDouGaLL seconded the resolution. He said he was responsible for the resolution being referred back for this discussion, and he could not help thinking the com- mittee had come to a somewhat premature conclusion, be- cause he understood that a meeting of the committee would not be called until after that meeting, when Mr. Lake un- dertook to apply for special powers. He (the speaker) had always held that the present building was most suitable for the Library in its present state ;—that was for a lending library, but several gentlemen brought forward certain objections to the building in the event of it developing into a reading room as well. Mr. HAZLEHURST (interrupting) said this matter was not before the Board.

Dr. McDoroaLL said he would leave the subject for the present. Mr. MEADOWCROFT remarked that Mr. Hazlehurst's pro- posal was indefinite and unsatisfactory. The adoption of the reco;ntnendation as a whole was as little as the commit- tee could do; and he was really most sick of the manner in which the matter had been referred back for consideration over and over again. It was high time the Board came to some decision as to what they intended to do with Waterloo House. They were paying £BO a year for it and making no use of it whatever. If they decided that the present offices were sufficient for all purposes, dispose of Waterloo- House; but if they were satisfied that the accommodation afforded by the present offices was insufficient remove to Waterloo House, and put into use a building now a great loss.
-?Mr. Hazlehurst's amendment was then put and carried. A discussion then commenced on the latter part of the resolution.

Dr. MeDorae.u. made a few remarks with regard to the library. Last Saturday afternoon the issues from the library were 206, a most gratifying number for one after- noon. The object in view in bringing forward that resolution was no doubt to extend the usefulness of the library, the working of which was getting so heavy, being only open two nights a week, that it was utterly impossible for the Librarian to do the work alone, but involved the necessity of three or four volunteers going [to assist him. Taking into consideration that the library had only been in existence about four weeks, and had got such a large issue, he was quite sure that the Board would not wish to stultify itself in any way. (Hear, bear.) It seemed to him that having established the library in that room, and after every- thing that had been said and done in connection with its establishment, it would be unfair to the ratepayers in other parts of the town, and put them to considerable inconveni- ence in consequence of the greater distance they would be from the books they wished to use, if the step contemplated was carried out. The CHAIRMAN: I think you are rather out of order. It has nothing to do with the ratepayers going to it. A MEMBER: We are speaking of the accommodation to be provided,

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday, when there were present—Messrs. Marsh (chairman), Dobell, Hall, Newsome, Leatherbarrow, Syder, Jackson, Fidler, P. Longton, Penke th, Buckley, Swift, Griffith, Lowe, Fisher, Gerrard, W. Long- ton, Rev. T. Chambers, and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk).

THE ORGANIST'S SALARY. - Mr. NEWSOME, in accordance with notice given at last meeting, rose to move that, having heard the letter read from the Rev. Father Henny making a request for the services of the organist (Miss Twist) her salary be increased to 20 per annum in c,insideration of her performing all the necessary services and duties in connection with the religious services:at the Workhouse. He did not think it was neces- sary for him to go into particulars, but he had calculated that the number of services in the year which it would be necessary for her to attend would be 290, and dividing the £2O by that number they would find that they only gave her for every time she went to and from the Workhouse Is. 411. which was not a large amount. Mr. CHAMBERS had very great pleasure in seconding the motion.
The CHAIRMLN : What is the salary we give at the present tinv,
Mr. HARTLEY : £lO.
The CHAIRMAN : Have not the Catholics more services than the others? Mr. HARTLEY : Just the same. Mr. Newaome's motion was then carried unanimously.

div.head: BELLING MEAL.
div.p: BELLING MEAL.
It was agreed to accept the tender of 173 per sack for the ground Indian meal stored at the Workhouse, from Mr. Melling, St. Helens.
TM! RETISION.
Mr. HALL moved that the Present reviaion be held on Thursdiy next, and sthrgested that the guArdians for Huy- ton be left to fix the date for their own revision according to their convenience.
It was suggested that Wednesday would be a more suit- able day for the revision, and Mr. Hall having altered his motion in accordance with this suggestion, it was agreed to.

ARFOSARS OF RATES. Mr. HALL called attention t.) the large.amount of arrears in the rates for some of the townships. Parr, he said, had paid nothing since June, and there was °win:, 016; there had been nrthing paid from Rainford since June, and there was owing £573. It was the same with Sutton, which owed £2,670. He thought something should be done, as it was a most serious matter. He begged to move that a communi- cation be sent to the overseers stating that unless a substan- tial sum was paid before the next meeting, some action would be taken.

Mr. FIDLER suggested that in consequence of the audit the motion be left over till next meeting. Mr. HALL could not see why the districts he had named should not pay in the same way as Prescot and other dis- tricts.
Mr. JACKSON said the money was collected and put in the bank.
Mr. NEWSOME said it appeared from the observation of Mr. Jackson that the money was collected and lodged in the bank. Mr. JACKSON: It is.

Mr. NEWSOME said if that was the case be decidedly ob- jected to it. He did not see why the overseers should use the ratepavers''money. (Cries of "They don't.") As soon as it was collected it should he lodged to the credit of the Union.

Mr. FIDLER : It is so, at Eccleston. Mr. JACKSON: It is very often the else that Sutton has to pay for Prescot. (Laughter.) A confused conversation then bok place, during which some uncomplimentary remarks were exchanged. Mr. CHAMBERS : I must protest against this mutual recrimination; it is exceedingly unpleasant for persons to listen to.

Mr. Jecssox : Nonsense. Mr. HARTLEY said it was his opinion that proceedings ought to be taken against the defaulting overseers. Mr. DOBELL then seconded Mr. Hall's proposition. In answer to a coestion the CLERK said the cell had been done many months. Mr. HALL'S proposition was ultimately carried. STAINED-GLASS WINDOW FOR 'THE WORKHOUSE CHAPEL.

Mr. CHAMBERS Said it was now time that something was done with regard to a new window for the chapel. He might tell them that he held £2C) 21. being the £27 cellected at the opening of the chapel, and two guineas sent by Mr. Birchall, of Rainhill, which it was no use keeping any longer. He had recently been in correspondence with Mr. Morris, who was well-known as the best glass. stainer in the United Kingdom. He had put 13 windows into his (Mr. Chamber's) church, and he had mentioned to him about this chapel window when he said he could do it for £23 lOs , and he (Mr. Chambers) was sure they could not leave it in better hands. He really thought they should take some action in the matter. A stained-glass window was a "thing of beatify," and was therefore "a joy for ever" (hear, hear) and would make the chapel a more pleasing place to the poor inmates of the Workhouse. He suggested that it be left to a committee to talk the matter over. Mr. FIDLER quite agreed to most of Mr. Chamber's remarks, but he thought it would be better to get the win- dow from some of the manufacturers at St. Helens than to go to another dealer. Mr. CHAMBERS: I beg your pardon, but I wor ' allow Mr. Morris to be called a dealer. He was one of ihtfirst artists in the country. Mr. FIDLER: I did not say he wasn't. Mr. CHAMBERS: You said he was a dealer.

Mr. FIDLER said be was confident that as good a window could be obtained from St. Helens as from any other part of the Kingdom. Mr.NEwsoms moved that a small committee be appointed to attend to the matter. Mr. HALL moved that it should be referred to the Furnish- ing Committee. Mr. CHAMBERS: I must differ with that; the Furnishing Committee has nothing to do with it. I will have the original Building Committee. Mr. HALL: You won't take that window Cut without the consent of the Board. . _
Mr. CHAMBERS (warmly): That window 313511 be put in, sir.
Mr. HALL: Whether it ia- pat in or not it is no matter to me.
I It was then agreed that the matter should be left to the ! Building Committee.

A PIOUS EPISTLE. Mr. HARTLEY reed the following communication:— Preseot Union Workhouse. From Solomon Wood, an inmate, aged 14 years, an episcopalian of the so-called Church of England, and a native of Widnes; to the Rev. Mr. Chambers and other gentlemen, as guardians representing the ratepayers of this Union. Gentlemen,—As I. the above-named Solomon Wood, wish to try to earn my own living, having been sup- ported at the expenditure of the kind ratepayers since Satur- day, June 10th, 1878, being admitted by an order of admission from Mr. Edwards, and chargeable to the township of Ecele- ston, for which kind protection and support I wish to return you—their representatives—my most grateful thanks; secondly, I also wish to express my gratitude to you as a Christian body, inasmich as you have provided for the spiritual wants of the inmates by providing a sanctuary wherein the true branches of Christ's Church may approach _their Creator without interrup, ion, and with solicitude and in reverence; thirdly, I speak of the inconvenient.° experienced for some years for want of proper accommodation for divine worship. As one having a long ex- perience I can appreciate the kindness of the Rev. Mr. Cham- bers and his kind supporters in the church scheme, through which. by God's mercy and the instrumentality of the Rey. Mr. Norris. I have got the scales removed from my eyes, and can, as it were, see men al trees walking. Fourthly, gentle- men, I must humbly solicit your kindness further so as to en- able me to earn the nourishment my sinking constitution re- qui- es to fight against the diseases of my corrupted body, as gentlemen your assistance in getting me some light employ- ment such as time-keeper or weigh-clerk Please accept this address, though inadequate, as the earnest sentiments of the thankful spirit, and allow me to remain your humble servant. HOLONION WOOD. For reference to character I have the honour of referring you to the Rev. Mr. Norris, whom I have always found ready to assist me with his usual kindness and seasonable advice; second, as a further reference. 1 am proud of having the good will of such an experienced per- son as the present master, Mr. Bicknall, second to none for economy and soberness. All I can say, in conclusion, is that I wish to return thanks to Mr, Bicknall for lifting me up from the dregs of paupei ism, and elevating me to the rank of the officials. A GUARDIAN: What soft sawder. _
Mr. CHAMBERS : I propose he is removed to Rainhill. (Laughter.) Mr. DOLL: I should think he is gone. Mr. CHAMBERS: Does no one second my proposition. (Llugbter.) The matter-then dropped.

MR. NEWSOME TOUCHES A SORE SPOT. Mr. NEWSOME wished to know if there were any standing oraers preventing the admission of representatives of the press to committee meetings. Mr. HAETLEY : We have no authority to enable them to attend.
Mr. NEWSOME : They attend the Rural Sanitary Authority. Mr. HARTLEY said he did not know of any pllce where they attended committee meetings, nor did he think they desired to attend.
Mr. NEWSOME submitted that they ought to be allowed to attend.

Mr. HARTLEY said as a matter of right representatives of the press had no right to be present even at the Board of Guardian meetings They were atrangers and could be treated as such. If the Guardians thought fit te allow them they could attend committee meetings. Mr. FIDLER said they could attend the Board meetings of ratepayers.
Mr. -HARTLEY said the ratepayets had not the privilege of attending. Mr. FIDLER referred to the case of Ton Councils..

Mr. HARTLEY said a different law altogether applied to Guardian meetings; that question had been decided some years ago in the case of a man named Mason. Some of them, he said, would remember a row which occurred in that room some time ago on one of the reporters refusing to heave the room when desired. He (Mr. Hartley) on that occasion wrote to the Local Government Board on the sub- ject, and they replied that the Board bad power to eject him. Mr. NEWSOME said there were many gnardians un- acquainted with the business transacted by the committees; for instance, there was the matter of the stones, which be was determined to bring up again. Over £153 worth of stones hal never been accounted for. Mr FIDLER : For Heaven's sake let that drop. Mr. NEWSOME said if all the guardians had been aware of the circumstance the stones would not have been lost. Mr. HARTLEY : The guardians are aware of it. Mr. Fintsn: Painfully aware of it. Mr. HARTLEY : It is not a matter of pushing things through.
Mr. NEwsomi3 : Well, the money is gone, and the stones too. Another scene of confusion now took place, the rest of the remarks being lost in a general conversation. This having somewhat subsided,
Mr. HARTLEY said the auditor was coming on Monday; he did not know whether any gentleman would like to come and see him. (Laughter.) The Board then adjourned.
PORT OF RUNCORN. Vessels arrived at and sailed from the Bridgewater Naviga- tion Company's Docks, in week ending August 8, 1882.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY. —Before Mr. Wm. Banki (chairman) and Mr. Henry
R.ynolds:

TnE BLACK LIST.—John Nichols was charg-d with being drunk and disorderly in Canal-street, on the 2,)th July, and on the evidence of P.B. Walley he was fined lOs and costs 93 6 I, For being drunk in High-street, on Saturday evenirg,Catherine Humphries, who said she came from Ches'er, was fined 5; and costs Cs latourer named Patrick Dagnall WAS brought up on a similar charge, and he was mulsted in the penalty of lOs and costs.
THIMMAT —Before Messrs John Brundrit and
B. B. Chadwick

DISREPUTABLE man, named Thomas Blakemore, wa.-- charged with behaving in an indecent mannei In High-street, on Tuesday.—Evidence s‘ as given by PO. Bossons and Thomas Booth, and he was fined lOs and costs 4d; or. in default, 14 days' hard labour.—Moses Peers, an old offender was charged with being drunk In Wellington- street, early this morning. and on the evidence of P.n. Mori Is. he was fined 5s and 53 4d cos; the Bench advi ing him to Mare the 'disreputable life he was leadln2,-. ARRESTED ON SUSPICION John Donavan and George Yesford were charged that, being, suspected persons, they did frequent the docks at Runcorn with intent to commit a fe'ony. on Tuesday night, the prosecutors walking about Albert Dock In a suspicious manner, and a canal trnstable, named James Weedall, warned them that they were liable to be apprehend° I. Subsequently a drunken sailor informed P.O.Morris that he had been robbed of es by the prisoners, who were the-capon apprehended. The sailor, however, failed to appear to give evidence.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson said the prisoners were tramps.—Mr. Brundrit remarked that there was a great deal of suspicion attaching to the prisoner's m,vements, but there was not sufficient evidence to warrant a conviction.—The prisoners were discharged.
WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Davies (in the chair) Alderman
Webster and Z. Arinitaze.

SCHOOL CAVC.—Matthew Heeson was charged with neglect- ing to send his by to school.—He pleaded not guilty. George, Riley. school attendance offl-,er, stated the facts of the case, which went to show that the boy was entirely neglected by the defendant, who let him run about much as he liked.—A fine of 53 and costs was imposed, 10s in all.

. . DRUNICENNESS.—John Hbby was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge street, on tin 29th July.Efe pleaded gulity.—P.o 14 stated the facts of the case. The consrabie had taken the defendant home as he was very drunk, and on reach- ing the house the defendant got hold of a poker and struck the constable.—He was 20s and costs, in default to go 14 lays to prisors.—John Edwards, who was represented by his wife, was charged with being drunk oaths) Ist inst. in Church-street, a plea of guilty was put in. and P 0. Taylor stated that he found the defendant lying across the street very chunk —A fi .e of 5s and costs was imposed with the usual alternative.— Thomas Hardy (18), for being drunk and disorderly in Horse- market-street, on the 29th July was fined lOs and costs.—P.O. Evans proved the case. THE Wtenm or CIRCITMSTANCES.—Ann Garland, who ap- peared in the dock with a child in her arms, was charged with committing a breach of the peace on Cocker's Brow.—P.O. Rowbottom stated that he saw the defendant fighting with Julia Ward, who was fined on Monday for drunkenness, I-1 Cocker's Brow. Along with P.O. Taylor he separate I them I and took Ward to gaol as she was very drunk. The defendant was sober.—lt was said that the defendant had been attacked by Ward, and the magistrates holding that she was the victim of circumstances, discharged her. STONE MEOWING By BOYB.—John Hampson and John Burke were charged with stone throwing In Back Ship-ya,rd.— They pieaded not gulity.—George Hankinson stated that they had thrown stones into his house, one of which struck him on the‘ve and cut him,—The Bench ilae4 thew 21, ‘4.1 uttier thA Borough Bye4aws.
